128	`wal/00000000000000000000.log`); subdirectories are created on demand.
129	**The data directory's parent must exist, and the node must be able to read
130	it.** `ProdDisk::new` creates the data directory itself when it is absent, and
131	never a directory above it: `./data` works on a fresh checkout, while
132	`/srv/app/node` with no `/srv/app` is refused at startup by name (`charpente
133	failed to start: the data directory "/srv/app/node" has no parent directory:
134	"/srv/app" is not an existing directory, ...`). Create the parent when you
135	provision the machine, and make it durable before the node starts — a bare
136	`mkdir -p` leaves the new entries in the page cache, so follow it with `sync`.
137	The reason is durability: an acknowledged write rests on every directory entry
138	above it. Every directory barrier fsyncs the whole chain from the directory it
139	names up to the data directory; `ProdDisk::new` fsyncs the data directory's
140	parent, which holds the data directory's own entry, at every start, before
141	anything is acknowledged; and the parent's own entry is yours. That start sync
142	also means a parent the node cannot read stops the start there, under the same
143	line, rather than inside your app's first barrier. An empty path is
144	refused by name too. `restore --to` follows the same rule.
145	
146	```rust
147	use charpente::prod::ProdDisk;
148	
149	/// Opens the app's one data directory, creating it if it doesn't exist yet
150	/// (its parent must).
151	fn open_data_dir(path: &str) -> std::io::Result<ProdDisk> {
152	    ProdDisk::new(path)
153	}
154	```
155	
156	Paths handed to a `Disk` must be relative flat names — never absolute, never
157	containing a `.` or `..` segment, never empty. Violating this is a contract
158	panic ("Disk paths are relative flat names like \"wal/000001.log\" — got
159	\"...\""), not a recoverable error.
160	
161	## 2. Tables
162	
163	A table is a plain struct annotated `#[table]`. The macro generates the
164	`Row` implementation (the byte encoding, the table's name, its index list)
165	plus one lookup function per `#[index]` field.
166	
167	### The `#[table]` contract
168	
169	- It declares its tenancy: `#[table(scoped_by = Org)]` if every row belongs
170	  to one tenant (§16), or `#[table(global)]` if its rows belong to none. A
171	  bare `#[table]` is a compile error naming both — the platform never guesses
172	  which a table is, and the built-in tables (`Session`, `ApiKey`, …) are
173	  `global` like any other.
174	- The struct must be a non-generic, braced struct with named fields — a
175	  table is one concrete row shape.
176	- It must have an `id` field of type `Id<Self>` — a typed primary key.
177	  `Id<Invoice>` is not `Id<Org>`, and neither is a bare `u64`. By
178	  convention (every example here follows it) `id` is declared first, but
179	  the macro only checks that the field exists and that its type is
180	  `Id<Self>` (the rejection list below), never its position.
181	- Every other field's type must implement `Codec` — charpente's own
182	  deterministic, versionless (v0) encoding, not serde. `Codec` is
183	  implemented for `u8`/`u16`/`u32`/`u64`/`i8`/`i16`/`i32`/`i64`, `bool`,
184	  `String`, `Vec<u8>`, `Option<T> where T: Codec`, and `Id<T>` for any `T`.
185	  A field type that isn't `Codec` fails as an ordinary trait-bound error at
186	  the macro's generated encode/decode code, not a custom message.
187	- Fields encode and decode **in declaration order** — reordering fields
188	  changes the byte layout of every row already durable on disk.
189	
190	```rust
191	use charpente::{Id, View, table};
192	
193	struct Org; // referenced only through its typed id below
194	
195	#[table(global)]
196	struct Invoice {
197	    id: Id<Invoice>,
198	    #[index]
199	    org: Id<Org>,
200	    amount_cents: i64,
201	    memo: Option<String>,
202	    paid: bool,
203	}
204	
205	/// `#[index]` on a field generates an exact-match lookup named
206	/// `by_<field>`. It takes any `View` — a `Snapshot` outside a transaction,
207	/// or a `Tx` inside one — and returns every row with that key, in id order.
208	fn invoices_for_org(view: &impl View, org: Id<Org>) -> std::io::Result<Vec<Invoice>> {
209	    Invoice::by_org(view, &org)
210	}
211	```
212	
213	`global` here because this section is about `#[index]`, not tenancy; a real invoice table
214	belongs to its tenant and would say `#[table(scoped_by = Org)]` (§16) — which also retires
215	the `org` column, because the scope is the key prefix.
216	
217	A table can carry any number of `#[index]` fields; each gets its own
218	function with this exact shape:
219	
220	```rust,ignore
221	fn by_<field>(view: &impl View, key: &<FieldType>) -> std::io::Result<Vec<Self>>
222	```
223	
224	### `#[index]` works on any `Codec` field, including a hand-rolled enum
225	
226	`#[index]`'s only requirement is the same one every table field already
227	has: the field type implements `Codec`. The generated index-key function
228	is nothing but `Codec::encode`, and the lookup it feeds
229	(`View::scan_by`) is bounded on `key: &impl Codec` — there is no separate
230	`Eq`/`Hash`/`Ord`/serde bound. A hand-rolled `Codec` enum — a status
231	field, say — can carry `#[index]` exactly like an `Id<T>` or a `String`
232	field can:
233	
234	```rust
235	use charpente::core::table::Codec;
236	use charpente::{Id, View, table};
237	use std::io;
238	
239	enum InvoiceState {
240	    Draft,
241	    Final,
242	    Paid,
243	}
244	
245	impl Codec for InvoiceState {
246	    fn encode(&self, out: &mut Vec<u8>) {
247	        let tag: u8 = match self {
248	            InvoiceState::Draft => 0,
249	            InvoiceState::Final => 1,
250	            InvoiceState::Paid => 2,
251	        };
252	        tag.encode(out);
253	    }
254	
255	    fn decode(input: &mut &[u8]) -> io::Result<Self> {
256	        match u8::decode(input)? {
257	            0 => Ok(InvoiceState::Draft),
258	            1 => Ok(InvoiceState::Final),
259	            2 => Ok(InvoiceState::Paid),
260	            other => Err(io::Error::other(format!(
261	                "invalid InvoiceState tag {other} — schema drift or corruption"
262	            ))),
263	        }
264	    }
265	}
266	
267	#[table(global)]
268	struct Invoice {
269	    id: Id<Invoice>,
270	    #[index]
271	    state: InvoiceState,
272	}
273	
274	/// Generated by `#[index]` on `state`, same shape as any other indexed
275	/// field: an exact-match lookup, in id order.
276	fn final_invoices(view: &impl View) -> std::io::Result<Vec<Invoice>> {
277	    Invoice::by_state(view, &InvoiceState::Final)
278	}
279	```
280	
281	When a query doesn't fit an exact-match index — a range or "greater
282	than" scan, which `#[index]` doesn't support in v0 — the fallback is
283	`tx.scan::<Invoice>()` filtered in Rust: correct, just not indexed. Reach
284	for that before assuming a `Codec` field can't be indexed at all.
285	
286	### Generating ids for rows created inside a transaction
287	
288	Every example above takes a row's `id` from somewhere outside the
289	transaction — a `:param` in the route path, or a value the caller
290	supplied. That works when a row has a natural external identity, but
291	breaks down for a row created *inside* a transaction with nothing to
292	source an id from — a child row for each entry of a request body's
293	`Vec<...>`, say.
294	
295	There is no platform id-generation primitive for `#[table]` rows in v0
296	(the platform's own internal job-id counter is not exposed to app code).
297	The pattern: a singleton counter row per id space, read, incremented, and
298	written back inside the same transaction that needs a fresh id. This is
299	safe without a lock or an atomic op because transactions are serialized
300	through one writer (§4) — two transactions racing to claim an id can
301	never both observe the same counter value, since the second one only
302	starts after the first has already committed its increment (or aborted
303	without writing anything at all).
304	
305	```rust
306	use charpente::{Id, Tx, View, table};
307	use std::io;
308	
309	#[table(global)]
310	struct IdCounter {
311	    id: Id<IdCounter>,
312	    next: u64,
313	}
314	
315	/// One counter row per id space you need (line items, reminders, …),
316	/// keyed by an arbitrary `seq` value you pick per space.
317	fn next_id<T>(tx: &mut Tx, seq: u64) -> io::Result<Id<T>> {
318	    let counter_id = Id::<IdCounter>::from_raw(seq);
319	    let mut counter = tx.get(counter_id)?.unwrap_or(IdCounter {
320	        id: counter_id,
321	        next: 0,
322	    });
323	    let value = counter.next;
324	    counter.next += 1;
325	    tx.put(&counter);
326	    Ok(Id::from_raw(value))
327	}
328	```
329	
330	Bit-packing an id out of a caller-supplied parent id (e.g. `(invoice_id
331	<< 20) | index`) is tempting but unsafe in general: a caller-supplied id
332	is an arbitrary `u64`, and shifting an arbitrary `u64` left can silently
333	wrap and collide with another parent's children. The counter-row pattern
334	above has no such ceiling.
335	
336	### What the macro rejects
337	
338	Every rejection happens at compile time, and the message names the contract
339	and the fix. The first rejection is the one every table meets once — a
340	declaration with no tenancy stance:
341	
342	<!-- pinned -->
343	```text
344	`<table>` declares no tenancy — a table says which. Add one of these to its `#[table(…)]`, keeping any arguments it already has: `scoped_by = Org` if every row belongs to one tenant (the key becomes `(scope, id)` and a bare `Tx` cannot read it), or `global` if its rows belong to no tenant. Neither is the default.
345	`global` and `scoped_by = <scope>` on one table — a table is one or the other; drop one
346	`global` given twice — write it once
347	```
348	
349	`<table>` is the struct's name. The other six rejections are about the
350	struct's shape:
351	
352	```rust,ignore
353	// no `id` field at all
354	#[table(global)]
355	struct Ping { hits: u64 }
356	// "missing `id: Id<Ping>` field — every #[table] row needs a typed primary
357	//  key (add `id: Id<Ping>`)"
358	
359	// `id` isn't `Id<Self>`
360	#[table(global)]
361	struct Ping { id: u64, hits: u64 }
362	// "the `id` field of a #[table] must be `Id<Ping>` — a typed id, never a
363	//  bare integer"
364	
365	// `#[index]` on the primary key
366	#[table(global)]
367	struct Ping { #[index] id: Id<Ping>, hits: u64 }
368	// "`id` is the primary key — it is already the fastest lookup; remove
369	//  #[index]"
370	
371	// not a braced struct with named fields (tuple structs and unit structs
372	// both hit this)
373	#[table(global)]
374	struct Ping(u64);
375	// "#[table] needs named fields — `Ping` must be a braced struct with an
376	//  `id: Id<Ping>` field"
377	
378	// enums and unions cannot be rows
379	#[table(global)]
380	enum Ping { A, B }
381	// "#[table] applies to structs — enums and unions cannot be rows"
382	
383	// generic structs — a table is one concrete row shape
384	#[table(global)]
385	struct Ping<T> { id: Id<Ping<T>>, data: T }
386	// "#[table] structs cannot be generic — a table is one concrete row shape;
387	//  make `Ping` non-generic"
388	```
389	
390	A row that fails to decode at runtime (schema drift, corruption, a
391	reordered field) fails with, for example, `"row decode: 3 trailing bytes
392	after a Ping row — schema drift or corruption"`.
393	
394	## 3. The database
395	
396	`Db` composes the write-ahead log with the typed table store behind one
397	writer:
398	
399	```rust,ignore
400	pub fn open(disk: Box<dyn Disk>, cfg: DbConfig, schema: Schema) -> std::io::Result<Db>
401	```
402	
403	`Schema` is a builder that registers every `#[table]` type your app writes.
404	Replay works from raw log bytes and needs each type's codec to reconstruct
405	rows and maintain indexes:
406	
407	```rust
408	use charpente::prod::ProdDisk;
409	use charpente::{Db, DbConfig, Id, Schema, table};
410	
411	#[table(global)]
412	struct Counter {
413	    id: Id<Counter>,
414	    hits: u64,
415	}
416	
417	fn open(data_dir: &str) -> std::io::Result<Db> {
418	    let disk = ProdDisk::new(data_dir)?;
419	    let schema = Schema::new().table::<Counter>();
420	    Db::open(Box::new(disk), DbConfig::default(), schema)
421	}
422	```
423	
424	Registering the same table type twice is a contract panic ("Schema: table
425	\"Counter\" registered twice — register each #[table] type once").
426	`Db::open` registers three tables of its own before yours — the job queue
427	`charpente.jobs`, the event log `charpente.events` and the migration record
428	`charpente.schema_versions` — so registering any of them yourself hits the same
429	panic. They are the platform's: no app code reads or writes one (§6, "Job rows are
430	the platform's"; §16, "Where the guarantee stops"), and code that holds the `Db` reads
431	them through `db.snapshot()`.
432	
433	`DbConfig` names the WAL's directory and segment rotation size, and the
434	table store's file name:
435	
436	```rust
437	use charpente::DbConfig;
438	use charpente::core::log::WalConfig;
439	
440	fn config() -> DbConfig {
441	    DbConfig {
442	        wal: WalConfig {
443	            dir: "wal".to_string(),
444	            segment_bytes: 64 << 20, // 64 MiB
445	        },
446	        store_path: "tables.redb".to_string(),
447	        retain_segments: 2,
448	        checkpoint_every: 4096,
449	        event_retention: 65_536,
450	        migration_batch_size: 1000,
451	    }
452	}
453	```
454	
455	`DbConfig::default()` already sets exactly these values — most apps never
456	construct one by hand. `retain_segments` and `checkpoint_every` govern
457	`Db::checkpoint`'s log GC, covered next. `event_retention` bounds the
458	built-in `charpente.events` table the same way: each checkpoint deletes all
459	but the newest `event_retention` event rows (`Db::event_floor()` reports the
460	smallest id still retained). `migration_batch_size` caps how many rows one
461	schema-migration transaction rewrites at a time, bounding a single migration
462	commit's WAL record size. It must be at least 1: a batch of 0 rewrites nothing,
463	so `migrate_schema` refuses by name, before writing anything, when a table is due
464	to migrate and the size is 0.
465	
466	### Recovery, behaviorally
467	
468	`Db::open` opens the table store first; if redb rejects the store file's
469	bytes (a crash mid-creation can leave bytes redb refuses to read), it's
470	discarded and rebuilt — the store is a materialization of the log, never a
471	second source of truth. Only that verdict costs the store: `Store::open`
472	reports it as `table::StoreRejected` (corrupted, a file format that needs a
473	manual upgrade, or not a redb file), and any other open failure — an IO
474	error from the disk — is returned by `Db::open` with the site and the fix
475	named and the store left as it was, so retrying the open is the fix. The one
476	exception says so in its text: a store file cut shorter than redb's header,
477	which no crash leaves and no retry fixes. Its fix depends on the log beside
478	it, and the text names the right one: while the log still reaches seq 0,
479	remove the file and the next boot rebuilds it; once the log is compacted,
480	restore the node from a replica or backup (DESIGN §4). On a replicated node
481	that restore is a re-seed, and every text that names it says so in the same
482	breath: clear the data directory and restart the node configured as a follower
483	of the current primary, never with a primary config (§10). A rebuild only works
484	while the log still holds everything back
485	to seq 0, though: `Db::checkpoint(&mut self)` durably persists the store,
486	then deletes WAL segments below the checkpoint (`DbConfig::retain_segments`
487	floors how much it keeps; `checkpoint_every` auto-fires the cadence every N
488	committed records, `0` to disable it and checkpoint only by hand). Once the
489	log has been compacted this way, a rejected store is unrecoverable
490	locally — `Db::open` returns a named error instead of a silent (wrong)
491	rebuild, naming the fix: restore from a replica/backup, or widen
492	`retain_segments` (for a store whose bytes name an older redb file format, it
493	says that no charpente release wrote one, so the version byte is damage, and
494	names redb 2.6's `Database::upgrade()` for a format-2 file something else
495	wrote). A store whose records stop short of the log's base is refused the same
496	way, by name, whatever the horizon breadcrumb beside it says: a store file that
497	is missing, or holds no records, beside a compacted log, or an older copy put
498	back without its log. Removing or replacing the store is never a fix once the
499	log is compacted. For a follower the text names the re-seed instead, with the
500	config it must restart under (§10). `Db::open` then recovers the write-ahead log and replays
501	every durable record after the store's last checkpoint back into it, so a
502	reopened `Db` reflects every transaction that ever committed, even one the
503	store hadn't caught up to when the process died. Recovery can itself fail
504	under an IO fault; `Db::open` is idempotent, so the caller's answer to a
505	failed open is simply to retry it. Outside a transaction, `Db::snapshot() ->
506	io::Result<Snapshot>` gives the same read surface (a `View`) for read-only
507	queries — inside a transaction, reads additionally see the transaction's
508	own writes, covered next.
509	
510	## 4. Transactions
511	
512	Every state change goes through one transaction:
513	
514	```rust,ignore
515	pub fn transact<T, E>(
516	    &mut self,
517	    f: impl FnOnce(&mut Tx) -> Result<T, E>,
518	) -> Result<T, TxError<E>>
519	```
520	
521	`f` runs synchronously against a `Tx`: reads see this transaction's own
522	writes first, then any writes already staged in the same commit batch —
523	`transact` runs a batch of exactly one, so that level is always empty here —
524	then the store snapshot the batch began from. `Tx` implements `View` (`get`,
525	`scan`, `scan_by`), so `Invoice::by_org` from §2 works on a `Tx` exactly as
526	it does on a `Snapshot`, for every table of the app's own. The platform's own
527	tables are read through a `Snapshot` alone (§16, "Where the guarantee stops").
528	On `Ok`, every buffered write, enqueue, and emit
529	commits as ONE durable log record — all or nothing — and only then applies
530	to the store. On `Err(TxError::App(_))`, nothing happened at all: no log
531	position consumed, nothing written. On `Err(TxError::Io(_))` the outcome is
532	unknown — the record may already be durable (below).
533	
534	```rust
535	use charpente::core::table::{Codec, Unscoped};
536	use charpente::{Db, Id, Job, Tx, TxError, View, event, table};
537	use std::io;
538	
539	#[table(global)]
540	struct Invoice {
541	    id: Id<Invoice>,
542	    amount_cents: i64,
543	    paid: bool,
544	}
545	
546	struct SendReceipt {
547	    invoice: u64,
548	}
549	
550	impl Codec for SendReceipt {
551	    fn encode(&self, out: &mut Vec<u8>) {
552	        self.invoice.encode(out);
553	    }
554	    fn decode(input: &mut &[u8]) -> io::Result<SendReceipt> {
555	        Ok(SendReceipt {
556	            invoice: u64::decode(input)?,
557	        })
558	    }
559	}
560	
561	impl Job for SendReceipt {
562	    const NAME: &'static str = "send_receipt";
563	    // The payload's shape, recorded beside every enqueue; a Pending job is
564	    // only ever decoded by a binary whose FINGERPRINT matches (§6). `#[job]`
565	    // computes it from the fields; by hand, change it whenever the fields
566	    // change.
567	    const FINGERPRINT: u64 = 0x5E4D_0001;
568	    // A global job: it belongs to no tenant (§6, §16).
569	    type Scope = Unscoped;
570	    // `RETRY` defaults to `RetryPolicy::DEFAULT` — retry/backoff and cron
571	    // are covered in a later section.
572	}
573	
574	#[event(global)]
575	struct InvoiceFinalized {
576	    invoice: Id<Invoice>,
577	}
578	
579	/// The row update, the receipt job, and the realtime event all commit in
580	/// the one transaction — or none of them do.
581	fn finalize(db: &mut Db, id: u64) -> Result<(), TxError<io::Error>> {
582	    db.transact(|tx: &mut Tx| {
583	        let mut inv = tx
584	            .get::<Invoice>(Id::from_raw(id))?
585	            .ok_or_else(|| io::Error::other("invoice not found"))?;
586	        if inv.paid {
587	            return Err(io::Error::other("invoice already paid"));
588	        }
589	        inv.paid = true;
590	        tx.put(&inv);
591	        tx.enqueue(SendReceipt { invoice: id });
592	        tx.emit(InvoiceFinalized {
593	            invoice: Id::from_raw(id),
594	        });
595	        Ok(())
596	    })
597	}
598	```
599	
600	`Job` needs `Codec`, a `NAME` and a `FINGERPRINT`, implemented by hand today
601	(v0); `#[job]` derives the rest of a job's registration for you (a later
602	section). `#[event]` derives everything an event needs in one step: `Codec`
603	(the log format), `Event` (`NAME` is the snake_case of the type name — §11 has
604	the exact splitting rule — and `FINGERPRINT` is the payload's structural
605	fingerprint, recorded beside every emit, §11 "Changing an event"), `Serialize`
606	(the wire format `#[route(SSE …)]` subscribers receive, §11), `Wire` (that wire
607	format's schema, so the contract can name it), and an `EventEntry` impl so
608	`events![...]` can register it (§11).
609	Because the payload IS what a subscriber receives, it obeys the wire rules a
610	route's types obey — which is why `InvoiceFinalized.invoice` above is
611	`Id<Invoice>` and not the bare `u64` the `SendReceipt` *job* beside it carries:
612	a job payload never leaves the process, an event payload is a JSON document
613	someone parses. `tx.put` and `tx.delete` cannot fail — they only
614	buffer a write into the transaction's overlay; `tx.get`/`scan`/`scan_by`
615	return `io::Result` because they read through the snapshot. A transaction
616	that never calls `put`/`delete`/`enqueue`/`emit` writes nothing and consumes
617	no log position — read-only queries are free.
618	
619	Enqueuing also takes the app's own key for the job: `tx.enqueue_keyed(key,
620	job)` carries it on the job's row, and the platform never dedupes on it. It is
621	not the idempotency key an outbound job's call carries — the platform mints
622	that one (see Outbound jobs below). An empty key is a contract panic
623	("contract: an `enqueue_keyed` app key names the job's external identity — it
624	cannot be empty"). One more hard limit: all of a
625	transaction's buffered effects together must fit in one 16 MiB log record —
626	a transaction that doesn't panics with "transaction effects are N bytes but
627	one log record holds at most 16777216 — split the work into smaller
628	transactions".
629	
630	### `TxError`'s four variants
631	
632	`TxError<E>` has four variants, and this block matches the real type — a
633	variant rename or addition breaks the guide's compile gate:
634	
635	```rust
636	use charpente::TxError;
637	
638	/// The four arms differ in what they promise: `App` means nothing was
639	/// written; `Io` means the outcome is unknown (details below); `NotPrimary`
640	/// means this node is a read-only follower and nothing was even attempted;
641	/// `Verifying` means this node cannot yet tell whether it is allowed to
642	/// write, and nothing was attempted either.
643	fn describe<E: std::fmt::Display>(err: &TxError<E>) -> String {
644	    match err {
645	        TxError::App(e) => format!("rejected by the app — nothing was written: {e}"),
646	        TxError::Io(e) => format!("platform IO failure — outcome unknown: {e}"),
647	        TxError::NotPrimary { primary } => {
648	            format!("read-only follower — writes go to {primary} instead")
649	        }
650	        TxError::Verifying { unreached } => {
651	            format!("still verifying witnesses {unreached:?} — writes are on hold")
652	        }
653	    }
654	}
655	```
656	
657	The distinction is load-bearing. `App(E)` is whatever `f` returned as
658	`Err` — your own rejection, or an IO failure hit while *reading* inside the
659	transaction (both surface through the closure's own `Result<T, E>`); either
660	way, **nothing was written**. `Io` is a platform failure outside `f`'s own
661	logic: opening the read snapshot before `f` runs, or appending/syncing the
662	committed record's log entry after `f` returned `Ok`. That second case is
663	genuinely ambiguous — the record may already be durable and will reappear
664	after the next recovery even though the caller was told the commit failed —
665	so treat `TxError::Io` as "unknown," never as "definitely didn't happen."
666	The exceptions are an `Io` carrying one of `Group::stage`'s two refusals,
667	each read with its own `of`. A `JobShapeRefusal`
668	(`charpente::core::db::JobShapeRefusal::of`) is an enqueue that disagrees with a
669	job name this binary mounts on its shape, its tenancy or whether it is outbound
670	(§6, "Changing a job's fields" and "Outbound jobs"). A
671	`TableWriteRefusal` (`charpente::core::db::TableWriteRefusal::of`) is a write
672	the `Schema` disagrees with about its table: a table it does not register
673	(add `.table::<T>()`), a scoped `Row` whose `TABLE` is an unscoped table's or
674	the reverse, or a put or delete through any Rust type other than the one
675	registered under that name. A `#[table]` type's table name is its struct
676	name, so two `#[table] struct Invoice` in different modules collide this way
677	even when their fields, and so their fingerprints, are the same. The text
678	names the type that wrote and the registered one: write the registered type,
679	or give the other one another name. Either refusal comes before anything was
680	written, so a retry cannot succeed. The HTTP layer answers
681	either with a 500 carrying the refusal's own text, and in a job handler
682	either is an attempt, retried and then dead-lettered. The broader
683	`Refusal::of` is not that predicate: it also matches a refusal apply raises
684	after the log sync (a replicated record decoded under a mismatched shape),
685	whose record may already be durable. A read through a type other than the
686	registered one, a `Tx` or `ScopedTx` read or an `across_tenants` scan, is
687	refused too, by the read itself, as a `TableReadRefusal`
688	(`charpente::core::db::TableReadRefusal::of`). It names the table, the type
689	that read and the registered one, offers the same two fixes, and returns no
690	row. It reaches your code through the read's `io::Result`, so a route that
691	returns it with `?` answers a 500 carrying its text, and in a job handler it
692	is an attempt.
693	`NotPrimary { primary }` fires only when `f` had at least one effect to
694	write and this node has been marked a read-only follower
695	(`Db::forbid_writes`, DESIGN §5) — reads and effect-free transactions never
696	see it; the HTTP layer maps it to 421, naming `primary`.
697	
698	`Verifying { unreached }` (M2 sub-project 0b) also fires only when `f` had
699	at least one effect to write — reads and effect-free transactions never see
700	it either. It means this node was a durable primary before it restarted and
701	has not yet confirmed that none of its followers (its "witnesses") were
702	promoted while it was down (`Db::verify_writes`). Unlike `NotPrimary`, there
703	is no primary address to name: this node does not know whether one exists
704	elsewhere, and it may still be the legitimate primary itself. `unreached` is
705	the witness set this node is verifying, fixed at the moment the gate closed;
706	the HTTP layer maps it to 503, naming them. It does not shrink as individual
707	witnesses answer — the stderr notice described in §10 is where the live
708	per-witness detail lives. The state is transient — writes resume automatically
709	(`Db::allow_writes`) the moment every witness confirms it was never
710	promoted, with no caller action needed.
711	
712	### What a transaction cannot do
713	
714	`f` only ever receives `&mut Tx` — no `Disk`, `Clock`, `Entropy`, or `Net`
715	handle reaches inside it. There is no way to await a network call from
716	inside a transaction: `f`'s signature is a plain, synchronous `FnOnce(&mut

718	compile error, not a runtime one:
719	
720	```rust,ignore
721	db.transact(|tx| {
722	    tx.put(&row);
723	    fetch_from_the_network().await?; // error[E0728]: `await` is only
724	                                      // allowed inside `async` functions
725	                                      // and blocks
726	    Ok::<_, std::io::Error>(())
727	})
728	```
729	
730	Nothing in the type system stops you from calling an ambient clock or
731	randomness function (`std::time::SystemTime::now()`, OS randomness, …)
732	inside `f` — charpente's own crates ban these mechanically with a clippy
733	`disallowed-methods`/`disallowed-types` deny-list (`clippy.toml`) enforced
734	in CI, not by review; adopt the same deny-list in your own app for the same
735	guarantee.

# Building an app on charpente

*(This file is compile-gated: every `rust` code block below is extracted
and built by `crates/guide-examples` — `cargo build -p guide-examples` fails
if a block stops compiling. A `text` block preceded by the line
`<!-- pinned -->` is gated too: `crates/guide-examples/tests/doc_truth.rs`
proves every fragment of 16+ characters outside a `<placeholder>` still
appears in a source or test file under `crates/` or `examples/`, so a quoted
error message cannot silently drift from what the code emits.
Sections 1–4 cover the persistence layer:
project setup, tables, the database, and transactions. Sections 5–7 cover
the deterministic kernel: HTTP, jobs, and cron. Section 8 covers sim
testing — writing `tests/sim.rs`, running `charpente test --sim`, and
replaying a failure's seed. Section 9 is an error index: look up the
message you're staring at. Section 10 covers replication; section 11
covers realtime SSE subscriptions; section 12 covers migrations —
evolving a `#[table]` row's shape safely; section 13 covers `describe` —
the machine-readable contract of a mounted app; section 14 covers the
generated TypeScript client — deriving `Wire`, 64-bit integers, and
`gen-client`/`check-client`; section 15 covers the archive — configuring
one, the notices it raises, and restoring a data directory from a
bucket; section 16 covers tenant scoping — `scoped_by`, opening a scope,
and the cross-tenant capability.)*

## 1. Project setup

Install the CLI once. The crate is `charpente-cli`; the binary it installs is `charpente`:

```text
cargo install charpente-cli
```

Then scaffold an app and run its two gates:

```text
charpente new myapp
cd myapp
cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings   # hard rule 1, in your app
charpente test --sim                        # seeded fault-injection runs
```

`charpente new` writes six files and does nothing else — no `git init`, no build, no
prompts. It refuses a name cargo would reject, a Rust keyword or a reserved crate or
build-directory name, and an existing path, each by name.

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `Cargo.toml` | the manifest below, byte for byte |
| `clippy.toml` | the fence: the standard-library calls a transaction must never make |
| `.gitignore` | `/target` and `/data` |
| `src/lib.rs` | one table, one route, one job, one event, and `build_app` |
| `src/main.rs` | `charpente::launch(...)` — one line (§13) |
| `tests/sim.rs` | three properties in the give-up idiom (§8), their inputs drawn with `sim.input()` and the recovery judged in a fault-free tail |

### `Cargo.toml`

A charpente app is a Rust crate that links against the `charpente` platform
crate and compiles into one binary. Deployment is one binary and one data
directory — no database server, queue service, or config store to
provision. Two dependencies: `charpente`, and `serde` for the request and
response types you define — `charpente` re-exports serde, but
`#[derive(Deserialize)]` looks the crate up by name in your own dependency
list (§5). This is the file `charpente new myapp` writes; a test holds the
two together:

```toml
[package]
name = "myapp"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"
rust-version = "1.99"

[dependencies]
charpente = "0.3"
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }

[dev-dependencies]
charpente-sim = "0.3"

[[test]]
name = "sim"
harness = false

[lints.clippy]
disallowed_methods = "deny"
disallowed_types = "deny"
```

`rust-version` is the oldest toolchain the app builds with. Cargo checks it
before compiling anything, and an older `rustc` is refused by name, with the
version the package requires and the one it found.

`charpente-sim` is dev-only: it drives your app's tables, routes, jobs, and
time through a deterministic simulator with seeded fault injection, and
never links into the shipped binary. The `[[test]] name = "sim", harness =
false` block is required for `charpente test --sim` (§8): it tells Cargo to
build a `tests/sim.rs` binary without the default libtest harness, so the
sim runner supplies its own `main` instead.

### The fence

`clippy.toml` names the standard-library calls a transaction must never
make — `SystemTime::now`, `Instant::now`, `thread::spawn`, the `std::fs`
functions, `TcpStream::connect`, `HashMap` — with the trait to use instead.
The `[lints.clippy]` lines above turn each into an error, so a handler that
reaches for the wall clock is refused at `cargo clippy` by name:

```text
error: use of a disallowed method `std::time::SystemTime::now`
  --> src/lib.rs:51:17
   |
   = note: ambient wall clock — use the Clock trait (DESIGN.md §1)
```

It is the platform's own fence (its CLAUDE.md hard rule 1) minus the entries
that guard platform internals, and a test keeps it a subset. Where a real
edge needs ambient IO — the production `Disk` your `main` mounts — the
sanctioned form is `#[allow(clippy::disallowed_methods)]` on that one
statement with a rationale comment, never at file level.

### The data directory

`charpente::prod::ProdDisk` is the production mount for the `Disk` trait —
the sanctioned place ambient filesystem calls happen. Every table's backing
file and the write-ahead log's segments live under one root directory, as
flat relative names (`tables.redb`; WAL segments are named by their
zero-padded 20-digit base sequence, so the first is
`wal/00000000000000000000.log`); subdirectories are created on demand.
**The data directory's parent must exist, and the node must be able to read
it.** `ProdDisk::new` creates the data directory itself when it is absent, and
never a directory above it: `./data` works on a fresh checkout, while
`/srv/app/node` with no `/srv/app` is refused at startup by name (`charpente
failed to start: the data directory "/srv/app/node" has no parent directory:
"/srv/app" is not an existing directory, ...`). Create the parent when you
provision the machine, and make it durable before the node starts — a bare
`mkdir -p` leaves the new entries in the page cache, so follow it with `sync`.
The reason is durability: an acknowledged write rests on every directory entry
above it. Every directory barrier fsyncs the whole chain from the directory it
names up to the data directory; `ProdDisk::new` fsyncs the data directory's
parent, which holds the data directory's own entry, at every start, before
anything is acknowledged; and the parent's own entry is yours. That start sync
also means a parent the node cannot read stops the start there, under the same
line, rather than inside your app's first barrier. An empty path is
refused by name too. `restore --to` follows the same rule.

```rust
use charpente::prod::ProdDisk;

/// Opens the app's one data directory, creating it if it doesn't exist yet
/// (its parent must).
fn open_data_dir(path: &str) -> std::io::Result<ProdDisk> {
    ProdDisk::new(path)
}
```

Paths handed to a `Disk` must be relative flat names — never absolute, never
containing a `.` or `..` segment, never empty. Violating this is a contract
panic ("Disk paths are relative flat names like \"wal/000001.log\" — got
\"...\""), not a recoverable error.

## 2. Tables

A table is a plain struct annotated `#[table]`. The macro generates the
`Row` implementation (the byte encoding, the table's name, its index list)
plus one lookup function per `#[index]` field.

### The `#[table]` contract

- It declares its tenancy: `#[table(scoped_by = Org)]` if every row belongs
  to one tenant (§16), or `#[table(global)]` if its rows belong to none. A
  bare `#[table]` is a compile error naming both — the platform never guesses
  which a table is, and the built-in tables (`Session`, `ApiKey`, …) are
  `global` like any other.
- The struct must be a non-generic, braced struct with named fields — a
  table is one concrete row shape.
- It must have an `id` field of type `Id<Self>` — a typed primary key.
  `Id<Invoice>` is not `Id<Org>`, and neither is a bare `u64`. By
  convention (every example here follows it) `id` is declared first, but
  the macro only checks that the field exists and that its type is
  `Id<Self>` (the rejection list below), never its position.
- Every other field's type must implement `Codec` — charpente's own
  deterministic, versionless (v0) encoding, not serde. `Codec` is
  implemented for `u8`/`u16`/`u32`/`u64`/`i8`/`i16`/`i32`/`i64`, `bool`,
  `String`, `Vec<u8>`, `Option<T> where T: Codec`, and `Id<T>` for any `T`.
  A field type that isn't `Codec` fails as an ordinary trait-bound error at
  the macro's generated encode/decode code, not a custom message.
- Fields encode and decode **in declaration order** — reordering fields
  changes the byte layout of every row already durable on disk.

```rust
use charpente::{Id, View, table};

struct Org; // referenced only through its typed id below

#[table(global)]
struct Invoice {
    id: Id<Invoice>,
    #[index]
    org: Id<Org>,
    amount_cents: i64,
    memo: Option<String>,
    paid: bool,
}

/// `#[index]` on a field generates an exact-match lookup named
/// `by_<field>`. It takes any `View` — a `Snapshot` outside a transaction,
/// or a `Tx` inside one — and returns every row with that key, in id order.
fn invoices_for_org(view: &impl View, org: Id<Org>) -> std::io::Result<Vec<Invoice>> {
    Invoice::by_org(view, &org)
}
```

`global` here because this section is about `#[index]`, not tenancy; a real invoice table
belongs to its tenant and would say `#[table(scoped_by = Org)]` (§16) — which also retires
the `org` column, because the scope is the key prefix.

A table can carry any number of `#[index]` fields; each gets its own
function with this exact shape:

```rust,ignore
fn by_<field>(view: &impl View, key: &<FieldType>) -> std::io::Result<Vec<Self>>
```

### `#[index]` works on any `Codec` field, including a hand-rolled enum

`#[index]`'s only requirement is the same one every table field already
has: the field type implements `Codec`. The generated index-key function
is nothing but `Codec::encode`, and the lookup it feeds
(`View::scan_by`) is bounded on `key: &impl Codec` — there is no separate
`Eq`/`Hash`/`Ord`/serde bound. A hand-rolled `Codec` enum — a status
field, say — can carry `#[index]` exactly like an `Id<T>` or a `String`
field can:

```rust
use charpente::core::table::Codec;
use charpente::{Id, View, table};
use std::io;

enum InvoiceState {
    Draft,
    Final,
    Paid,
}

impl Codec for InvoiceState {
    fn encode(&self, out: &mut Vec<u8>) {
        let tag: u8 = match self {
            InvoiceState::Draft => 0,
            InvoiceState::Final => 1,
            InvoiceState::Paid => 2,
        };
        tag.encode(out);
    }

    fn decode(input: &mut &[u8]) -> io::Result<Self> {
        match u8::decode(input)? {
            0 => Ok(InvoiceState::Draft),
            1 => Ok(InvoiceState::Final),
            2 => Ok(InvoiceState::Paid),
            other => Err(io::Error::other(format!(
                "invalid InvoiceState tag {other} — schema drift or corruption"
            ))),
        }
    }
}

#[table(global)]
struct Invoice {
    id: Id<Invoice>,
    #[index]
    state: InvoiceState,
}

/// Generated by `#[index]` on `state`, same shape as any other indexed
/// field: an exact-match lookup, in id order.
fn final_invoices(view: &impl View) -> std::io::Result<Vec<Invoice>> {
    Invoice::by_state(view, &InvoiceState::Final)
}
```

When a query doesn't fit an exact-match index — a range or "greater
than" scan, which `#[index]` doesn't support in v0 — the fallback is
`tx.scan::<Invoice>()` filtered in Rust: correct, just not indexed. Reach
for that before assuming a `Codec` field can't be indexed at all.

### Generating ids for rows created inside a transaction

Every example above takes a row's `id` from somewhere outside the
transaction — a `:param` in the route path, or a value the caller
supplied. That works when a row has a natural external identity, but
breaks down for a row created *inside* a transaction with nothing to
source an id from — a child row for each entry of a request body's
`Vec<...>`, say.

There is no platform id-generation primitive for `#[table]` rows in v0
(the platform's own internal job-id counter is not exposed to app code).
The pattern: a singleton counter row per id space, read, incremented, and
written back inside the same transaction that needs a fresh id. This is
safe without a lock or an atomic op because transactions are serialized
through one writer (§4) — two transactions racing to claim an id can
never both observe the same counter value, since the second one only
starts after the first has already committed its increment (or aborted
without writing anything at all).

```rust
use charpente::{Id, Tx, View, table};
use std::io;

#[table(global)]
struct IdCounter {
    id: Id<IdCounter>,
    next: u64,
}

/// One counter row per id space you need (line items, reminders, …),
/// keyed by an arbitrary `seq` value you pick per space.
fn next_id<T>(tx: &mut Tx, seq: u64) -> io::Result<Id<T>> {
    let counter_id = Id::<IdCounter>::from_raw(seq);
    let mut counter = tx.get(counter_id)?.unwrap_or(IdCounter {
        id: counter_id,
        next: 0,
    });
    let value = counter.next;
    counter.next += 1;
    tx.put(&counter);
    Ok(Id::from_raw(value))
}
```

Bit-packing an id out of a caller-supplied parent id (e.g. `(invoice_id
<< 20) | index`) is tempting but unsafe in general: a caller-supplied id
is an arbitrary `u64`, and shifting an arbitrary `u64` left can silently
wrap and collide with another parent's children. The counter-row pattern
above has no such ceiling.

### What the macro rejects

Every rejection happens at compile time, and the message names the contract
and the fix. The first rejection is the one every table meets once — a
declaration with no tenancy stance:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
`<table>` declares no tenancy — a table says which. Add one of these to its `#[table(…)]`, keeping any arguments it already has: `scoped_by = Org` if every row belongs to one tenant (the key becomes `(scope, id)` and a bare `Tx` cannot read it), or `global` if its rows belong to no tenant. Neither is the default.
`global` and `scoped_by = <scope>` on one table — a table is one or the other; drop one
`global` given twice — write it once
```

`<table>` is the struct's name. The other six rejections are about the
struct's shape:

```rust,ignore
// no `id` field at all
#[table(global)]
struct Ping { hits: u64 }
// "missing `id: Id<Ping>` field — every #[table] row needs a typed primary
//  key (add `id: Id<Ping>`)"

// `id` isn't `Id<Self>`
#[table(global)]
struct Ping { id: u64, hits: u64 }
// "the `id` field of a #[table] must be `Id<Ping>` — a typed id, never a
//  bare integer"

// `#[index]` on the primary key
#[table(global)]
struct Ping { #[index] id: Id<Ping>, hits: u64 }
// "`id` is the primary key — it is already the fastest lookup; remove
//  #[index]"

// not a braced struct with named fields (tuple structs and unit structs
// both hit this)
#[table(global)]
struct Ping(u64);
// "#[table] needs named fields — `Ping` must be a braced struct with an
//  `id: Id<Ping>` field"

// enums and unions cannot be rows
#[table(global)]
enum Ping { A, B }
// "#[table] applies to structs — enums and unions cannot be rows"

// generic structs — a table is one concrete row shape
#[table(global)]
struct Ping<T> { id: Id<Ping<T>>, data: T }
// "#[table] structs cannot be generic — a table is one concrete row shape;
//  make `Ping` non-generic"
```

A row that fails to decode at runtime (schema drift, corruption, a
reordered field) fails with, for example, `"row decode: 3 trailing bytes
after a Ping row — schema drift or corruption"`.

## 3. The database

`Db` composes the write-ahead log with the typed table store behind one
writer:

```rust,ignore
pub fn open(disk: Box<dyn Disk>, cfg: DbConfig, schema: Schema) -> std::io::Result<Db>
```

`Schema` is a builder that registers every `#[table]` type your app writes.
Replay works from raw log bytes and needs each type's codec to reconstruct
rows and maintain indexes:

```rust
use charpente::prod::ProdDisk;
use charpente::{Db, DbConfig, Id, Schema, table};

#[table(global)]
struct Counter {
    id: Id<Counter>,
    hits: u64,
}

fn open(data_dir: &str) -> std::io::Result<Db> {
    let disk = ProdDisk::new(data_dir)?;
    let schema = Schema::new().table::<Counter>();
    Db::open(Box::new(disk), DbConfig::default(), schema)
}
```

Registering the same table type twice is a contract panic ("Schema: table
\"Counter\" registered twice — register each #[table] type once").
`Db::open` registers three tables of its own before yours — the job queue
`charpente.jobs`, the event log `charpente.events` and the migration record
`charpente.schema_versions` — so registering any of them yourself hits the same
panic. They are the platform's: no app code reads or writes one (§6, "Job rows are
the platform's"; §16, "Where the guarantee stops"), and code that holds the `Db` reads
them through `db.snapshot()`.

`DbConfig` names the WAL's directory and segment rotation size, and the
table store's file name:

```rust
use charpente::DbConfig;
use charpente::core::log::WalConfig;

fn config() -> DbConfig {
    DbConfig {
        wal: WalConfig {
            dir: "wal".to_string(),
            segment_bytes: 64 << 20, // 64 MiB
        },
        store_path: "tables.redb".to_string(),
        retain_segments: 2,
        checkpoint_every: 4096,
        event_retention: 65_536,
        migration_batch_size: 1000,
    }
}
```

`DbConfig::default()` already sets exactly these values — most apps never
construct one by hand. `retain_segments` and `checkpoint_every` govern
`Db::checkpoint`'s log GC, covered next. `event_retention` bounds the
built-in `charpente.events` table the same way: each checkpoint deletes all
but the newest `event_retention` event rows (`Db::event_floor()` reports the
smallest id still retained). `migration_batch_size` caps how many rows one
schema-migration transaction rewrites at a time, bounding a single migration
commit's WAL record size. It must be at least 1: a batch of 0 rewrites nothing,
so `migrate_schema` refuses by name, before writing anything, when a table is due
to migrate and the size is 0.

### Recovery, behaviorally

`Db::open` opens the table store first; if redb rejects the store file's
bytes (a crash mid-creation can leave bytes redb refuses to read), it's
discarded and rebuilt — the store is a materialization of the log, never a
second source of truth. Only that verdict costs the store: `Store::open`
reports it as `table::StoreRejected` (corrupted, a file format that needs a
manual upgrade, or not a redb file), and any other open failure — an IO
error from the disk — is returned by `Db::open` with the site and the fix
named and the store left as it was, so retrying the open is the fix. The one
exception says so in its text: a store file cut shorter than redb's header,
which no crash leaves and no retry fixes. Its fix depends on the log beside
it, and the text names the right one: while the log still reaches seq 0,
remove the file and the next boot rebuilds it; once the log is compacted,
restore the node from a replica or backup (DESIGN §4). On a replicated node
that restore is a re-seed, and every text that names it says so in the same
breath: clear the data directory and restart the node configured as a follower
of the current primary, never with a primary config (§10). A rebuild only works
while the log still holds everything back
to seq 0, though: `Db::checkpoint(&mut self)` durably persists the store,
then deletes WAL segments below the checkpoint (`DbConfig::retain_segments`
floors how much it keeps; `checkpoint_every` auto-fires the cadence every N
committed records, `0` to disable it and checkpoint only by hand). Once the
log has been compacted this way, a rejected store is unrecoverable
locally — `Db::open` returns a named error instead of a silent (wrong)
rebuild, naming the fix: restore from a replica/backup, or widen
`retain_segments` (for a store whose bytes name an older redb file format, it
says that no charpente release wrote one, so the version byte is damage, and
names redb 2.6's `Database::upgrade()` for a format-2 file something else
wrote). A store whose records stop short of the log's base is refused the same
way, by name, whatever the horizon breadcrumb beside it says: a store file that
is missing, or holds no records, beside a compacted log, or an older copy put
back without its log. Removing or replacing the store is never a fix once the
log is compacted. For a follower the text names the re-seed instead, with the
config it must restart under (§10). `Db::open` then recovers the write-ahead log and replays
every durable record after the store's last checkpoint back into it, so a
reopened `Db` reflects every transaction that ever committed, even one the
store hadn't caught up to when the process died. Recovery can itself fail
under an IO fault; `Db::open` is idempotent, so the caller's answer to a
failed open is simply to retry it. Outside a transaction, `Db::snapshot() ->
io::Result<Snapshot>` gives the same read surface (a `View`) for read-only
queries — inside a transaction, reads additionally see the transaction's
own writes, covered next.

## 4. Transactions

Every state change goes through one transaction:

```rust,ignore
pub fn transact<T, E>(
    &mut self,
    f: impl FnOnce(&mut Tx) -> Result<T, E>,
) -> Result<T, TxError<E>>
```

`f` runs synchronously against a `Tx`: reads see this transaction's own
writes first, then any writes already staged in the same commit batch —
`transact` runs a batch of exactly one, so that level is always empty here —
then the store snapshot the batch began from. `Tx` implements `View` (`get`,
`scan`, `scan_by`), so `Invoice::by_org` from §2 works on a `Tx` exactly as
it does on a `Snapshot`, for every table of the app's own. The platform's own
tables are read through a `Snapshot` alone (§16, "Where the guarantee stops").
On `Ok`, every buffered write, enqueue, and emit
commits as ONE durable log record — all or nothing — and only then applies
to the store. On `Err(TxError::App(_))`, nothing happened at all: no log
position consumed, nothing written. On `Err(TxError::Io(_))` the outcome is
unknown — the record may already be durable (below).

```rust
use charpente::core::table::{Codec, Unscoped};
use charpente::{Db, Id, Job, Tx, TxError, View, event, table};
use std::io;

#[table(global)]
struct Invoice {
    id: Id<Invoice>,
    amount_cents: i64,
    paid: bool,
}

struct SendReceipt {
    invoice: u64,
}

impl Codec for SendReceipt {
    fn encode(&self, out: &mut Vec<u8>) {
        self.invoice.encode(out);
    }
    fn decode(input: &mut &[u8]) -> io::Result<SendReceipt> {
        Ok(SendReceipt {
            invoice: u64::decode(input)?,
        })
    }
}

impl Job for SendReceipt {
    const NAME: &'static str = "send_receipt";
    // The payload's shape, recorded beside every enqueue; a Pending job is
    // only ever decoded by a binary whose FINGERPRINT matches (§6). `#[job]`
    // computes it from the fields; by hand, change it whenever the fields
    // change.
    const FINGERPRINT: u64 = 0x5E4D_0001;
    // A global job: it belongs to no tenant (§6, §16).
    type Scope = Unscoped;
    // `RETRY` defaults to `RetryPolicy::DEFAULT` — retry/backoff and cron
    // are covered in a later section.
}

#[event(global)]
struct InvoiceFinalized {
    invoice: Id<Invoice>,
}

/// The row update, the receipt job, and the realtime event all commit in
/// the one transaction — or none of them do.
fn finalize(db: &mut Db, id: u64) -> Result<(), TxError<io::Error>> {
    db.transact(|tx: &mut Tx| {
        let mut inv = tx
            .get::<Invoice>(Id::from_raw(id))?
            .ok_or_else(|| io::Error::other("invoice not found"))?;
        if inv.paid {
            return Err(io::Error::other("invoice already paid"));
        }
        inv.paid = true;
        tx.put(&inv);
        tx.enqueue(SendReceipt { invoice: id });
        tx.emit(InvoiceFinalized {
            invoice: Id::from_raw(id),
        });
        Ok(())
    })
}
```

`Job` needs `Codec`, a `NAME` and a `FINGERPRINT`, implemented by hand today
(v0); `#[job]` derives the rest of a job's registration for you (a later
section). `#[event]` derives everything an event needs in one step: `Codec`
(the log format), `Event` (`NAME` is the snake_case of the type name — §11 has
the exact splitting rule — and `FINGERPRINT` is the payload's structural
fingerprint, recorded beside every emit, §11 "Changing an event"), `Serialize`
(the wire format `#[route(SSE …)]` subscribers receive, §11), `Wire` (that wire
format's schema, so the contract can name it), and an `EventEntry` impl so
`events![...]` can register it (§11).
Because the payload IS what a subscriber receives, it obeys the wire rules a
route's types obey — which is why `InvoiceFinalized.invoice` above is
`Id<Invoice>` and not the bare `u64` the `SendReceipt` *job* beside it carries:
a job payload never leaves the process, an event payload is a JSON document
someone parses. `tx.put` and `tx.delete` cannot fail — they only
buffer a write into the transaction's overlay; `tx.get`/`scan`/`scan_by`
return `io::Result` because they read through the snapshot. A transaction
that never calls `put`/`delete`/`enqueue`/`emit` writes nothing and consumes
no log position — read-only queries are free.

Enqueuing also takes the app's own key for the job: `tx.enqueue_keyed(key,
job)` carries it on the job's row, and the platform never dedupes on it. It is
not the idempotency key an outbound job's call carries — the platform mints
that one (see Outbound jobs below). An empty key is a contract panic
("contract: an `enqueue_keyed` app key names the job's external identity — it
cannot be empty"). One more hard limit: all of a
transaction's buffered effects together must fit in one 16 MiB log record —
a transaction that doesn't panics with "transaction effects are N bytes but
one log record holds at most 16777216 — split the work into smaller
transactions".

### `TxError`'s four variants

`TxError<E>` has four variants, and this block matches the real type — a
variant rename or addition breaks the guide's compile gate:

```rust
use charpente::TxError;

/// The four arms differ in what they promise: `App` means nothing was
/// written; `Io` means the outcome is unknown (details below); `NotPrimary`
/// means this node is a read-only follower and nothing was even attempted;
/// `Verifying` means this node cannot yet tell whether it is allowed to
/// write, and nothing was attempted either.
fn describe<E: std::fmt::Display>(err: &TxError<E>) -> String {
    match err {
        TxError::App(e) => format!("rejected by the app — nothing was written: {e}"),
        TxError::Io(e) => format!("platform IO failure — outcome unknown: {e}"),
        TxError::NotPrimary { primary } => {
            format!("read-only follower — writes go to {primary} instead")
        }
        TxError::Verifying { unreached } => {
            format!("still verifying witnesses {unreached:?} — writes are on hold")
        }
    }
}
```

The distinction is load-bearing. `App(E)` is whatever `f` returned as
`Err` — your own rejection, or an IO failure hit while *reading* inside the
transaction (both surface through the closure's own `Result<T, E>`); either
way, **nothing was written**. `Io` is a platform failure outside `f`'s own
logic: opening the read snapshot before `f` runs, or appending/syncing the
committed record's log entry after `f` returned `Ok`. That second case is
genuinely ambiguous — the record may already be durable and will reappear
after the next recovery even though the caller was told the commit failed —
so treat `TxError::Io` as "unknown," never as "definitely didn't happen."
The exceptions are an `Io` carrying one of `Group::stage`'s two refusals,
each read with its own `of`. A `JobShapeRefusal`
(`charpente::core::db::JobShapeRefusal::of`) is an enqueue that disagrees with a
job name this binary mounts on its shape, its tenancy or whether it is outbound
(§6, "Changing a job's fields" and "Outbound jobs"). A
`TableWriteRefusal` (`charpente::core::db::TableWriteRefusal::of`) is a write
the `Schema` disagrees with about its table: a table it does not register
(add `.table::<T>()`), a scoped `Row` whose `TABLE` is an unscoped table's or
the reverse, or a put or delete through any Rust type other than the one
registered under that name. A `#[table]` type's table name is its struct
name, so two `#[table] struct Invoice` in different modules collide this way
even when their fields, and so their fingerprints, are the same. The text
names the type that wrote and the registered one: write the registered type,
or give the other one another name. Either refusal comes before anything was
written, so a retry cannot succeed. The HTTP layer answers
either with a 500 carrying the refusal's own text, and in a job handler
either is an attempt, retried and then dead-lettered. The broader
`Refusal::of` is not that predicate: it also matches a refusal apply raises
after the log sync (a replicated record decoded under a mismatched shape),
whose record may already be durable. A read through a type other than the
registered one, a `Tx` or `ScopedTx` read or an `across_tenants` scan, is
refused too, by the read itself, as a `TableReadRefusal`
(`charpente::core::db::TableReadRefusal::of`). It names the table, the type
that read and the registered one, offers the same two fixes, and returns no
row. It reaches your code through the read's `io::Result`, so a route that
returns it with `?` answers a 500 carrying its text, and in a job handler it
is an attempt.
`NotPrimary { primary }` fires only when `f` had at least one effect to
write and this node has been marked a read-only follower
(`Db::forbid_writes`, DESIGN §5) — reads and effect-free transactions never
see it; the HTTP layer maps it to 421, naming `primary`.

`Verifying { unreached }` (M2 sub-project 0b) also fires only when `f` had
at least one effect to write — reads and effect-free transactions never see
it either. It means this node was a durable primary before it restarted and
has not yet confirmed that none of its followers (its "witnesses") were
promoted while it was down (`Db::verify_writes`). Unlike `NotPrimary`, there
is no primary address to name: this node does not know whether one exists
elsewhere, and it may still be the legitimate primary itself. `unreached` is
the witness set this node is verifying, fixed at the moment the gate closed;
the HTTP layer maps it to 503, naming them. It does not shrink as individual
witnesses answer — the stderr notice described in §10 is where the live
per-witness detail lives. The state is transient — writes resume automatically
(`Db::allow_writes`) the moment every witness confirms it was never
promoted, with no caller action needed.

### What a transaction cannot do

`f` only ever receives `&mut Tx` — no `Disk`, `Clock`, `Entropy`, or `Net`
handle reaches inside it. There is no way to await a network call from
inside a transaction: `f`'s signature is a plain, synchronous `FnOnce(&mut
Tx) -> Result<T, E>`, not `async`, so writing `.await` inside it is a
compile error, not a runtime one:

```rust,ignore
db.transact(|tx| {
    tx.put(&row);
    fetch_from_the_network().await?; // error[E0728]: `await` is only
                                      // allowed inside `async` functions
                                      // and blocks
    Ok::<_, std::io::Error>(())
})
```

Nothing in the type system stops you from calling an ambient clock or
randomness function (`std::time::SystemTime::now()`, OS randomness, …)
inside `f` — charpente's own crates ban these mechanically with a clippy
`disallowed-methods`/`disallowed-types` deny-list (`clippy.toml`) enforced
in CI, not by review; adopt the same deny-list in your own app for the same
guarantee.

- The first argument must be named exactly `tx`, typed `&mut Tx`.

  helper that returns something borrowed out of a `Ctx` must say which
