The handler returns `Result<T, ApiError>` where `T: serde::Serialize + Wire`
— the `Result<_, _>` shape itself is enforced too, and named (a bare return
value is a compile error naming the fix, `-> Result<YourResponseType,
ApiError>`); on `Ok`, the glue emits `Response::json(200, &value)`.

```rust
use charpente::core::table::Id;
use charpente::http::{ApiError, App, AppConfig, Ctx};
use charpente::prod::{ProdDisk, ProdEntropy};
use charpente::{Schema, Tx, View, Wire, route, routes, table};
use serde::Deserialize;

#[table(global)]
struct Note {
    id: Id<Note>,
    text: String,
}

// A route's request body must be `Wire` too (§13) — `#[derive(Wire)]` sits
// alongside `Deserialize`, one for the schema, one for the actual parse.
#[derive(Wire, Deserialize)]
struct NoteBody {
    text: String,
}

// tx, then :id (named `id`, path order), then the JSON body, then `ctx`. A
// path param is a wire position too, so it is `Id<Note>`, not a bare `u64`.
#[route(POST "/notes/:id", public)]
fn create_note(tx: &mut Tx, id: Id<Note>, body: NoteBody, ctx: &Ctx) -> Result<Id<Note>, ApiError> {
    let _ = ctx; // available; this route just doesn't need a session
    tx.put(&Note {
        id,
        text: body.text,
    });
    Ok(id)
}

#[route(GET "/notes/:id", public)]
fn get_note(tx: &mut Tx, id: Id<Note>) -> Result<String, ApiError> {
    Ok(tx.get(id)?.ok_or(ApiError::NotFound)?.text)
}

fn build_app(data_dir: &str) -> std::io::Result<App> {
    Ok(App::open(
        Box::new(ProdDisk::new(data_dir)?),
        Schema::new().table::<Note>(),
        Box::new(ProdEntropy::new()?),
        AppConfig::default(),
    )?
    .mount(routes![create_note, get_note]))
}
```

`routes![...]` accepts path-qualified handlers too, not just bare
identifiers in scope — `routes![handlers::create_note]` works exactly like
`routes![create_note]` after `use handlers::create_note;`.

`Request`'s shape (what a handler ultimately runs against, one layer down):
`method: Method`, `path: String`, `query: BTreeMap<String, String>`,
`headers: BTreeMap<String, String>` (keys lowercased), `body: Vec<u8>`.
`query` is parsed from the URL's `?...` suffix at construction; a plain
`#[route]` handler still has no argument-convention access to it (only
`#[route(SSE ...)]`'s platform-extracted resume cursor reads it today).

### Returning rows from a route: storage shape vs. wire shape

A handler's return type only needs `T: serde::Serialize + Wire` (above) —
nothing requires `T` to be a `#[table]` row, and `#[table]` does not derive
`Serialize` or `Wire` for you: a row's storage shape (`Id<T>`'s own `Codec`, §2) and
its wire shape are separate concerns on purpose, kept apart even though
`Id<T>` also implements `Serialize`/`Deserialize` — as a decimal string,
never a JSON number, because `u64` values above 2^53 lose precision
silently in JavaScript clients.

The fix is the one every other example in this guide already uses without
saying so: convert to a plain response type first. `Id<T>` belongs directly
in that view type — there's no need to unwrap it to a bare `u64` with
`.raw()` to make it serializable.

```rust
use charpente::http::{ApiError, App, AppConfig};
use charpente::prod::{ProdDisk, ProdEntropy};
use charpente::{Id, Schema, Tx, View, Wire, route, routes, table};
use serde::Serialize;

#[table(global)]
struct Note {
    id: Id<Note>,
    text: String,
}

/// The wire shape: `Id<Note>` crosses as a decimal string, so it appears
/// directly here — no `.raw()` unwrap, no separate id type. `#[derive(Wire)]`
/// is what lets this type appear in a route's response schema (§13).
#[derive(Wire, Serialize)]
struct NoteView {
    id: Id<Note>,
    text: String,
}

impl From<Note> for NoteView {
    fn from(row: Note) -> Self {
        NoteView {
            id: row.id,
            text: row.text,
        }
    }
}

#[route(GET "/notes/:id", public)]
fn get_note(tx: &mut Tx, id: Id<Note>) -> Result<NoteView, ApiError> {
    Ok(tx.get(id)?.ok_or(ApiError::NotFound)?.into())
}

fn build_app(data_dir: &str) -> std::io::Result<App> {
    Ok(App::open(
        Box::new(ProdDisk::new(data_dir)?),
        Schema::new().table::<Note>(),
        Box::new(ProdEntropy::new()?),
        AppConfig::default(),
    )?
    .mount(routes![get_note]))
}
```

Storage rows and wire responses are different concerns regardless of the
serde question — this DTO conversion is good hygiene even for a `Codec`
field type that happens to also implement `Serialize`.

### Mounting routes, and the conflict panic

`App::open(...)` returns the platform-registered `App`; `.mount(routes![...])`
adds a batch of routes, checking every new route against every route already
mounted. Two routes with the **same method and the same shape** — the same
sequence of literal-vs-`:param` segments, so both could match one real path
— panic at mount time, not at request time:

```rust
use charpente::http::{ApiError, App};
use charpente::{Id, Tx, route, routes, table};

#[table(global)]
struct Note {
    id: Id<Note>,
}

// A path param is a wire position too — `Id<Note>`, not a bare `u64`.
#[route(GET "/notes/:id", public)]
fn by_id(tx: &mut Tx, id: Id<Note>) -> Result<Id<Note>, ApiError> {
    let _ = tx;
    Ok(id)
}

#[route(GET "/notes/:key", public)]
fn by_key(tx: &mut Tx, key: String) -> Result<String, ApiError> {
    let _ = tx;
    Ok(key)
}

// `/notes/:id` and `/notes/:key` are the same shape under the same method —
// both could match `GET /notes/42` — so mounting both panics with:
// "route conflict: GET /notes/:key (fn by_key) collides with GET
//  /notes/:id (fn by_id) — two routes with the same method and shape can
//  both match one path; change one pattern"
fn mount_conflicting(app: App) -> App {
    app.mount(routes![by_id, by_key])
}
```

A literal segment beats a `:param` at the same position instead of
conflicting — `/notes/all` and `/notes/:id` can coexist, and a request for
`/notes/all` always prefers the literal route.

### Auth: sessions, API keys, and the resolution ladder

`App::open` registers two platform tables of its own alongside yours —
`Session` (`id: Id<Session>`, `#[index] token_hash: String`, `subject:
String`, `expires_at: WallTime`) and `ApiKey` (`id: Id<ApiKey>`, `#[index]
key_hash: String`, `subject: String`, `created_at: WallTime`) — both inside the
commit point, so a login or a minted key is a durable, replicated
transaction like any other. **Only the hash is ever stored:**
`token_hash`/`key_hash` are lowercase-hex SHA-256 of the raw credential; the
raw string exists only in the response that mints it and never reaches disk
(a sim property scans every durable file in the run and proves it).

Every request gets a `Ctx`, built inside the same transaction as your
handler, carrying:

- `ctx.principal() -> Option<&Principal>` — the authenticated identity, if
  any. `principal.subject()` is the subject the credential was minted for,
  and `principal.via()` names which rung authenticated it
  (`Via::Session(id)`, `Via::ApiKey(id)`, or `Via::Oidc`; `charpente::auth::Via`, whose
  `id` is the matched row's `Id<Session>` or `Id<ApiKey>`). Read the subject
  from here on any `auth` route, whatever the credential kind. A `Principal`
  is read-only to your code: its fields are private, so the only principals
  are the ones the ladder produced. It is not `Clone` either, so the only one
  your code holds is the `&Principal` this request's `Ctx` lends, which ends
  with the request: no principal can be parked in a `static` for a later
  request to hand `tx.open_scope`. So `Tenant::authorize` can trust the one
  it is handed: the ladder produced it, for the request that is asking.
- `ctx.session() -> Option<&Session>` — a compatibility accessor: the
  `Session` row, but only when the principal authenticated `via` a session
  (bearer or cookie); `None` for an API-key or OIDC principal.
- `ctx.create_session(tx, subject) -> String` — inserts a `Session` row and
  returns its raw token (a login). `expires_at` is this request's wall-clock
  `now` plus `AppConfig::session_ttl` (default 30 days).
- `ctx.create_api_key(tx, subject) -> String` — inserts an `ApiKey` row and
  returns the raw key: `"ck_"` + 64 hex chars (the prefix makes a leaked key
  grep-able for scanners). Revoke a key by deleting its row —
  `tx.delete::<ApiKey>(id)`, an ordinary write — after checking that the row's
  `subject` is the caller's: an id names a key, it does not show the caller holds
  it (`revoke_key` below). Revoking a key ends that key alone: a session or key
  minted by a request that presented it stays live.
- `ctx.revoke(tx)` — deletes the current session (logout); a no-op without
  one.

One credential mint per request, of either kind. The raw token/key is 32
entropy bytes drawn once *before* the transaction starts, so
`create_session` and `create_api_key` share a single mint budget — calling
either a second time in one request panics: "Ctx::create_session/create_api_key
called twice in one request — one credential mint per request".

A `Session`'s or `ApiKey`'s `id` is the first 64 bits of that same draw: the
raw token's first 16 hex characters (after `ck_` for a key). The ladder finds a
row by the hash of the whole raw token, and the other 192 bits stay secret, so
showing a holder the id of their own credential (to revoke it, say) is fine.
Show it to no one else: each id is a quarter of a credential.

**The resolution ladder.** Before your handler runs, the platform turns the
request's credential into a `Principal`, in this order:

1. `Authorization: Bearer <t>` where `<t>` contains exactly two `.` — judged
   as a JWT and OIDC-verified (below). With no verifier mounted, a JWT-shaped
   bearer is an unrecognized credential, never a fall-through to the hash
   path.
2. Any other bearer — SHA-256'd and matched against the `ApiKey` index, then
   the `Session` index (a session past its `expires_at` is treated as
   absent).
3. A `charpente_session=<t>` cookie — the same hash path as 2. Only a
   `Bearer` header is ever OIDC-verified; a cookie value that happens to
   contain two dots still goes down the hash path.
4. Nothing presented — `principal` is `None`.

`#[route(METHOD "/path", auth)]` rejects the request before your handler runs
when the principal is `None`. With `public`, the route always runs and
`ctx.principal()` is whatever the ladder resolved (possibly `None`) — though a
handler that then opens a tenant scope with no principal gets a 401 of its
own, unless the route declared `public(Org)` (below) — but a
*presented* credential is still resolved and rejected even on a public
route, so a garbage bearer never reaches a handler.

The 401s are named and fixed — copy these verbatim if you assert against
them:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
authentication required — send "Authorization: Bearer <token>" or the charpente_session cookie
unrecognized credential — it may have been revoked; obtain a new one
session expired — log in again
```

The first fires when an `auth` route saw no credential; the second for a
bearer/cookie that matched no live row (garbage, revoked, or a JWT-shaped
bearer with no OIDC configured); the third for a session past its TTL. Expiry
is judged on wall time: `expires_at` is a `WallTime` (UTC nanoseconds since the
Unix epoch, `charpente::core::io::WallTime`), and under the kernel each
request's `now` is the node's `Clock::wall` reading, held so that it never runs
backwards (§7, "Clock errors"). So a TTL means the same thing after a restart or
a failover as before it, within one bound for each backward step of the clock
(steps add up, §7): a session that expired just before a
restart or a failover can resolve again for at most `CLOCK_TOLERANCE` (60 s)
plus the time since the data directory last recorded a time, and never when the
clocks are right. Expiry is *lazy*: a row is invisible the moment `now` passes
`expires_at` — a built-in daily cron sweeps the dead rows for hygiene, but
resolution never waits on it.

`App::handle` is the one seam outside the kernel's clock: it judges at
`WallTime::UNIX_EPOCH`, so a session it mints expires `session_ttl` after 1970
and reads as expired the moment a kernel presents it. When a kernel will present
the credential, mint it through the kernel, or call `app.handle_at(request,
clock.wall())` with the node's clock.

```rust
use charpente::auth::{ApiKey, Via};
use charpente::http::{ApiError, App, AppConfig, Ctx};
use charpente::prod::{ProdDisk, ProdEntropy};
use charpente::{Id, Schema, Tx, View, route, routes};

// A login trades a credential the ladder has already verified, an API key or
// an OIDC token (below), for a session in the same subject. It refuses a
// session: a session that could buy a session would renew itself past its TTL
// and outlive its holder's logout. A session bought with a key still outlives a
// revoke of that key (above). charpente has no password check, so never mint
// for a subject a request body names: that lets anyone log in as anyone. The
// first credential comes from something the app trusts, such as an IdP or a
// signup route that mints a key for a subject it has just created.
#[route(POST "/login", auth)]
fn login(tx: &mut Tx, ctx: &Ctx) -> Result<String, ApiError> {
    let principal = ctx.principal().expect("auth route");
    if matches!(principal.via(), Via::Session(_)) {
        return Err(ApiError::BadRequest(
            "log in with an API key or an OIDC token, not a session".to_string(),
        ));
    }
    let subject = principal.subject().to_string();
    Ok(ctx.create_session(tx, subject))
}

#[route(GET "/me", auth)]
fn whoami(tx: &mut Tx, ctx: &Ctx) -> Result<String, ApiError> {
    let _ = tx;
    Ok(ctx
        .principal()
        .expect("auth routes always have a principal")
        .subject()
        .to_string())
}

#[route(POST "/logout", auth)]
fn logout(tx: &mut Tx, ctx: &Ctx) -> Result<&'static str, ApiError> {
    ctx.revoke(tx);
    Ok("bye")
}

// Mint an API key for the caller's own subject; revoke by deleting the row.
#[route(POST "/keys", auth)]
fn mint_key(tx: &mut Tx, ctx: &Ctx) -> Result<String, ApiError> {
    let subject = ctx.principal().expect("auth route").subject().to_string();
    Ok(ctx.create_api_key(tx, subject))
}

// `ApiKey` is a global table, so any id reaches any subject's key. Revoke only
// the caller's own, and answer another subject's key as absent.
#[route(DELETE "/keys/:id", auth)]
fn revoke_key(tx: &mut Tx, id: Id<ApiKey>, ctx: &Ctx) -> Result<&'static str, ApiError> {
    let caller = ctx.principal().expect("auth route").subject();
    match tx.get(id)? {
        Some(key) if key.subject == caller => {
            tx.delete::<ApiKey>(id);
            Ok("revoked")
        }
        _ => Err(ApiError::NotFound),
    }
}

fn build_app(data_dir: &str) -> std::io::Result<App> {
    Ok(App::open(
        Box::new(ProdDisk::new(data_dir)?),
        Schema::new(), // Session and ApiKey are registered by App::open itself
        Box::new(ProdEntropy::new()?),
        AppConfig::default(),
    )?
    .mount(routes![login, whoami, logout, mint_key, revoke_key]))
}
```

### OIDC (static JWKS)

`App::with_oidc` mounts a verifier for RS256-signed JWTs against a static
JWKS — pure signature-and-claims checking on the kernel thread, no network
fetch (dynamic JWKS is a later milestone). Configure it with the IdP's
issuer, your audience, and the JWKS document verbatim:

```rust
use charpente::auth::OidcConfig;
use charpente::http::App;

fn mount_oidc(app: App) -> App {
    app.with_oidc(OidcConfig {
        issuer: "https://idp.example.com".to_string(),
        audience: "my-charpente-api".to_string(),
        // The IdP's JWKS document, verbatim — one or more RSA keys.
        jwks_json: r#"{"keys":[{"kty":"RSA","kid":"k1","n":"0vx7...","e":"AQAB"}]}"#.to_string(),
    })
}
```

The JWKS is parsed once, at mount — a malformed document or an unusable key
panics *then*, naming the offending key and the fix, never at request time
(`<kid>` is the key's `kid`, or its position when absent):

```text
OidcConfig::jwks_json is not valid JSON: <detail> — pass the IdP's JWKS document verbatim (a {"keys": [...]} object)
OidcConfig::jwks_json has no keys — the "keys" array is empty; add at least one RSA key
OIDC JWKS key <kid> has kty "EC" — only "RSA" is supported in v1; remove non-RSA keys from the JWKS
OIDC JWKS key <kid> has alg "RS384" — only "RS256" is supported; fix or remove the key's "alg" field
OIDC JWKS key <kid> is invalid: modulus "n" is not valid base64url: <detail>
```

A verified token yields a `Principal` whose `via()` is `Via::Oidc` and whose
`subject()` is the token's `sub` claim — ephemeral, no row, nothing to revoke
but a short `exp`. `exp`/`nbf` (Unix seconds) are checked against the node's
wall clock with a 60-second skew tolerance (`CLOCK_TOLERANCE`). Each failed
check is its own named 401 (the
`iss`/`aud` ones name presented-vs-configured; `<presented>`/`<configured>`
are the actual values):

<!-- pinned -->
```text
malformed OIDC token — expected "header.payload.signature" (three dot-separated segments); got 2 segment(s)
unsupported OIDC token alg "HS256" — only "RS256" is verified; mint the token with an RS256-signed key
OIDC token signature does not verify against any configured JWKS key — the token was not issued by a trusted key; obtain a new one
OIDC token expired — its "exp" claim is in the past; obtain a new one
OIDC token is not yet valid — its "nbf" claim is in the future; wait or mint a fresh token
OIDC token has issuer "<presented>" but this server is configured for issuer "<configured>" — mint the token against the configured issuer or fix OidcConfig::issuer
OIDC token has audience "<presented>" but this server is configured for audience "<configured>" — mint the token for the configured audience or fix OidcConfig::audience
```

The replication port has its own peer-authentication secret, unrelated to
this request-side auth — see §10.

### A route's stance, and who reaches a tenant

Every route declares one of three stances after its path, and the stance decides what
`tx.scope::<Org>(org, ctx)?` (§16) does for each caller:

| Stance | Who reaches the handler | What the scope line does |
|---|---|---|
| `auth` | a caller with a credential | runs `Org::authorize` once, about that principal |
| `public` | every caller | with a credential, the same; with none, the 401 below |
| `public(Org)` | every caller | admits every caller into the `Org` tenant it names; no `authorize` runs |

The scope line applies three rules, in order:

1. If the route declared `public(S)` for this very `S`, the scope is admitted by that
   declaration. No `authorize` runs, whoever the caller is. A credentialed caller whose
   membership check would refuse is admitted too: the route said every caller may act
   here.
2. Otherwise, with a principal present, `S::authorize` runs once, about that principal,
   and its `Err` is the handler's `Err`.
3. Otherwise the caller has no credential, and the request is answered 401, by name.
   Nothing below the scope line runs.

An `auth` request never reaches rule 3, because the `auth` gate refused the anonymous caller
before your handler ran. So your `authorize` is only ever asked about a real principal. A
`public(Org)` route that opens a *different* scope type gets rules 2 and 3 for it, and the
401 names `public(Org)` as the route's stance.

The rule-3 401, for a `POST /orgs/:org/incidents` declared plain `public`:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
authentication required — `POST /orgs/:org/incidents` is declared `public` and opened the tenant scope `Org` for a caller with no credential; only a route declared `public(Org)` admits one. Send "Authorization: Bearer <token>" or the charpente_session cookie, or, if every caller may act inside this tenant here, declare `public(Org)` in place of `public` in this route's `#[route(…)]` attribute, keeping its other flags. A tenant type is named here by its NAME; name the type in the attribute: `Org` is the tenant type `<path>`
```

The site is the word the route was declared with (`SSE` for a stream) and its pattern;
the scope is its tenant type's `NAME` (§16). Both fixes are there: the caller's (send a credential)
and the author's (declare the tenant public, if that really is the policy). The author's
names the change to make where the stance is written and restates no attribute, so a route's
other flags, `cross_tenant` or `emits(…)`, stay as they are. A `NAME` need not be how your
source spells the type (`billing::Org` and `crm::Org` take two), so the text ends with each
named type's `std::any::type_name` (`<path>` above), which says which type to write in the
attribute. On a route declared `public(BillingOrg)` that opened `CrmOrg`, it names both. §16's
"Who reaches a tenant" shows the three side by side.

### `ApiError` and status mapping

A handler rejects with `ApiError`; `From<io::Error> for ApiError` converts
to `Internal`, so `?` works on `tx` reads exactly like it does inside a
plain transaction (§4). Every response body is a JSON envelope
`{"error": "<message>"}` except a 200, which is the handler's own returned
value:

- `BadRequest(String)` → 400. What `FromParam`/JSON-body decoding produce
  (below), or your own rejection.
- The 401 family → 401. Auth rejections, produced before your handler runs
  (the resolution ladder, above): `Unauthorized` (no credential),
  `UnrecognizedCredential`, `SessionExpired`, and `Oidc(..)` (one per failed
  OIDC check); and, at the scope line inside it, `AnonymousScope(..)`, a
  scope line reached with no credential on a route that did not declare that
  tenant public (above). Their exact, named texts are in the auth and stance
  sections above — you rarely construct these yourself; the `auth` gate, the
  ladder and `tx.scope` emit them.
- `NotFound` → 404. Fixed message `"not found"` — the same text an
  unmatched path gets from the router directly.
- `Internal(String)` → 500. Carries `e.to_string()` when it arrived via
  `?`, or your own message.

There is no 403. To refuse a caller the ladder did authenticate (an `authorize`
that says no, a row the caller does not own), pick one of the variants above:
this guide's membership checks answer `BadRequest` naming the tenant, and
`revoke_key` above answers `NotFound`, which does not say whether the row exists.

Two more statuses never go through `ApiError` at all: an unmatched path is
404 ("not found") and a matched path with the wrong method is 405 ("method
not allowed for this path") — both produced by the router before a
transaction ever opens, so nothing was attempted, let alone written.

A path param that doesn't parse is a named 400 — e.g. a non-numeric `:id`
against a `u64` argument: `"path parameter :id must be an unsigned integer
— got \"abc\""`. A missing or malformed JSON body is a named 400 too, e.g.
`"this route requires a JSON body of type NoteBody"` (empty body) or
`"invalid JSON body for NoteBody: <serde_json's own message>"`.

### The 1 MiB body cap

`AppConfig::body_cap` (default `1 << 20` — 1,048,576 bytes, 1 MiB) fences
the request body — and, transitively, `Db::transact`'s 16 MiB record-size
assert (§4) from ever seeing raw network input. It is enforced in two
places:

- In production, `charpente::serve` enforces it at the wire — a
  length-limited body read rejects an oversized body *before* the request
  is even routed, so it applies uniformly to every path, matched or not.
  With a 64-byte cap and a 65-byte body, the wire's 413 reads exactly:
  `"request body exceeds the 64-byte cap — raise AppConfig.body_cap or
  send less"`.
- Inside the kernel (`App::handle` — what the sim drives directly, and
  what `serve` calls after decoding), the same cap is checked again, but
  only **after** routing succeeds: an oversized body sent to an unmatched
  path 404s, not 413, since the router runs first. With the same 64/65
  numbers, this 413 reads: `"request body is 65 bytes but the cap is 64 —
  raise AppConfig.body_cap or send less"`.

Apps exercised only through `App::handle` (sim tests, and anything built
directly against the kernel) only ever see the second message — the wire
check is production-only edge behavior.

```rust
use charpente::http::AppConfig;

fn small_cap_config() -> AppConfig {
    AppConfig {
        body_cap: 4096,
        ..AppConfig::default()
    }
}
```

### Ack-after-durable

A 200 is emitted only once the handler's transaction has returned `Ok` —
which, per §4, only happens after that transaction's one log record has
synced to disk. There is no path that returns a 200 before durability.

The other statuses fall out of §4's `TxError` split precisely:
`ApiError`-mapped statuses (400/401/404, and a handler-level 500 from
`Internal`/`?`) are `TxError::App(e)` — the transaction aborted, **nothing
was written**, so there is nothing ambiguous about them. The remaining
case, `TxError::Io` — a platform failure appending or syncing the record
itself, outside the handler's own logic — is genuinely unknown: the record
may already be durable. It surfaces as its own 500, with a message that
says so instead of guessing: `"internal storage failure — the request may
or may not have committed; retry after the server recovers: {e}"`.

**Since group commit, one request's failure can be another request's 500 —
and a 500 can name a write that committed.** The kernel commits everything
it drained in one loop iteration under a single fsync, up to 64 requests.
An append or sync failure still commits no record in the batch — but "acks
nothing" would overstate it, and the fourth bullet below is the reason: a
request that ran ahead of every staged record observed only committed state,
so it is not invalidated and keeps its 200. What such a failure invalidates is
every request from the first staged record onward. The case with no analogue in
a one-at-a-time kernel is a failure to
*apply* a record after the batch has already synced: at that point every
record in the batch is on disk and none of them is in the store, because the
store takes a whole batch in one transaction — an apply failure anywhere rolls
every record in it back rather than leaving a prefix behind. So the platform
answers 500 to every request that staged a record in that batch, and to every
request that *read* one of those records through the batch's shared view. A
request that ran ahead of every staged record still keeps its 200: it only ever
observed committed state. Read it as the
rule above says: **a 500 never promises rejection, only the absence of
confirmation.** What that means in practice:

- **The write may be committed.** After an apply failure every record in the
  batch is durable and applies when the process restarts. The client was told
  "unknown"; the durable answer turns out to be "yes". Plan for it — this is
  a named contract, not an edge case you are expected to discover.
- **The reverse remains impossible.** No 200 is ever emitted for something
  that is not durable. Every reply in a batch is held until the commit
  returns, so the ack still follows the sync.
- **The node stops.** An apply failure means machine state no longer matches
  the log, so the engine poisons and the kernel stops rather than serving on
  (§9's "Poisoned-engine errors"). The fix is a restart, which replays the
  WAL and is idempotent.
- **A request that ran ahead of the failure keeps its answer.** The rule is
  what a request *saw*, not where it sat in the batch: a read that only ever
  observed committed

143	            id: row.id,
144	            text: row.text,
145	        }
146	    }
147	}
148	
149	#[route(GET "/notes/:id", public)]
150	fn get_note(tx: &mut Tx, id: Id<Note>) -> Result<NoteView, ApiError> {
151	    Ok(tx.get(id)?.ok_or(ApiError::NotFound)?.into())
152	}
153	
154	fn build_app(data_dir: &str) -> std::io::Result<App> {
155	    Ok(App::open(
156	        Box::new(ProdDisk::new(data_dir)?),
157	        Schema::new().table::<Note>(),
158	        Box::new(ProdEntropy::new()?),
159	        AppConfig::default(),
160	    )?
161	    .mount(routes![get_note]))
162	}
163	```

165	Storage rows and wire responses are different concerns regardless of the
166	serde question — this DTO conversion is good hygiene even for a `Codec`
167	field type that happens to also implement `Serialize`.

169	### Mounting routes, and the conflict panic
170	
171	`App::open(...)` returns the platform-registered `App`; `.mount(routes![...])`
172	adds a batch of routes, checking every new route against every route already
173	mounted. Two routes with the **same method and the same shape** — the same
174	sequence of literal-vs-`:param` segments, so both could match one real path
175	— panic at mount time, not at request time:
176	
177	```rust
178	use charpente::http::{ApiError, App};
179	use charpente::{Id, Tx, route, routes, table};
180	
181	#[table(global)]
182	struct Note {
183	    id: Id<Note>,
184	}
185	
186	// A path param is a wire position too — `Id<Note>`, not a bare `u64`.
187	#[route(GET "/notes/:id", public)]
188	fn by_id(tx: &mut Tx, id: Id<Note>) -> Result<Id<Note>, ApiError> {
189	    let _ = tx;
190	    Ok(id)
191	}
192	
193	#[route(GET "/notes/:key", public)]
194	fn by_key(tx: &mut Tx, key: String) -> Result<String, ApiError> {
195	    let _ = tx;
196	    Ok(key)
197	}
198	
199	// `/notes/:id` and `/notes/:key` are the same shape under the same method —
200	// both could match `GET /notes/42` — so mounting both panics with:
201	// "route conflict: GET /notes/:key (fn by_key) collides with GET
202	//  /notes/:id (fn by_id) — two routes with the same method and shape can
203	//  both match one path; change one pattern"
204	fn mount_conflicting(app: App) -> App {
205	    app.mount(routes![by_id, by_key])
206	}
207	```
208	
209	A literal segment beats a `:param` at the same position instead of
210	conflicting — `/notes/all` and `/notes/:id` can coexist, and a request for
211	`/notes/all` always prefers the literal route.

213	### Auth: sessions, API keys, and the resolution ladder
214	
215	`App::open` registers two platform tables of its own alongside yours —
216	`Session` (`id: Id<Session>`, `#[index] token_hash: String`, `subject:
217	String`, `expires_at: WallTime`) and `ApiKey` (`id: Id<ApiKey>`, `#[index]
218	key_hash: String`, `subject: String`, `created_at: WallTime`) — both inside the
219	commit point, so a login or a minted key is a durable, replicated
220	transaction like any other. **Only the hash is ever stored:**
221	`token_hash`/`key_hash` are lowercase-hex SHA-256 of the raw credential; the
222	raw string exists only in the response that mints it and never reaches disk
223	(a sim property scans every durable file in the run and proves it).
224	
225	Every request gets a `Ctx`, built inside the same transaction as your
226	handler, carrying:
227	
228	- `ctx.principal() -> Option<&Principal>` — the authenticated identity, if
229	  any. `principal.subject()` is the subject the credential was minted for,
230	  and `principal.via()` names which rung authenticated it
231	  (`Via::Session(id)`, `Via::ApiKey(id)`, or `Via::Oidc`; `charpente::auth::Via`, whose
232	  `id` is the matched row's `Id<Session>` or `Id<ApiKey>`). Read the subject
233	  from here on any `auth` route, whatever the credential kind. A `Principal`
234	  is read-only to your code: its fields are private, so the only principals
235	  are the ones the ladder produced. It is not `Clone` either, so the only one
236	  your code holds is the `&Principal` this request's `Ctx` lends, which ends
237	  with the request: no principal can be parked in a `static` for a later
238	  request to hand `tx.open_scope`. So `Tenant::authorize` can trust the one
239	  it is handed: the ladder produced it, for the request that is asking.
240	- `ctx.session() -> Option<&Session>` — a compatibility accessor: the
241	  `Session` row, but only when the principal authenticated `via` a session
242	  (bearer or cookie); `None` for an API-key or OIDC principal.
243	- `ctx.create_session(tx, subject) -> String` — inserts a `Session` row and
244	  returns its raw token (a login). `expires_at` is this request's wall-clock
245	  `now` plus `AppConfig::session_ttl` (default 30 days).
246	- `ctx.create_api_key(tx, subject) -> String` — inserts an `ApiKey` row and
247	  returns the raw key: `"ck_"` + 64 hex chars (the prefix makes a leaked key
248	  grep-able for scanners). Revoke a key by deleting its row —
249	  `tx.delete::<ApiKey>(id)`, an ordinary write — after checking that the row's
250	  `subject` is the caller's: an id names a key, it does not show the caller holds
251	  it (`revoke_key` below). Revoking a key ends that key alone: a session or key
252	  minted by a request that presented it stays live.
253	- `ctx.revoke(tx)` — deletes the current session (logout); a no-op without
254	  one.
255	
256	One credential mint per request, of either kind. The raw token/key is 32
257	entropy bytes drawn once *before* the transaction starts, so
258	`create_session` and `create_api_key` share a single mint budget — calling
259	either a second time in one request panics: "Ctx::create_session/create_api_key
260	called twice in one request — one credential mint per request".
261	
262	A `Session`'s or `ApiKey`'s `id` is the first 64 bits of that same draw: the
263	raw token's first 16 hex characters (after `ck_` for a key). The ladder finds a
264	row by the hash of the whole raw token, and the other 192 bits stay secret, so
265	showing a holder the id of their own credential (to revoke it, say) is fine.
266	Show it to no one else: each id is a quarter of a credential.
267	
268	**The resolution ladder.** Before your handler runs, the platform turns the
269	request's credential into a `Principal`, in this order:
270	
271	1. `Authorization: Bearer <t>` where `<t>` contains exactly two `.` — judged
272	   as a JWT and OIDC-verified (below). With no verifier mounted, a JWT-shaped
273	   bearer is an unrecognized credential, never a fall-through to the hash
274	   path.
275	2. Any other bearer — SHA-256'd and matched against the `ApiKey` index, then
276	   the `Session` index (a session past its `expires_at` is treated as
277	   absent).
278	3. A `charpente_session=<t>` cookie — the same hash path as 2. Only a
279	   `Bearer` header is ever OIDC-verified; a cookie value that happens to
280	   contain two dots still goes down the hash path.
281	4. Nothing presented — `principal` is `None`.
282	
283	`#[route(METHOD "/path", auth)]` rejects the request before your handler runs
284	when the principal is `None`. With `public`, the route always runs and
285	`ctx.principal()` is whatever the ladder resolved (possibly `None`) — though a
286	handler that then opens a tenant scope with no principal gets a 401 of its
287	own, unless the route declared `public(Org)` (below) — but a
288	*presented* credential is still resolved and rejected even on a public
289	route, so a garbage bearer never reaches a handler.
290	
291	The 401s are named and fixed — copy these verbatim if you assert against
292	them:
293	
294	<!-- pinned -->
295	```text
296	authentication required — send "Authorization: Bearer <token>" or the charpente_session cookie
297	unrecognized credential — it may have been revoked; obtain a new one
298	session expired — log in again
299	```
300	
301	The first fires when an `auth` route saw no credential; the second for a
302	bearer/cookie that matched no live row (garbage, revoked, or a JWT-shaped
303	bearer with no OIDC configured); the third for a session past its TTL. Expiry
304	is judged on wall time: `expires_at` is a `WallTime` (UTC nanoseconds since the
305	Unix epoch, `charpente::core::io::WallTime`), and under the kernel each
306	request's `now` is the node's `Clock::wall` reading, held so that it never runs
307	backwards (§7, "Clock errors"). So a TTL means the same thing after a restart or
308	a failover as before it, within one bound for each backward step of the clock
309	(steps add up, §7): a session that expired just before a
310	restart or a failover can resolve again for at most `CLOCK_TOLERANCE` (60 s)
311	plus the time since the data directory last recorded a time, and never when the
312	clocks are right. Expiry is *lazy*: a row is invisible the moment `now` passes
313	`expires_at` — a built-in daily cron sweeps the dead rows for hygiene, but
314	resolution never waits on it.
315	
316	`App::handle` is the one seam outside the kernel's clock: it judges at
317	`WallTime::UNIX_EPOCH`, so a session it mints expires `session_ttl` after 1970
318	and reads as expired the moment a kernel presents it. When a kernel will present
319	the credential, mint it through the kernel, or call `app.handle_at(request,
320	clock.wall())` with the node's clock.
321	
322	```rust
323	use charpente::auth::{ApiKey, Via};
324	use charpente::http::{ApiError, App, AppConfig, Ctx};
325	use charpente::prod::{ProdDisk, ProdEntropy};
326	use charpente::{Id, Schema, Tx, View, route, routes};
327	
328	// A login trades a credential the ladder has already verified, an API key or
329	// an OIDC token (below), for a session in the same subject. It refuses a
330	// session: a session that could buy a session would renew itself past its TTL
331	// and outlive its holder's logout. A session bought with a key still outlives a
332	// revoke of that key (above). charpente has no password check, so never mint
333	// for a subject a request body names: that lets anyone log in as anyone. The
334	// first credential comes from something the app trusts, such as an IdP or a
335	// signup route that mints a key for a subject it has just created.
336	#[route(POST "/login", auth)]
337	fn login(tx: &mut Tx, ctx: &Ctx) -> Result<String, ApiError> {
338	    let principal = ctx.principal().expect("auth route");
339	    if matches!(principal.via(), Via::Session(_)) {
340	        return Err(ApiError::BadRequest(
341	            "log in with an API key or an OIDC token, not a session".to_string(),
342	        ));
343	    }
344	    let subject = principal.subject().to_string();
345	    Ok(ctx.create_session(tx, subject))
346	}
347	
348	#[route(GET "/me", auth)]
349	fn whoami(tx: &mut Tx, ctx: &Ctx) -> Result<String, ApiError> {
350	    let _ = tx;
351	    Ok(ctx
352	        .principal()
353	        .expect("auth routes always have a principal")
354	        .subject()
355	        .to_string())
356	}
357	
358	#[route(POST "/logout", auth)]
359	fn logout(tx: &mut Tx, ctx: &Ctx) -> Result<&'static str, ApiError> {
360	    ctx.revoke(tx);
361	    Ok("bye")
362	}
363	
364	// Mint an API key for the caller's own subject; revoke by deleting the row.
365	#[route(POST "/keys", auth)]
366	fn mint_key(tx: &mut Tx, ctx: &Ctx) -> Result<String, ApiError> {
367	    let subject = ctx.principal().expect("auth route").subject().to_string();
368	    Ok(ctx.create_api_key(tx, subject))
369	}
370	
371	// `ApiKey` is a global table, so any id reaches any subject's key. Revoke only
372	// the caller's own, and answer another subject's key as absent.
373	#[route(DELETE "/keys/:id", auth)]
374	fn revoke_key(tx: &mut Tx, id: Id<ApiKey>, ctx: &Ctx) -> Result<&'static str, ApiError> {
375	    let caller = ctx.principal().expect("auth route").subject();
376	    match tx.get(id)? {
377	        Some(key) if key.subject == caller => {
378	            tx.delete::<ApiKey>(id);
379	            Ok("revoked")
380	        }
381	        _ => Err(ApiError::NotFound),
382	    }
383	}
384	
385	fn build_app(data_dir: &str) -> std::io::Result<App> {
386	    Ok(App::open(
387	        Box::new(ProdDisk::new(data_dir)?),
388	        Schema::new(), // Session and ApiKey are registered by App::open itself
389	        Box::new(ProdEntropy::new()?),
390	        AppConfig::default(),
391	    )?
392	    .mount(routes![login, whoami, logout, mint_key, revoke_key]))
393	}

396	### OIDC (static JWKS)
397	
398	`App::with_oidc` mounts a verifier for RS256-signed JWTs against a static
399	JWKS — pure signature-and-claims checking on the kernel thread, no network
400	fetch (dynamic JWKS is a later milestone). Configure it with the IdP's
401	issuer, your audience, and the JWKS document verbatim:
402	
403	```rust
404	use charpente::auth::OidcConfig;
405	use charpente::http::App;
406	
407	fn mount_oidc(app: App) -> App {
408	    app.with_oidc(OidcConfig {
409	        issuer: "https://idp.example.com".to_string(),
410	        audience: "my-charpente-api".to_string(),
411	        // The IdP's JWKS document, verbatim — one or more RSA keys.
412	        jwks_json: r#"{"keys":[{"kty":"RSA","kid":"k1","n":"0vx7...","e":"AQAB"}]}"#.to_string(),
413	    })
414	}
415	```
416	
417	The JWKS is parsed once, at mount — a malformed document or an unusable key
418	panics *then*, naming the offending key and the fix, never at request time
419	(`<kid>` is the key's `kid`, or its position when absent):
420	
421	```text
422	OidcConfig::jwks_json is not valid JSON: <detail> — pass the IdP's JWKS document verbatim (a {"keys": [...]} object)
423	OidcConfig::jwks_json has no keys — the "keys" array is empty; add at least one RSA key
424	OIDC JWKS key <kid> has kty "EC" — only "RSA" is supported in v1; remove non-RSA keys from the JWKS
425	OIDC JWKS key <kid> has alg "RS384" — only "RS256" is supported; fix or remove the key's "alg" field
426	OIDC JWKS key <kid> is invalid: modulus "n" is not valid base64url: <detail>
427	```
428	
429	A verified token yields a `Principal` whose `via()` is `Via::Oidc` and whose
430	`subject()` is the token's `sub` claim — ephemeral, no row, nothing to revoke
431	but a short `exp`. `exp`/`nbf` (Unix seconds) are checked against the node's
432	wall clock with a 60-second skew tolerance (`CLOCK_TOLERANCE`). Each failed
433	check is its own named 401 (the
434	`iss`/`aud` ones name presented-vs-configured; `<presented>`/`<configured>`
435	are the actual values):
436	
437	<!-- pinned -->
438	```text
439	malformed OIDC token — expected "header.payload.signature" (three dot-separated segments); got 2 segment(s)
440	unsupported OIDC token alg "HS256" — only "RS256" is verified; mint the token with an RS256-signed key
441	OIDC token signature does not verify against any configured JWKS key — the token was not issued by a trusted key; obtain a new one
442	OIDC token expired — its "exp" claim is in the past; obtain a new one
443	OIDC token is not yet valid — its "nbf" claim is in the future; wait or mint a fresh token
444	OIDC token has issuer "<presented>" but this server is configured for issuer "<configured>" — mint the token against the configured issuer or fix OidcConfig::issuer
445	OIDC token has audience "<presented>" but this server is configured for audience "<configured>" — mint the token for the configured audience or fix OidcConfig::audience
446	```
447	
448	The replication port has its own peer-authentication secret, unrelated to
449	this request-side auth — see §10.
450	
451	### A route's stance, and who reaches a tenant
452	
453	Every route declares one of three stances after its path, and the stance decides what
454	`tx.scope::<Org>(org, ctx)?` (§16) does for each caller:
455	
456	| Stance | Who reaches the handler | What the scope line does |
457	|---|---|---|
458	| `auth` | a caller with a credential | runs `Org::authorize` once, about that principal |
459	| `public` | every caller | with a credential, the same; with none, the 401 below |
460	| `public(Org)` | every caller | admits every caller into the `Org` tenant it names; no `authorize` runs |
461	
462	The scope line applies three rules, in order:
463	
464	1. If the route declared `public(S)` for this very `S`, the scope is admitted by that
465	   declaration. No `authorize` runs, whoever the caller is. A credentialed caller whose
466	   membership check would refuse is admitted too: the route said every caller may act
467	   here.
468	2. Otherwise, with a principal present, `S::authorize` runs once, about that principal,
469	   and its `Err` is the handler's `Err`.
470	3. Otherwise the caller has no credential, and the request is answered 401, by name.
471	   Nothing below the scope line runs.
472	
473	An `auth` request never reaches rule 3, because the `auth` gate refused the anonymous caller
474	before your handler ran. So your `authorize` is only ever asked about a real principal. A
475	`public(Org)` route that opens a *different* scope type gets rules 2 and 3 for it, and the
476	401 names `public(Org)` as the route's stance.
477	
478	The rule-3 401, for a `POST /orgs/:org/incidents` declared plain `public`:
479	
480	<!-- pinned -->
481	```text
482	authentication required — `POST /orgs/:org/incidents` is declared `public` and opened the tenant scope `Org` for a caller with no credential; only a route declared `public(Org)` admits one. Send "Authorization: Bearer <token>" or the charpente_session cookie, or, if every caller may act inside this tenant here, declare `public(Org)` in place of `public` in this route's `#[route(…)]` attribute, keeping its other flags. A tenant type is named here by its NAME; name the type in the attribute: `Org` is the tenant type `<path>`
483	```
484	
485	The site is the word the route was declared with (`SSE` for a stream) and its pattern;
486	the scope is its tenant type's `NAME` (§16). Both fixes are there: the caller's (send a credential)
487	and the author's (declare the tenant public, if that really is the policy). The author's
488	names the change to make where the stance is written and restates no attribute, so a route's
489	other flags, `cross_tenant` or `emits(…)`, stay as they are. A `NAME` need not be how your
490	source spells the type (`billing::Org` and `crm::Org` take two), so the text ends with each
491	named type's `std::any::type_name` (`<path>` above), which says which type to write in the
492	attribute. On a route declared `public(BillingOrg)` that opened `CrmOrg`, it names both. §16's
493	"Who reaches a tenant" shows the three side by side.
494	
495	### `ApiError` and status mapping
496	
497	A handler rejects with `ApiError`; `From<io::Error> for ApiError` converts
498	to `Internal`, so `?` works on `tx` reads exactly like it does inside a
499	plain transaction (§4). Every response body is a JSON envelope
500	`{"error": "<message>"}` except a 200, which is the handler's own returned
501	value:
502	
503	- `BadRequest(String)` → 400. What `FromParam`/JSON-body decoding produce
504	  (below), or your own rejection.
505	- The 401 family → 401. Auth rejections, produced before your handler runs
506	  (the resolution ladder, above): `Unauthorized` (no credential),
507	  `UnrecognizedCredential`, `SessionExpired`, and `Oidc(..)` (one per failed
508	  OIDC check); and, at the scope line inside it, `AnonymousScope(..)`, a
509	  scope line reached with no credential on a route that did not declare that
510	  tenant public (above). Their exact, named texts are in the auth and stance
511	  sections above — you rarely construct these yourself; the `auth` gate, the
512	  ladder and `tx.scope` emit them.
513	- `NotFound` → 404. Fixed message `"not found"` — the same text an
514	  unmatched path gets from the router directly.
515	- `Internal(String)` → 500. Carries `e.to_string()` when it arrived via
516	  `?`, or your own message.
517	
518	There is no 403. To refuse a caller the ladder did authenticate (an `authorize`
519	that says no, a row the caller does not own), pick one of the variants above:
520	this guide's membership checks answer `BadRequest` naming the tenant, and
521	`revoke_key` above answers `NotFound`, which does not say whether the row exists.
522	
523	Two more statuses never go through `ApiError` at all: an unmatched path is
524	404 ("not found") and a matched path with the wrong method is 405 ("method
525	not allowed for this path") — both produced by the router before a
526	transaction ever opens, so nothing was attempted, let alone written.
527	
528	A path param that doesn't parse is a named 400 — e.g. a non-numeric `:id`
529	against a `u64` argument: `"path parameter :id must be an unsigned integer
530	— got \"abc\""`. A missing or malformed JSON body is a named 400 too, e.g.
531	`"this route requires a JSON body of type NoteBody"` (empty body) or
532	`"invalid JSON body for NoteBody: <serde_json's own message>"`.
533	
534	### The 1 MiB body cap
535	
536	`AppConfig::body_cap` (default `1 << 20` — 1,048,576 bytes, 1 MiB) fences
537	the request body — and, transitively, `Db::transact`'s 16 MiB record-size
538	assert (§4) from ever seeing raw network input. It is enforced in two
539	places:
540	
541	- In production, `charpente::serve` enforces it at the wire — a
542	  length-limited body read rejects an oversized body *before* the request
543	  is even routed, so it applies uniformly to every path, matched or not.
544	  With a 64-byte cap and a 65-byte body, the wire's 413 reads exactly:
545	  `"request body exceeds the 64-byte cap — raise AppConfig.body_cap or
546	  send less"`.
547	- Inside the kernel (`App::handle` — what the sim drives directly, and
548	  what `serve` calls after decoding), the same cap is checked again, but
549	  only **after** routing succeeds: an oversized body sent to an unmatched
550	  path 404s, not 413, since the router runs first. With the same 64/65
551	  numbers, this 413 reads: `"request body is 65 bytes but the cap is 64 —
552	  raise AppConfig.body_cap or send less"`.
553	
554	Apps exercised only through `App::handle` (sim tests, and anything built
555	directly against the kernel) only ever see the second message — the wire
556	check is production-only edge behavior.
557	
558	```rust
559	use charpente::http::AppConfig;
560	
561	fn small_cap_config() -> AppConfig {
562	    AppConfig {
563	        body_cap: 4096,
564	        ..AppConfig::default()
565	    }
566	}
567	```
568	
569	### Ack-after-durable
570	
571	A 200 is emitted only once the handler's transaction has returned `Ok` —
572	which, per §4, only happens after that transaction's one log record has
573	synced to disk. There is no path that returns a 200 before durability.
574	
575	The other statuses fall out of §4's `TxError` split precisely:
576	`ApiError`-mapped statuses (400/401/404, and a handler-level 500 from
577	`Internal`/`?`) are `TxError::App(e)` — the transaction aborted, **nothing
578	was written**, so there is nothing ambiguous about them. The remaining
579	case, `TxError::Io` — a platform failure appending or syncing the record
580	itself, outside the handler's own logic — is genuinely unknown: the record
581	may already be durable. It surfaces as its own 500, with a message that
582	says so instead of guessing: `"internal storage failure — the request may
583	or may not have committed; retry after the server recovers: {e}"`.
584	
585	**Since group commit, one request's failure can be another request's 500 —
586	and a 500 can name a write that committed.** The kernel commits everything
587	it drained in one loop iteration under a single fsync, up to 64 requests.
588	An append or sync failure still commits no record in the batch — but "acks
589	nothing" would overstate it, and the fourth bullet below is the reason: a
590	request that ran ahead of every staged record observed only committed state,
591	so it is not invalidated and keeps its 200. What such a failure invalidates is
592	every request from the first staged record onward. The case with no analogue in
593	a one-at-a-time kernel is a failure to
594	*apply* a record after the batch has already synced: at that point every
595	record in the batch is on disk and none of them is in the store, because the
596	store takes a whole batch in one transaction — an apply failure anywhere rolls
597	every record in it back rather than leaving a prefix behind. So the platform
598	answers 500 to every request that staged a record in that batch, and to every
599	request that *read* one of those records through the batch's shared view. A
600	request that ran ahead of every staged record still keeps its 200: it only ever
601	observed committed state. Read it as the
602	rule above says: **a 500 never promises rejection, only the absence of
603	confirmation.** What that means in practice:
604	
605	- **The write may be committed.** After an apply failure every record in the
606	  batch is durable and applies when the process restarts. The client was told
607	  "unknown"; the durable answer turns out to be "yes". Plan for it — this is
608	  a named contract, not an edge case you are expected to discover.
609	- **The reverse remains impossible.** No 200 is ever emitted for something
610	  that is not durable. Every reply in a batch is held until the commit
611	  returns, so the ack still follows the sync.
612	- **The node stops.** An apply failure means machine state no longer matches
613	  the log, so the engine poisons and the kernel stops rather than serving on
614	  (§9's "Poisoned-engine errors"). The fix is a restart, which replays the
615	  WAL and is idempotent.
616	- **A request that ran ahead of the failure keeps its answer.** The rule is
617	  what a request *saw*, not where it sat in the batch: a read that only ever
618	  observed committed state is not invalidated by a later sibling's failure.
619	
620	Operationally this is the same epistemic class as any `TxError::Io`, so
621	handle it the same way: a blind retry is safe only where the operation is
622	idempotent in your own schema — the platform does not dedupe for you, and
623	§6 is explicit that an `enqueue_keyed` key is carried, not indexed. After the
624	restart, the honest way to learn what happened is to read the state back
625	rather than infer it from the status code.
626	
627	### Starting the server
628	
629	`charpente::serve::serve(addr: &str, app: App) -> io::Result<Server>` spawns
630	the kernel (requests, due jobs, and cron ticks — §6 and §7 ride the same
631	loop) on one thread and the hyper listener on another, then returns as soon
632	as both are up — it does not block. `Server::wait` blocks until the kernel
633	stops and returns the exit code the process should end with. A kernel that
634	stopped — on a platform IO failure or a named refusal, each printed on
635	stderr with its fix — must end the process, or a supervisor sees a live
636	process answering every request 500 and never restarts it.
637	
638	```rust
639	use charpente::core::table::Id;
640	use charpente::http::{ApiError, App, AppConfig};
641	use charpente::prod::{ProdDisk, ProdEntropy};
642	use charpente::{Schema, Tx, View, Wire, route, routes, table};
643	use serde::Deserialize;
644	
645	#[table(global)]
646	struct Note {
647	    id: Id<Note>,
648	    text: String,
649	}
650	
651	#[derive(Wire, Deserialize)]
652	struct NoteBody {
653	    text: String,
654	}
655	
656	#[route(POST "/notes/:id", public)]
657	fn create_note(tx: &mut Tx, id: Id<Note>, body: NoteBody) -> Result<Id<Note>, ApiError> {
658	    tx.put(&Note {
659	        id,
660	        text: body.text,
661	    });
662	    Ok(id)
663	}
664	
665	#[route(GET "/notes/:id", public)]
666	fn get_note(tx: &mut Tx, id: Id<Note>) -> Result<String, ApiError> {
667	    Ok(tx.get(id)?.ok_or(ApiError::NotFound)?.text)
668	}
669	
670	fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
671	    let app = App::open(
672	        Box::new(ProdDisk::new("./data")?),
673	        Schema::new().table::<Note>(),
674	        Box::new(ProdEntropy::new()?),
675	        AppConfig::default(),
676	    )?
677	    .mount(routes![create_note, get_note]);
678	
679	    let server = charpente::serve::serve("0.0.0.0:8080", app)?;
680	    // `serve` returned once the listener was up; `wait` blocks until the
681	    // kernel stops. Exiting with its code is what lets a supervisor see a
682	    // stopped kernel and restart it (no graceful shutdown in v0).
683	    std::process::exit(server.wait());
684	}
685	```
686	
687	An app whose jobs call outside services (§6) gets its HTTP client from the
688	server. `serve(addr, app)` is `serve_with(addr, app,
689	OutboundOptions::default())`, and `serve_with(addr: &str, app: App, outbound:
690	OutboundOptions) -> io::Result<Server>` takes the operator's settings:
691	`OutboundOptions { bases, cas }` (both `Vec`s, `Default` empty). `bases`
692	holds `(host, base)` pairs that move where a declared host is reached
693	(`--outbound-base`), and `cas` holds paths of PEM CA certificates to trust
694	beside the built-in roots (`--outbound-ca`). `launch` (§13) fills both from
695	its flags.
696	
697	```rust
698	use charpente::http::App;
699	use charpente::serve::{OutboundOptions, Server, serve_with};
700	
701	fn serve_against_a_local_fake(app: App) -> std::io::Result<Server> {
702	    serve_with(
703	        "127.0.0.1:8080",
704	        app,
705	        OutboundOptions {
706	            bases: vec![("pay.test".into(), "https://127.0.0.1:8443".into())],
707	            cas: vec!["./tls/ca.pem".into()],
708	        },
709	    )
710	}
711	```
712	
713	The client is built before the listener is bound, reading each credential
714	variable once, so a setup refusal (an unset credential, a bad base or CA
715	file) returns an `Err` holding a `Refusal`, with nothing running. An app
716	whose jobs call nothing gets no client and no thread for one, but its
717	settings are still checked: any base is refused, since it names a host no job
718	calls, and each CA file is read, so a bad one refuses the start.
719	`serve_replicated`, `backup` and `archive` build the client the same way,
720	with no operator settings, so they reach only hosts whose certificates chain
721	to a public CA, at their real addresses.
722	
723	On the command line of an app built on `charpente::launch` (§13), the two
724	settings are the serve form's flags, each repeatable for a different `HOST` or
725	`PATH`:
726	
727	- `--outbound-base HOST=URL` reaches the declared host `HOST` at `URL`
728	  instead of `https://HOST:443`. `URL` is a scheme, an IP address or
729	  `localhost`, and an optional port (`https://127.0.0.1:8443`,
730	  `https://[::1]:8443`), with no path. Only the address moves: TLS still
731	  verifies `HOST`, and the request's `host` header still names it, so a
732	  stand-in remote must present a certificate for `HOST` that a trusted CA
733	  issued. That is why a DNS name is refused as a base: it would read as
734	  moving the name, which never moves. Plain `http://` is accepted only for a
735	  loopback address. A `HOST` no mounted job calls is refused, naming the
736	  hosts the app does call, or saying it calls none.
737	- `--outbound-ca PATH` trusts the PEM CA certificates in `PATH`, for every
738	  host, beside Mozilla's roots. A file that cannot be read or holds no
739	  certificate refuses the start, even for an app that calls no host.
740	
741	A flag that is unknown, has no value, names a `HOST` or a `PATH` a second
742	time, or (for `--outbound-base`) is not `HOST=URL` exits 2 with `launch`'s
743	usage before the data directory is touched; anything `serve_with` refuses
744	prints `charpente refused to start: <the refusal>` and exits 1 (§13).
745	
746	### What `#[route]` rejects
747	
748	Every rejection is a compile error naming the contract and the fix. The
749	first is the one every route meets once:
750	
751	<!-- pinned -->
752	```text
753	`<handler>` declares neither `auth` nor `public` — a route says which callers reach it. Add one of these to the flags of its `#[route(<method> "<path>", …)]`, keeping any it already has: `auth` to require a principal (`ctx.principal()` is `Some`), `public` to serve anonymous callers, or `public(Org)` to also let every caller act inside the `Org` tenant it opens. None is the default.
754	`auth` and `public` on one route — a route is one or the other; drop one
755	`public` given twice — write it once
756	```
757	
758	The rest are about the handler's shape:
759	
760	```rust,ignore
761	// first argument isn't named `tx`
762	#[route(GET "/ping", public)]
763	fn ping(ctx: &Ctx) -> Result<&'static str, ApiError> {
764	    Ok("pong")
765	}
766	// "a #[route] handler's first argument must be `tx: &mut Tx` — `ping` is
767	//  missing it"
768	
769	// argument count doesn't match the :param count
770	#[route(GET "/notes/:id", public)]
771	fn get_note(tx: &mut Tx) -> Result<String, ApiError> {
772	    Ok(String::new())
773	}
774	// "`get_note` takes 0 argument(s) after `tx` (excluding `ctx`) but the path
775	//  \"/notes/:id\" has 1 :param(s) — write one argument per :param (same
776	//  name, path order) plus at most one JSON body argument"
777	
778	// argument name doesn't match the :param name
779	#[route(GET "/notes/:id", public)]
780	fn get_note(tx: &mut Tx, key: u64) -> Result<String, ApiError> {
781	    Ok(String::new())
782	}
783	// "this argument must be named `id` to match :id in \"/notes/:id\" — got
784	//  `key`"
785	
786	// route path isn't a string literal, or doesn't start with '/', or names
787	// an unknown method — each fails at the same macro-argument-parsing step
788	// with its own named message (e.g. "route path must start with '/' — got
789	// \"notes\"", "unknown method PUSH — one of GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, SSE").
790	```
791	
792	## 6. Jobs
793	
794	Jobs ride the same kernel loop as HTTP requests (§5's `charpente::serve`
795	starts it): mounting a job or a schedule needs no separate worker process
796	or entry point.

798	### `#[job]` and its retry policy
799	
800	`#[job]` derives a job payload's `Codec`, its `NAME`, its `FINGERPRINT`,
801	and the `JobEntry` glue `jobs![...]` collects — the same shape `#[table]`
