is the whole surface — the sim drives `handle` directly, and
`charpente::serve` is what feeds it from real hyper traffic in production.
Every request that reaches a matched route runs inside exactly one
transaction: routing runs first (an unmatched request never opens one),
then the session lookup and your handler run inside the same `db.transact`
call covered in §4.

### The `#[route]` argument convention

`#[route(METHOD "/path/:param", ...)]` goes on a free function (`METHOD` is
one of `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `SSE`; exactly one of `, auth`,
`, public` or `, public(Org)` follows the path — a route says which callers
reach it, and `public(Org)` adds that every caller may act inside the `Org`
tenant it opens (see "A route's stance" below); a route that says none is a
compile error naming all three; `auth` is covered under Sessions below). The
macro checks the
function's argument list against the path and emits the glue that extracts,
decodes, and dispatches to it:

- The first argument must be named exactly `tx`, typed `&mut Tx`.
- Then one argument per `:param` in the path, **in path order**, each named
  exactly like its param (`:id` needs an argument named `id`). Its type
  must implement **both** `FromParam` (parses the path segment; a bad one
  fails as a named 400, not a panic) **and** `Wire` (§13 — the client needs
  a schema for it too). `String` and `Id<T>` (any `T`) satisfy both. `u64`
  implements `FromParam` but not `Wire` — a bare `u64` path param is a
  compile error naming the fix (`Id<T>` for a row id, or `WireU64`); use
  `Id<T>` for a row id.
- Then at most one JSON body argument, of any type that is both an owned
  deserializable AND `Wire` (`serde::de::DeserializeOwned + Wire` — the
  glue's actual bound); a type borrowing from the input won't compile, and
  neither will one missing `#[derive(Wire)]`.
- Then, optionally, a trailing argument named exactly `ctx`, typed `&Ctx`
  (session access — see Sessions below). `Ctx` borrows from the request's
  group (`Ctx<'g>`), and `&Ctx` elides that, so a handler never names it. A
  helper that returns something borrowed out of a `Ctx` must say which
  borrow: `fn subject_of<'c>(ctx: &'c Ctx) -> Option<&'c str>`. Left elided,
  it is `error[E0106]: missing lifetime specifier`.

The handler returns `Result<T, ApiError>` where `T: serde::Serialize + Wire`
— the `Result<_, _>` shape itself is enforced too, and named (a bare return
value is a compile error naming the fix, `-> Result<YourResponseType,
ApiError>`); on `Ok`, the glue emits `Response::json(200, &value)`.

```rust
use charpente::core::table::Id;
use charpente::http::{ApiError, App, AppConfig, Ctx};
use charpente::prod::{ProdDisk, ProdEntropy};
use charpente::{Schema, Tx, View, Wire, route, routes, table};
use serde::Deserialize;

#[table(global)]
struct Note {
    id: Id<Note>,
    text: String,
}

// A route's request body must be `Wire` too (§13) — `#[derive(Wire)]` sits
// alongside `Deserialize`, one for the schema, one for the actual parse.
#[derive(Wire, Deserialize)]
struct NoteBody {
    text: String,
}

// tx, then :id (named `id`, path order), then the JSON body, then `ctx`. A
// path param is a wire position too, so it is `Id<Note>`, not a bare `u64`.
#[route(POST "/notes/:id", public)]
fn create_note(tx: &mut Tx, id: Id<Note>, body: NoteBody, ctx: &Ctx) -> Result<Id<Note>, ApiError> {
    let _ = ctx; // available; this route just doesn't need a session
    tx.put(&Note {
        id,
        text: body.text,
    });
    Ok(id)
}

#[route(GET "/notes/:id", public)]
fn get_note(tx: &mut Tx, id: Id<Note>) -> Result<String, ApiError> {
    Ok(tx.get(id)?.ok_or(ApiError::NotFound)?.text)
}

fn build_app(data_dir: &str) -> std::io::Result<App> {
    Ok(App::open(
        Box::new(ProdDisk::new(data_dir)?),
        Schema::new().table::<Note>(),
        Box::new(ProdEntropy::new()?),
        AppConfig::default(),
    )?
    .mount(routes![create_note, get_note]))
}
```

`routes![...]` accepts path-qualified handlers too, not just bare
identifiers in scope — `routes![handlers::create_note]` works exactly like
`routes![create_note]` after `use handlers::create_note;`.

`Request`'s shape (what a handler ultimately runs against, one layer down):
`method: Method`, `path: String`, `query: BTreeMap<String, String>`,
`headers: BTreeMap<String, String>` (keys lowercased), `body: Vec<u8>`.
`query` is parsed from the URL's `?...` suffix at construction; a plain
`#[route]` handler still has no argument-convention access to it (only
`#[route(SSE ...)]`'s platform-extracted resume cursor reads it today).

### Returning rows from a route: storage shape vs. wire shape

A handler's return type only needs `T: serde::Serialize + Wire` (above) —
nothing requires `T` to be a `#[table]` row, and `#[table]` does not derive
`Serialize` or `Wire` for you: a row's storage shape (`Id<T>`'s own `Codec`, §2) and
its wire shape are separate concerns on purpose, kept apart even though
`Id<T>` also implements `Serialize`/`Deserialize` — as a decimal string,
never a JSON number, because `u64` values above 2^53 lose precision
silently in JavaScript clients.

The fix is the one every other example in this guide already uses without
saying so: convert to a plain response type first. `Id<T>` belongs directly
in that view type — there's no need to unwrap it to a bare `u64` with
`.raw()` to make it serializable.

```rust
use charpente::http::{ApiError, App, AppConfig};
use charpente::prod::{ProdDisk, ProdEntropy};
use charpente::{Id, Schema, Tx, View, Wire, route, routes, table};
use serde::Serialize;

#[table(global)]
struct Note {
    id: Id<Note>,
    text: String,
}

/// The wire shape: `Id<Note>` crosses as a decimal string, so it appears
/// directly here — no `.raw()` unwrap, no separate id type. `#[derive(Wire)]`
/// is what lets this type appear in a route's response schema (§13).
#[derive(Wire, Serialize)]
struct NoteView {
    id: Id<Note>,
    text: String,
}

impl From<Note> for NoteView {
    fn from(row: Note) -> Self {
        NoteView {
            id: row.id,
            text: row.text,
        }
    }
}

#[route(GET "/notes/:id", public)]
fn get_note(tx: &mut Tx, id: Id<Note>) -> Result<NoteView, ApiError> {
    Ok(tx.get(id)?.ok_or(ApiError::NotFound)?.into())
}

fn build_app(data_dir: &str) -> std::io::Result<App> {
    Ok(App::open(
        Box::new(ProdDisk::new(data_dir)?),
        Schema::new().table::<Note>(),
        Box::new(ProdEntropy::new()?),
        AppConfig::default(),
    )?
    .mount(routes![get_note]))
}
```

Storage rows and wire responses are different concerns regardless of the
serde question — this DTO conversion is good hygiene even for a `Codec`
field type that happens to also implement `Serialize`.

### Mounting routes, and the conflict panic

`App::open(...)` returns the platform-registered `App`; `.mount(routes![...])`
adds a batch of routes, checking every new route against every route already
mounted. Two routes with the **same method and the same shape** — the same
sequence of literal-vs-`:param` segments, so both could match one real path
— panic at mount time, not at request time:

```rust
use charpente::http::{ApiError, App};
use charpente::{Id, Tx, route, routes, table};

#[table(global)]
struct Note {
    id: Id<Note>,
}

// A path param is a wire position too — `Id<Note>`, not a bare `u64`.
#[route(GET "/notes/:id", public)]
fn by_id(tx: &mut Tx, id: Id<Note>) -> Result<Id<Note>, ApiError> {
    let _ = tx;
    Ok(id)
}

#[route(GET "/notes/:key", public)]
fn by_key(tx: &mut Tx, key: String) -> Result<String, ApiError> {
    let _ = tx;
    Ok(key)
}

// `/notes/:id` and `/notes/:key` are the same shape under the same method —
// both could match `GET /notes/42` — so mounting both panics with:
// "route conflict: GET /notes/:key (fn by_key) collides with GET
//  /notes/:id (fn by_id) — two routes with the same method and shape can
//  both match one path; change one pattern"
fn mount_conflicting(app: App) -> App {
    app.mount(routes![by_id, by_key])
}
```

A literal segment beats a `:param` at the same position instead of
conflicting — `/notes/all` and `/notes/:id` can coexist, and a request for
`/notes/all` always prefers the literal route.

### Auth: sessions, API keys, and the resolution ladder

`App::open` registers two platform tables of its own alongside yours —
`Session` (`id: Id<Session>`, `#[index] token_hash: String`, `subject:
String`, `expires_at: WallTime`) and `ApiKey` (`id: Id<ApiKey>`, `#[index]
key_hash: String`, `subject: String`, `created_at: WallTime`) — both inside the
commit point, so a login or a minted key is a durable, replicated
transaction like any other. **Only the hash is ever stored:**
`token_hash`/`key_hash` are lowercase-hex SHA-256 of the raw credential; the
raw string exists only in the response that mints it and never reaches disk
(a sim property scans every durable file in the run and proves it).

Every request gets a `Ctx`, built inside the same transaction as your
handler, carrying:

- `ctx.principal() -> Option<&Principal>` — the authenticated identity, if
  any. `principal.subject()` is the subject the credential was minted for,
  and `principal.via()` names which rung authenticated it
  (`Via::Session(id)`, `Via::ApiKey(id)`, or `Via::Oidc`; `charpente::auth::Via`, whose
  `id` is the matched row's `Id<Session>` or `Id<ApiKey>`). Read the subject
  from here on any `auth` route, whatever the credential kind. A `Principal`
  is read-only to your code: its fields are private, so the only principals
  are the ones the ladder produced. It is not `Clone` either, so the only one
  your code holds is the `&Principal` this request's `Ctx` lends, which ends
  with the request: no principal can be parked in a `static` for a later
  request to hand `tx.open_scope`. So `Tenant::authorize` can trust the one
  it is handed: the ladder produced it, for the request that is asking.
- `ctx.session() -> Option<&Session>` — a compatibility accessor: the
  `Session` row, but only when the principal authenticated `via` a session
  (bearer or cookie); `None` for an API-key or OIDC principal.
- `ctx.create_session(tx, subject) -> String` — inserts a `Session` row and
  returns its raw token (a login). `expires_at` is this request's wall-clock
  `now` plus `AppConfig::session_ttl` (default 30 days).
- `ctx.create_api_key(tx, subject) -> String` — inserts an `ApiKey` row and
  returns the raw key: `"ck_"` + 64 hex chars (the prefix makes a leaked key
  grep-able for scanners). Revoke a key by deleting its row —
  `tx.delete::<ApiKey>(id)`, an ordinary write — after checking that the row's
  `subject` is the caller's: an id names a key, it does not show the caller holds
  it (`revoke_key` below). Revoking a key ends that key alone: a session or key
  minted by a request that presented it stays live.
- `ctx.revoke(tx)` — deletes the current session (logout); a no-op without
  one.

One credential mint per request, of either kind. The raw token/key is 32
entropy bytes drawn once *before* the transaction starts, so
`create_session` and `create_api_key` share a single mint budget — calling
either a second time in one request panics: "Ctx::create_session/create_api_key
called twice in one request — one credential mint per request".

A `Session`'s or `ApiKey`'s `id` is the first 64 bits of that same draw: the
raw token's first 16 hex characters (after `ck_` for a key). The ladder finds a
row by the hash of the whole raw token, and the other 192 bits stay secret, so
showing a holder the id of their own credential (to revoke it, say) is fine.
Show it to no one else: each id is a quarter of a credential.

**The resolution ladder.** Before your handler runs, the platform turns the
request's credential into a `Principal`, in this order:

1. `Authorization: Bearer <t>` where `<t>` contains exactly two `.` — judged
   as a JWT and OIDC-verified (below). With no verifier mounted, a JWT-shaped
   bearer is an unrecognized credential, never a fall-through to the hash
   path.
2. Any other bearer — SHA-256'd and matched against the `ApiKey` index, then
   the `Session` index (a session past its `expires_at` is treated as
   absent).
3. A `charpente_session=<t>` cookie — the same hash path as 2. Only a
   `Bearer` header is ever OIDC-verified; a cookie value that happens to
   contain two dots still goes down the hash path.
4. Nothing presented — `principal` is `None`.

`#[route(METHOD "/path", auth)]` rejects the request before your handler runs
when the principal is `None`. With `public`, the route always runs and
`ctx.principal()` is whatever the ladder resolved (possibly `None`) — though a
handler that then opens a tenant scope with no principal gets a 401 of its
own, unless the route declared `public(Org)` (below) — but a
*presented* credential is still resolved and rejected even on a public
route, so a garbage bearer never reaches a handler.

The 401s are named and fixed — copy these verbatim if you assert against
them:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
authentication required — send "Authorization: Bearer <token>" or the charpente_session cookie
unrecognized credential — it may have been revoked; obtain a new one
session expired — log in again
```

The first fires when an `auth` route saw no credential; the second for a
bearer/cookie that matched no live row (garbage, revoked, or a JWT-shaped
bearer with no OIDC configured); the third for a session past its TTL. Expiry
is judged on wall time: `expires_at` is a `WallTime` (UTC nanoseconds since the
Unix epoch, `charpente::core::io::WallTime`), and under the kernel each
request's `now` is the node's `Clock::wall` reading, held so that it never runs
backwards (§7, "Clock errors"). So a TTL means the same thing after a restart or
a failover as before it, within one bound for each backward step of the clock
(steps add up, §7): a session that expired just before a
restart or a failover can resolve again for at most `CLOCK_TOLERANCE` (60 s)
plus the time since the data directory last recorded a time, and never when the
clocks are right. Expiry is *lazy*: a row is invisible the moment `now` passes
`expires_at` — a built-in daily cron sweeps the dead rows for hygiene, but
resolution never waits on it.

`App::handle` is the one seam outside the kernel's clock: it judges at
`WallTime::UNIX_EPOCH`, so a session it mints expires `session_ttl` after 1970
and reads as expired the moment a kernel presents it. When a kernel will present
the credential, mint it through the kernel, or call `app.handle_at(request,
clock.wall())` with the node's clock.

```rust
use charpente::auth::{ApiKey, Via};
use charpente::http::{ApiError, App, AppConfig, Ctx};
use charpente::prod::{ProdDisk, ProdEntropy};
use charpente::{Id, Schema, Tx, View, route, routes};

// A login trades a credential the ladder has already verified, an API key or
// an OIDC token (below), for a session in the same subject. It refuses a
// session: a session that could buy a session would renew itself past its TTL
// and outlive its holder's logout. A session bought with a key still outlives a
// revoke of that key (above). charpente has no password check, so never mint
// for a subject a request body names: that lets anyone log in as anyone. The
// first credential comes from something the app trusts, such as an IdP or a
// signup route that mints a key for a subject it has just created.
#[route(POST "/login", auth)]
fn login(tx: &mut Tx, ctx: &Ctx) -> Result<String, ApiError> {
    let principal = ctx.principal().expect("auth route");
    if matches!(principal.via(), Via::Session(_)) {
        return Err(ApiError::BadRequest(
            "log in with an API key or an OIDC token, not a session".to_string(),
        ));
    }
    let subject = principal.subject().to_string();
    Ok(ctx.create_session(tx, subject))
}

#[route(GET "/me", auth)]
fn whoami(tx: &mut Tx, ctx: &Ctx) -> Result<String, ApiError> {
    let _ = tx;
    Ok(ctx
        .principal()
        .expect("auth routes always have a principal")
        .subject()
        .to_string())
}

#[route(POST "/logout", auth)]
fn logout(tx: &mut Tx, ctx: &Ctx) -> Result<&'static str, ApiError> {
    ctx.revoke(tx);
    Ok("bye")
}

// Mint an API key for the caller's own subject; revoke by deleting the row.
#[route(POST "/keys", auth)]
fn mint_key(tx: &mut Tx, ctx: &Ctx) -> Result<String, ApiError> {
    let subject = ctx.principal().expect("auth route").subject().to_string();
    Ok(ctx.create_api_key(tx, subject))
}

// `ApiKey` is a global table, so any id reaches any subject's key. Revoke only
// the caller's own, and answer another subject's key as absent.
#[route(DELETE "/keys/:id", auth)]
fn revoke_key(tx: &mut Tx, id: Id<ApiKey>, ctx: &Ctx) -> Result<&'static str, ApiError> {
    let caller = ctx.principal().expect("auth route").subject();
    match tx.get(id)? {
        Some(key) if key.subject == caller => {
            tx.delete::<ApiKey>(id);
            Ok("revoked")
        }
        _ => Err(ApiError::NotFound),
    }
}

fn build_app(data_dir: &str) -> std::io::Result<App> {
    Ok(App::open(
        Box::new(ProdDisk::new(data_dir)?),
        Schema::new(), // Session and ApiKey are registered by App::open itself
        Box::new(ProdEntropy::new()?),
        AppConfig::default(),
    )?
    .mount(routes![login, whoami, logout, mint_key, revoke_key]))
}
```

### OIDC (static JWKS)

`App::with_oidc` mounts a verifier for RS256-signed JWTs against a static
JWKS — pure signature-and-claims checking on the kernel thread, no network
fetch (dynamic JWKS is a later milestone). Configure it with the IdP's
issuer, your audience, and the JWKS document verbatim:

```rust
use charpente::auth::OidcConfig;
use charpente::http::App;

fn mount_oidc(app: App) -> App {
    app.with_oidc(OidcConfig {
        issuer: "https://idp.example.com".to_string(),
        audience: "my-charpente-api".to_string(),
        // The IdP's JWKS document, verbatim — one or more RSA keys.
        jwks_json: r#"{"keys":[{"kty":"RSA","kid":"k1","n":"0vx7...","e":"AQAB"}]}"#.to_string(),
    })
}
```

The JWKS is parsed once, at mount — a malformed document or an unusable key
panics *then*, naming the offending key and the fix, never at request time
(`<kid>` is the key's `kid`, or its position when absent):

```text
OidcConfig::jwks_json is not valid JSON: <detail> — pass the IdP's JWKS document verbatim (a {"keys": [...]} object)
OidcConfig::jwks_json has no keys — the "keys" array is empty; add at least one RSA key
OIDC JWKS key <kid> has kty "EC" — only "RSA" is supported in v1; remove non-RSA keys from the JWKS
OIDC JWKS key <kid> has alg "RS384" — only "RS256" is supported; fix or remove the key's "alg" field
OIDC JWKS key <kid> is invalid: modulus "n" is not valid base64url: <detail>
```

A verified token yields a `Principal` whose `via()` is `Via::Oidc` and whose
`subject()` is the token's `sub` claim — ephemeral, no row, nothing to revoke
but a short `exp`. `exp`/`nbf` (Unix seconds) are checked against the node's
wall clock with a 60-second skew tolerance (`CLOCK_TOLERANCE`). Each failed
check is its own named 401 (the
`iss`/`aud` ones name presented-vs-configured; `<presented>`/`<configured>`
are the actual values):

<!-- pinned -->
```text
malformed OIDC token — expected "header.payload.signature" (three dot-separated segments); got 2 segment(s)
unsupported OIDC token alg "HS256" — only "RS256" is verified; mint the token with an RS256-signed key
OIDC token signature does not verify against any configured JWKS key — the token was not issued by a trusted key; obtain a new one
OIDC token expired — its "exp" claim is in the past; obtain a new one
OIDC token is not yet valid — its "nbf" claim is in the future; wait or mint a fresh token
OIDC token has issuer "<presented>" but this server is configured for issuer "<configured>" — mint the token against the configured issuer or fix OidcConfig::issuer
OIDC token has audience "<presented>" but this server is configured for audience "<configured>" — mint the token for the configured audience or fix OidcConfig::audience
```

The replication port has its own peer-authentication secret, unrelated to
this request-side auth — see §10.

### A route's stance, and who reaches a tenant

Every route declares one of three stances after its path, and the stance decides what
`tx.scope::<Org>(org, ctx)?` (§16) does for each caller:

| Stance | Who reaches the handler | What the scope line does |
|---|---|---|
| `auth` | a caller with a credential | runs `Org::authorize` once, about that principal |
| `public` | every caller | with a credential, the same; with none, the 401 below |
| `public(Org)` | every caller | admits every caller into the `Org` tenant it names; no `authorize` runs |

The scope line applies three rules, in order:

1. If the route declared `public(S)` for this very `S`, the scope is admitted by that
   declaration. No `authorize` runs, whoever the caller is. A credentialed caller whose
   membership check would refuse is admitted too: the route said every caller may act
   here.
2. Otherwise, with a principal present, `S::authorize` runs once, about that principal,
   and its `Err` is the handler's `Err`.
3. Otherwise the caller has no credential, and the request is answered 401, by name.
   Nothing below the scope line runs.

An `auth` request never reaches rule 3, because the `auth` gate refused the anonymous caller
before your handler ran. So your `authorize` is only ever asked about a real principal. A
`public(Org)` route that opens a *different* scope type gets rules 2 and 3 for it, and the
401 names `public(Org)` as the route's stance.

The rule-3 401, for a `POST /orgs/:org/incidents` declared plain `public`:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
authentication required — `POST /orgs/:org/incidents` is declared `public` and opened the tenant scope `Org` for a caller with no credential; only a route declared `public(Org)` admits one. Send "Authorization: Bearer <token>" or the charpente_session cookie, or, if every caller may act inside this tenant here, declare `public(Org)` in place of `public` in this route's `#[route(…)]` attribute, keeping its other flags. A tenant type is named here by its NAME; name the type in the attribute: `Org` is the tenant type `<path>`
```

The site is the word the route was declared with (`SSE` for a stream) and its pattern;
the scope is its tenant type's `NAME` (§16). Both fixes are there: the caller's (send a credential)
and the author's (declare the tenant public, if that really is the policy). The author's
names the change to make where the stance is written and restates no attribute, so a route's
other flags, `cross_tenant` or `emits(…)`, stay as they are. A `NAME` need not be how your
source spells the type (`billing::Org` and `crm::Org` take two), so the text ends with each
named type's `std::any::type_name` (`<path>` above), which says which type to write in the
attribute. On a route declared `public(BillingOrg)` that opened `CrmOrg`, it names both. §16's
"Who reaches a tenant" shows the three side by side.

### `ApiError` and status mapping

A handler rejects with `ApiError`; `From<io::Error> for ApiError` converts
to `Internal`, so `?` works on `tx` reads exactly like it does inside a
plain transaction (§4). Every response body is a JSON envelope
`{"error": "<message>"}` except a 200, which is the handler's own returned
value:

- `BadRequest(String)` → 400. What `FromParam`/JSON-body decoding produce
  (below), or your own rejection.
- The 401 family → 401. Auth rejections, produced before your handler runs
  (the resolution ladder, above): `Unauthorized` (no credential),
  `UnrecognizedCredential`, `SessionExpired`, and `Oidc(..)` (one per failed
  OIDC check); and, at the scope line inside it, `AnonymousScope(..)`, a
  scope line reached with no credential on a route that did not declare that
  tenant public (above). Their exact, named texts are in the auth and stance
  sections above — you rarely construct these yourself; the `auth` gate, the
  ladder and `tx.scope` emit them.
- `NotFound` → 404. Fixed message `"not found"` — the same text an
  unmatched path gets from the router directly.
- `Internal(String)` → 500. Carries `e.to_string()` when it arrived via
  `?`, or your own message.

There is no 403. To refuse a caller the ladder did authenticate (an `authorize`
that says no, a row the caller does not own), pick one of the variants above:
this guide's membership checks answer `BadRequest` naming the tenant, and
`revoke_key` above answers `NotFound`, which does not say whether the row exists.

Two more statuses never go through `ApiError` at all: an unmatched path is
404 ("not found") and a matched path with the wrong method is 405 ("method
not allowed for this path") — both produced by the router before a
transaction ever opens, so nothing was attempted, let alone written.

A path param that doesn't parse is a named 400 — e.g. a non-numeric `:id`
against a `u64` argument: `"path parameter :id must be an unsigned integer
— got \"abc\""`. A missing or malformed JSON body is a named 400 too, e.g.
`"this route requires a JSON body of type NoteBody"` (empty body) or
`"invalid JSON body for NoteBody: <serde_json's own message>"`.

### The 1 MiB body cap

`AppConfig::body_cap` (default `1 << 20` — 1,048,576 bytes, 1 MiB) fences
the request body — and, transitively, `Db::transact`'s 16 MiB record-size
assert (§4) from ever seeing raw network input. It is enforced in two
places:

- In production, `charpente::serve` enforces it at the wire — a
  length-limited body read rejects an oversized body *before* the request
  is even routed, so it applies uniformly to every path, matched or not.
  With a 64-byte cap and a 65-byte body, the wire's 413 reads exactly:
  `"request body exceeds the 64-byte cap — raise AppConfig.body_cap or
  send less"`.
- Inside the kernel (`App::handle` — what the sim drives directly, and
  what `serve` calls after decoding), the same cap is checked again, but
  only **after** routing succeeds: an oversized body sent to an unmatched
  path 404s, not 413, since the router runs first. With the same 64/65
  numbers, this 413 reads: `"request body is 65 bytes but the cap is 64 —
  raise AppConfig.body_cap or send less"`.

Apps exercised only through `App::handle` (sim tests, and anything built
directly against the kernel) only ever see the second message — the wire
check is production-only edge behavior.

```rust
use charpente::http::AppConfig;

fn small_cap_config() -> AppConfig {
    AppConfig {
        body_cap: 4096,
        ..AppConfig::default()
    }
}
```

### Ack-after-durable

A 200 is emitted only once the handler's transaction has returned `Ok` —
which, per §4, only happens after that transaction's one log record has
synced to disk. There is no path that returns a 200 before durability.

The other statuses fall out of §4's `TxError` split precisely:
`ApiError`-mapped statuses (400/401/404, and a handler-level 500 from
`Internal`/`?`) are `TxError::App(e)` — the transaction aborted, **nothing
was written**, so there is nothing ambiguous about them. The remaining
case, `TxError::Io` — a platform failure appending or syncing the record
itself, outside the handler's own logic — is genuinely unknown: the record
may already be durable. It surfaces as its own 500, with a message that
says so instead of guessing: `"internal storage failure — the request may
or may not have committed; retry after the server recovers: {e}"`.

**Since group commit, one request's failure can be another request's 500 —
and a 500 can name a write that committed.** The kernel commits everything
it drained in one loop iteration under a single fsync, up to 64 requests.
An append or sync failure still commits no record in the batch — but "acks
nothing" would overstate it, and the fourth bullet below is the reason: a
request that ran ahead of every staged record observed only committed state,
so it is not invalidated and keeps its 200. What such a failure invalidates is
every request from the first staged record onward. The case with no analogue in
a one-at-a-time kernel is a failure to
*apply* a record after the batch has already synced: at that point every
record in the batch is on disk and none of them is in the store, because the
store takes a whole batch in one transaction — an apply failure anywhere rolls
every record in it back rather than leaving a prefix behind. So the platform
answers 500 to every request that staged a record in that batch, and to every
request that *read* one of those records through the batch's shared view. A
request that ran ahead of every staged record still keeps its 200: it only ever
observed committed state. Read it as the
rule above says: **a 500 never promises rejection, only the absence of
confirmation.** What that means in practice:

- **The write may be committed.** After an apply failure every record in the
  batch is durable and applies when the process restarts. The client was told
  "unknown"; the durable answer turns out to be "yes". Plan for it — this is
  a named contract, not an edge case you are expected to discover.
- **The reverse remains impossible.** No 200 is ever emitted for something
  that is not durable. Every reply in a batch is held until the commit
  returns, so the ack still follows the sync.
- **The node stops.** An apply failure means machine state no longer matches
  the log, so the engine poisons and the kernel stops rather than serving on
  (§9's "Poisoned-engine errors"). The fix is a restart, which replays the
  WAL and is idempotent.
- **A request that ran ahead of the failure keeps its answer.** The rule is
  what a request *saw*, not where it sat in the batch: a read that only ever
  observed committed state is not invalidated by a later sibling's failure.

Operationally this is the same epistemic class as any `TxError::Io`, so
handle it the same way: a blind retry is safe only where the operation is
idempotent in your own schema — the platform does not dedupe for you, and
§6 is explicit that an `enqueue_keyed` key is carried, not indexed. After the
restart, the honest way to learn what happened is to read the state back
rather than infer it from the status code.

### Starting the server

`charpente::serve::serve(addr: &str, app: App) -> io::Result<Server>` spawns
the kernel (requests, due jobs, and cron ticks — §6 and §7 ride the same
loop) on one thread and the hyper listener on another, then returns as soon
as both are up — it does not block. `Server::wait` blocks until the kernel
stops and returns the exit code the process should end with. A kernel that
stopped — on a platform IO failure or a named refusal, each printed on
stderr with its fix — must end the process, or a supervisor sees a live
process answering every request 500 and never restarts it.

```rust
use charpente::core::table::Id;
use charpente::http::{ApiError, App, AppConfig};
use charpente::prod::{ProdDisk, ProdEntropy};
use charpente::{Schema, Tx, View, Wire, route, routes, table};
use serde::Deserialize;

#[table(global)]
struct Note {
    id: Id<Note>,
    text: String,
}

#[derive(Wire, Deserialize)]
struct NoteBody {
    text: String,
}

#[route(POST "/notes/:id", public)]
fn create_note(tx: &mut Tx, id: Id<Note>, body: NoteBody) -> Result<Id<Note>, ApiError> {
    tx.put(&Note {
        id,
        text: body.text,
    });
    Ok(id)
}

#[route(GET "/notes/:id", public)]
fn get_note(tx: &mut Tx, id: Id<Note>) -> Result<String, ApiError> {
    Ok(tx.get(id)?.ok_or(ApiError::NotFound)?.text)
}

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let app = App::open(
        Box::new(ProdDisk::new("./data")?),
        Schema::new().table::<Note>(),
        Box::new(ProdEntropy::new()?),
        AppConfig::default(),
    )?
    .mount(routes![create_note, get_note]);

    let server = charpente::serve::serve("0.0.0.0:8080", app)?;
    // `serve` returned once the listener was up; `wait` blocks until the
    // kernel stops. Exiting with its code is what lets a supervisor see a
    // stopped kernel and restart it (no graceful shutdown in v0).
    std::process::exit(server.wait());
}
```

An app whose jobs call outside services (§6) gets its HTTP client from the
server. `serve(addr, app)` is `serve_with(addr, app,
OutboundOptions::default())`, and `serve_with(addr: &str, app: App, outbound:
OutboundOptions) -> io::Result<Server>` takes the operator's settings:
`OutboundOptions { bases, cas }` (both `Vec`s, `Default` empty). `bases`
holds `(host, base)` pairs that move where a declared host is reached
(`--outbound-base`), and `cas` holds paths of PEM CA certificates to trust
beside the built-in roots (`--outbound-ca`). `launch` (§13) fills both from
its flags.

```rust
use charpente::http::App;
use charpente::serve::{OutboundOptions, Server, serve_with};

fn serve_against_a_local_fake(app: App) -> std::io::Result<Server> {
    serve_with(
        "127.0.0.1:8080",
        app,
        OutboundOptions {
            bases: vec![("pay.test".into(), "https://127.0.0.1:8443".into())],
            cas: vec!["./tls/ca.pem".into()],
        },
    )
}
```

The client is built before the listener is bound, reading each credential
variable once, so a setup refusal (an unset credential, a bad base or CA
file) returns an `Err` holding a `Refusal`, with nothing running. An app
whose jobs call nothing gets no client and no thread for one, but its
settings are still checked: any base is refused, since it names a host no job
calls, and each CA file is read, so a bad one refuses the start.
`serve_replicated`, `backup` and `archive` build the client the same way,
with no operator settings, so they reach only hosts whose certificates chain
to a public CA, at their real addresses.

On the command line of an app built on `charpente::launch` (§13), the two
settings are the serve form's flags, each repeatable for a different `HOST` or
`PATH`:

- `--outbound-base HOST=URL` reaches the declared host `HOST` at `URL`
  instead of `https://HOST:443`. `URL` is a scheme, an IP address or
  `localhost`, and an optional port (`https://127.0.0.1:8443`,
  `https://[::1]:8443`), with no path. Only the address moves: TLS still
  verifies `HOST`, and the request's `host` header still names it, so a
  stand-in remote must present a certificate for `HOST` that a trusted CA
  issued. That is why a DNS name is refused as a base: it would read as
  moving the name, which never moves. Plain `http://` is accepted only for a
  loopback address. A `HOST` no mounted job calls is refused, naming the
  hosts the app does call, or saying it calls none.
- `--outbound-ca PATH` trusts the PEM CA certificates in `PATH`, for every
  host, beside Mozilla's roots. A file that cannot be read or holds no
  certificate refuses the start, even for an app that calls no host.

A flag that is unknown, has no value, names a `HOST` or a `PATH` a second
time, or (for `--outbound-base`) is not `HOST=URL` exits 2 with `launch`'s
usage before the data directory is touched; anything `serve_with` refuses
prints `charpente refused to start: <the refusal>` and exits 1 (§13).

### What `#[route]` rejects

Every rejection is a compile error naming the contract and the fix. The
first is the one every route meets once:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
`<handler>` declares neither `auth` nor `public` — a route says which callers reach it. Add one of these to the flags of its `#[route(<method> "<path>", …)]`, keeping any it already has: `auth` to require a principal (`ctx.principal()` is `Some`), `public` to serve anonymous callers, or `public(Org)` to also let every caller act inside the `Org` tenant it opens. None is the default.
`auth` and `public` on one route — a route is one or the other; drop one
`public` given twice — write it once
```

The rest are about the handler's shape:

```rust,ignore
// first argument isn't named `tx`
#[route(GET "/ping", public)]
fn ping(ctx: &Ctx) -> Result<&'static str, ApiError> {
    Ok("pong")
}
// "a #[route] handler's first argument must be `tx: &mut Tx` — `ping` is
//  missing it"

// argument count doesn't match the :param count
#[route(GET "/notes/:id", public)]
fn get_note(tx: &mut Tx) -> Result<String, ApiError> {
    Ok(String::new())
}
// "`get_note` takes 0 argument(s) after `tx` (excluding `ctx`) but the path
//  \"/notes/:id\" has 1 :param(s) — write one argument per :param (same
//  name, path order) plus at most one JSON body argument"

// argument name doesn't match the :param name
#[route(GET "/notes/:id", public)]
fn get_note(tx: &mut Tx, key: u64) -> Result<String, ApiError> {
    Ok(String::new())
}
// "this argument must be named `id` to match :id in \"/notes/:id\" — got
//  `key`"

// route path isn't a string literal, or doesn't start with '/', or names
// an unknown method — each fails at the same macro-argument-parsing step
// with its own named message (e.g. "route path must start with '/' — got
// \"notes\"", "unknown method PUSH — one of GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, SSE").
```

Jobs ride the same kernel loop as HTTP requests (§5's `charpente::serve`
starts it): mounting a job or a schedule needs no separate worker process
or entry point.

`#[job]` derives a job payload's `Codec`, its `NAME`, its `FINGERPRINT`,
and the `JobEntry` glue `jobs![...]` collects — the same shape `#[table]`

Everything in §1–§7 routes ambient IO through `Disk`, `Entropy`, and
`Clock` instead of touching the OS directly — that is the whole reason
`charpente-sim` can exist. `charpente_sim::Sim` implements all three traits
against one seed: a `u64` that determines virtual time, every entropy draw,
and a fault matrix (write errors, sync errors, crashes between any two disk
operations, torn writes). The whole app is what the simulator drives:

same kernel loop (§6–§7) production runs — see "Driving the whole app in a

becomes "testable" specially, because it was already built on the traits.
The product's core promise: the same seed always produces the same
run, so a failure a workload returns is not just a bug report — it is
a one-command reproduction, forever.

35	literal or a `const`, not a `format!`ed `String`; plus the sim's own auto-covered
36	`fault:*`/`crash:*`/`restart` keys) that must be hit at least once across
37	that test's runs in a batch run, or the batch fails even if every
38	run individually passed. A `require`d key that never fires is telling
39	you something real: either the workload never drives the system into that
40	state, or the run count is too low to make it likely.
41	
42	```rust
43	use charpente::{Db, DbConfig, Id, Schema, TxError, View, table};
44	use charpente_sim::Sim;
45	use charpente_sim::checks::{boot_through_fallout, is_fault_fallout, replays_identically};
46	
47	#[table(global)]
48	struct Counter {
49	    id: Id<Counter>,
50	    hits: u64,
51	}
52	
53	// This is the shape of `tests/sim.rs`'s top level — the macro generates the
54	// binary's `fn main`, wiring these two workloads (and their `require` keys,
55	// if any) into the harness's arg parsing and reporting.
56	charpente_sim::sim_tests! {
57	    counter_roundtrip require ["restart"],
58	    counter_replays,
59	}
60	
61	/// `sim_tests!` workloads return `Result<(), String>` — this one delegates
62	/// to a helper that returns the interesting value instead, so the
63	/// determinism checker below can reuse the exact same logic. `None` asserted
64	/// nothing, and a pass needs a verdict, so it gives the run up ("Giving
65	/// up" below).
66	fn counter_roundtrip(sim: &mut Sim) -> Result<(), String> {
67	    if counter_roundtrip_result(sim)?.is_none() {
68	        sim.give_up("nothing to assert: the write never acked, or a boot never came up", "");
69	    }
70	    Ok(())
71	}
72	
73	/// `replays_identically` is the determinism oracle: it runs `workload` twice
74	/// on two fresh `Sim`s seeded identically and demands both the return value
75	/// and the durable end-state match byte-for-byte.
76	fn counter_replays(sim: &mut Sim) -> Result<(), String> {
77	    replays_identically(sim.seed(), counter_roundtrip_result)
78	}
79	
80	/// Puts a row, restarts the simulated disk (crashes and reopens), and reads
81	/// it back. Returns `None` — not a failure — when there is nothing to
82	/// assert: an injected fault kept the write from its ack, or either
83	/// `Db::open` never booted through fault fallout (the harness's own fault
84	/// paths, not this workload's contract, are under test elsewhere). Only a
85	/// `TxError::Io` can be fallout: the closure's own `App` error, or a
86	/// follower's refusal, is this workload's bug. `is_fault_fallout` recognizes the
87	/// sim's own injected-fault wording, the WAL/engine poison wording, and
88	/// redb's "close and re-open the database" latch; `boot_through_fallout`
89	/// boots again on those, and excuses a refusal for durable corruption only
90	/// where the harness injected some. Anything else is treated as a real bug
91	/// and fails the run.
92	fn counter_roundtrip_result(sim: &mut Sim) -> Result<Option<u64>, String> {
93	    let schema = || Schema::new().table::<Counter>();
94	    let open = || Db::open(Box::new(sim.disk()), DbConfig::default(), schema());
95	    let Some(mut db) = boot_through_fallout(sim, 8, is_fault_fallout, open)
96	        .map_err(|e| e.to_string())?
97	    else {
98	        return Ok(None);
99	    };
100	    let acked = match db.transact(|tx| {
101	        tx.put(&Counter {
102	            id: Id::from_raw(1),
103	            hits: 1,
104	        });
105	        Ok::<_, std::io::Error>(())
106	    }) {
107	        Ok(()) => true,
108	        Err(TxError::Io(e)) if is_fault_fallout(&e.to_string()) => false,
109	        Err(e) => return Err(format!("{e:?}")),
110	    };
111	
112	    sim.restart(); // power-cycles the simulated disk: unsynced writes tear or vanish
113	    drop(db); // the old handle is dead after restart — reopen, per its own contract
114	
115	    let open = || Db::open(Box::new(sim.disk()), DbConfig::default(), schema());
116	    let Some(db) = boot_through_fallout(sim, 8, is_fault_fallout, open)
117	        .map_err(|e| e.to_string())?
118	    else {
119	        return Ok(None);
120	    };
121	    if !acked {
122	        return Ok(None);
123	    }
124	    let snap = db.snapshot().map_err(|e| e.to_string())?;
125	    match snap.get::<Counter>(Id::from_raw(1)).map_err(|e| e.to_string())? {
126	        Some(row) => Ok(Some(row.hits)),
127	        None => Err("acked Counter row lost across a crash".to_string()),
128	    }
129	}
130	```

132	### Examples to copy
133	
134	Three compiled examples ship in the `charpente` crate, each a small batch
135	that prints the report "Reading a batch" describes and exits with its code.
136	Each is a whole `tests/sim.rs`: `sim_tests!` supplies `main`, and the file
137	declares its own tables, routes and jobs.
138	
139	- **In your app**, copy one to `tests/sim.rs` and run `charpente test --sim`.
140	  It needs only the manifest `charpente new` writes.
141	- **In a charpente checkout**, run `cargo run -p charpente --example <name>`.
142	  Cargo refuses `-p charpente` anywhere else. The batch's last line names
143	  `charpente test --sim --master-seed 0x…`; for an example, pass the same flags
144	  after `--` instead: `cargo run -p charpente --example <name> -- --master-seed
145	  0x…` reruns that batch byte for byte.
146	
147	| Example | File, in the `charpente` crate | It shows |
148	|---|---|---|
149	| `drawn_inputs` | `examples/drawn_inputs.rs` | bids drawn with `sim.input()` (`between`, `pick`, `shuffle`, `text`), a check that holds for any of them, and a `require` on a key the check marks when it judged something |
150	| `modelled_remote` | `examples/modelled_remote.rs` | an outbound job against a `Remote` with its own `Rng`, a calm switch for the fault-free tail, and the three outbound checkers |
151	| `restart_under_faults` | `examples/restart_under_faults.rs` | `boot_through_fallout`, a restart, a fault-free tail that waits out a clock refusal, and a `require ["restart"]` |
152	
153	In all three a skipped run gives a constant `reason` and puts the run's own
154	text in the `detail`. The files are in the registry copy of the crate, under
155	`crates/charpente/examples/` in a checkout, and this guide is the
156	`charpente::guide` page on docs.rs.
157	
158	### Drawing inputs
159	
160	`sim.input()` is for the inputs a property must hold for: a name, an amount, an
161	order of operations. Each draw comes from a stream of its own, so drawing moves
162	no fault, and the harness records each draw's choice in a sequence it can replay
163	and shrink. The choice is the one the draw used: the stream's raw value reduced
164	into the draw's range, which is the smallest raw value that draws the same
165	value. So a choice and its value are one to one, and two equal values drawn
166	with the same bounds are equal choices.
167	
168	```text
169	let i = sim.input();
170	let qty = i.between("qty", 1, 500);        // inclusive; shrinks toward 1
171	let kind = i.pick("kind", &["a", "b"]);    // shrinks toward the first item
172	i.shuffle("order", &mut ops);              // shrinks toward the given order
173	let note = i.text("note", &["x", "y"], 1, 4);
174	```
175	
176	It is the workload's own script only: a modelled remote keeps its own `Rng`. A
177	drawn input tests how the app handles what its model stand-in returns, never
178	the real model's behaviour. `between` panics when `lo > hi`, and `pick` on an
179	empty slice. `text` panics when `min_words > max_words`, and on an empty
180	`words` when `max_words` is above 0; with a `max_words` of 0 it draws `""`.
181	Each message names the call and the draw, and says which argument to change.
182	
183	When a check fails, its first failure is shrunk to smaller draws that still
184	fail it, and the failure block lists them by name on its `inputs:` line
185	("Shrinking a failure" below).
186	
187	A batch counts, on each check's line, how many distinct inputs its tested runs
188	drew: two runs that drew the same values, under the same names and in the same
189	order, count once.
190	It is a count, never a threshold. A check whose workload draws nothing is named
191	above the check lines, because every one of its runs tested the same scripted
192	case, whatever the faults did ("Reading a batch" below).
193	
194	### Giving up: a skipped run
195	
196	Sooner or later a workload hits a run where the faults are severe enough
197	that it cannot test its claim at all: the database never opened, the write was
198	never acknowledged, every recovery attempt was exhausted, or durable corruption
199	cut the very record the claim was about. That is not a pass —
200	nothing was proven — and it is not a failure either; the harness did exactly
201	what it was told.
202	
203	Say so:
204	
205	```rust
206	use charpente::{Db, DbConfig, Id, Schema, TxError, View, table};
207	use charpente_sim::Sim;
208	use charpente_sim::checks::{boot_through_fallout, durable_corruption_fired, is_fault_fallout};
209	
210	#[table(global)]
211	struct Counter {
212	    id: Id<Counter>,
213	    hits: u64,
214	}
215	
216	fn counter_survives(sim: &mut Sim) -> Result<(), String> {
217	    let schema = || Schema::new().table::<Counter>();
218	    // A boot that meets an injected fault restarts and boots again, as a
219	    // supervised process would: `Db::open`'s contract for an IO failure.
220	    let open = || Db::open(Box::new(sim.disk()), DbConfig::default(), schema());
221	    let Some(mut db) = boot_through_fallout(sim, 8, is_fault_fallout, open)
222	        .map_err(|e| e.to_string())?
223	    else {
224	        // Nothing to adjudicate: the disk never let the claim become testable.
225	        sim.give_up("Db::open never booted in 8 boots", "");
226	        return Ok(());
227	    };
228	    let put = db.transact(|tx| {
229	        tx.put(&Counter {
230	            id: Id::from_raw(1),
231	            hits: 1,
232	        });
233	        Ok::<_, std::io::Error>(())
234	    });
235	    match put {
236	        Ok(()) => {}
237	        // An injected fault kept the write from its ack: no claim to check.
238	        // Any other error is the platform's, and fails, as the opens do.
239	        Err(TxError::Io(e)) if is_fault_fallout(&e.to_string()) => {
240	            sim.give_up("the write was never acknowledged, so there is no claim to check", e);
241	            return Ok(());
242	        }
243	        Err(e) => return Err(format!("{e:?}")),
244	    }
245	
246	    sim.restart(); // a crash: unsynced writes tear or vanish
247	    drop(db); // the old handle is dead after restart
248	    let open = || Db::open(Box::new(sim.disk()), DbConfig::default(), schema());
249	    let Some(db) = boot_through_fallout(sim, 8, is_fault_fallout, open)
250	        .map_err(|e| e.to_string())?
251	    else {
252	        sim.give_up("the reopen never booted in 8 boots", "");
253	        return Ok(());
254	    };
255	    match db.snapshot().and_then(|snap| snap.get::<Counter>(Id::from_raw(1))) {
256	        Ok(Some(_)) => Ok(()),
257	        // The one loss the platform excuses on a single node, and an excused
258	        // run GIVES UP: the row's durability was not adjudicated, and a pass
259	        // needs a verdict.
260	        Ok(None) if durable_corruption_fired(sim) => {
261	            sim.give_up("durable corruption cut the acked row, so durability was not adjudicated", "");
262	            Ok(())
263	        }
264	        Ok(None) => Err("acked Counter row lost across a crash".to_string()),
265	        Err(e) if is_fault_fallout(&e.to_string()) => {
266	            sim.give_up("the read-back hit fault fallout", e);
267	            Ok(())
268	        }
269	        Err(e) => Err(e.to_string()),
270	    }
271	}
272	```
273	
274	- `sim.give_up(reason, detail)` records the give-up **on the run**, not in
275	  the value you return. That is deliberate: a `Result` can be mapped back to
276	  `Ok(())` by a wrapper before the runner ever sees it, and for a long time
277	  that is exactly what happened — a property could report green having
278	  concluded nothing over most of its runs.
279	- **The reason is fixed text; the detail is this run's own.** `reason` is a
280	  `&'static str` that names the *kind* of give-up and embeds nothing that
281	  varies between runs: no error text, count or seq. A batch groups each
282	  check's skipped runs by reason and counts each group, so a reason with a seq
283	  in it makes every run its own group and the counts say nothing. What varies
284	  goes in `detail` (anything `Display`, such as the fallout error `e`): that one
285	  run's own text, which a batch does not print and `--seed` prints under the skipped check as `detail:`. A
286	  constant such as a retry count is fixed text, so it belongs in the reason
287	  (`"Db::open never booted in 8 boots"`), not the detail. A give-up with
288	  nothing to add passes `""`, and an empty detail is none.
289	  `sim.gave_up()` reads the reason and `sim.gave_up_detail()` the detail;
290	  `Outcome::GaveUp` carries both.
291	- First call wins, reason and detail together; later ones are consequences of
292	  the first.
293	- **Give up and stop.** The record is sticky and nothing enforces terminality,
294	  so if you give up inside a retry arm and the loop then goes on to adjudicate,
295	  the run is still reported as skipped and that verdict is thrown away.
296	  `give_up` and the `return`/`break` belong on the same arm. This bites hardest
297	  in a multi-round checker on your own `sim` (`acked_implies_durable`).
298	- A workload that gives up and then returns `Err` is still a **failure**.
299	  Failures outrank give-ups.
300	- It also marks the coverage key `run:skipped` — once per run, not
301	  once per call — so a give-up *rate* is counted like any other sometimes-key,
302	  and it cross-checks the reported count exactly. `ceiling:
303	  [("run:skipped", N)]` on `run_universes_swarm!`/`run_universes_swarm_with!`
304	  caps it: the batch fails when more than N runs gave up, naming the key,
305	  the count and the cap. Twenty of the platform's own swarm properties carry
306	  one:
307	  - kernel's exactly-once and job-tenancy properties;
308	  - the flagship properties of tenant, transactions, http, group_commit and
309	    typed_tables, and archive's two convergence properties;
310	  - realtime's flagship, scoped settled-client and tenant-feed properties,
311	    migrations' two, and the WAL suite's fault-matrix, bit-flip, misdirected-write, read-error,
312	    dir-entry and gc properties.
313	
314	  The rest carry none yet, so a drift in their give-up rates is visible only in
315	  the split: realtime's mixed-shapes and follower properties, replication's,
316	  auth's, kernel's job-shape property, transactions' crashed-reseed property,
317	  and engine's. A give-up is
318	  reported and never failed, so without a cap a property can drift toward
319	  adjudicating nothing with every batch green; a floor on the key would bound
320	  give-ups from below, which guards nothing. An app's `sim_tests!` takes no
321	  `ceiling:`. Its property `require`s instead the key its verdict marks, past
322	  every give-up arm. That fails a batch in which no run reached a verdict,
323	  but not one whose rate merely drifted.
324	- A cap bounds what a property fails to conclude, not how much it checks, so
325	  pair it with a `floor: [("key", N)]` on the key that counts its checks
326	  (written before `ceiling:`, on either macro). A change that skips a round's
327	  work without giving up meets every cap. At a pinned base the floor is the
328	  exact count; at an ambient one it is a margin, the mean over ten or more
329	  fresh batches less four standard deviations (§8).
330	- If your workload already funnels give-ups through a wrapper (the
331	  `Err("universe-inconclusive: …")` idiom the platform's own suites use), put
332	  the `sim.give_up(INCONCLUSIVE, e)` call there, beside the `sim.cover(...)` mark. Keep
333	  both: the coverage keys are a floorable distribution over *causes*, and the
334	  outcome is the scalar the runner reports. Neither replaces the other.
335	
336	Every batch states, check by check, how many runs tested the check and, when any
337	were skipped, how many and why. A check with nothing skipped shows no skipped
338	count and is left out of the reasons block, and a batch that skipped nothing
339	prints no reasons block at all. This is a pinned batch of `crates/sim-fixture`,
340	`charpente test --sim --runs 64 --master-seed 0x5eed --filter counter_roundtrip`:
341	
342	<!-- pinned -->
343	```text
344	skipped runs hit a fault before reaching the check, so they prove nothing either way:
345	  counter_roundtrip
346	    10  Db::open after the crash never booted in 8 boots
347	     2  the write was never acked, so durability has nothing to prove
348	
349	these checks draw no inputs, so every run tested the same case — draw them with sim.input() (GUIDE §8):
350	  counter_roundtrip
351	
352	check counter_roundtrip ... ok  (52 tested, 12 skipped)
353	
354	sim result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed. 52 of 64 runs tested a check.
355	rerun exactly this batch: charpente test --sim --master-seed 0x5eed --runs 64 --filter counter_roundtrip
356	```
357	
358	A check in which every run was skipped is `untested`, never `ok`, because a
359	property that adjudicated nothing is vacuous no matter how green it looks. A
360	batch whose every check is untested says `nothing tested`, and still exits 0.
361	This is the harness's own fixture pair, a check that passes and one that always
362	gives up, over six runs:
363

366	  always_gives_up — never tested: every run was skipped
367	    6  the fixture always gives up
368	
369	these checks draw no inputs, so every run tested the same case — draw them with sim.input() (GUIDE §8):
370	  always_passes
371	
372	check always_passes ..... ok  (6 tested)
373	check always_gives_up ... untested  (0 tested, 6 skipped)

400	### A fault-free tail for an end-of-run check
401	
402	A check that runs at the end of a run — a checkpoint, a graceful close, a
403	byte comparison of two nodes' files — does IO, and the run's
404	`FaultConfig` still applies to it. "No fault has fired so far" is a fact about
405	the past: the check's own fsync can still draw an injected failure. Call
406	`sim.quiesce_disk_faults()` first. For the rest of the run, on every disk,
407	it disarms any pending crash countdown, and no injected read, write, sync or
408	directory-barrier error, misdirected write or restart bit flip fires after it.
409	Each skipped roll draws nothing, so a run that never calls it
410	replays exactly as before. After it, an error in the check is a real failure,
411	not fallout to classify. Network and object-store faults are untouched, and a
412	restart still power-cycles: unsynced writes and directory entries collapse under
413	the crash model as usual (`crash_apply`, `crash_torn`, `dir_entry_loss`).
414	
415	An outbound workload's tail needs the outbound half as well.
416	`sim.quiesce_outbound_faults()` ends the five outbound fault axes for the rest of
417	the run: no call started after it is refused, lost, throttled or slowed, or
418	loses its reply. Each skipped roll draws nothing, so a run that never calls
419	it replays exactly as before. Latency stays, since it is not a fault, and a
420	request already in flight keeps the fate it drew. Call both, then run past the
421	last backoff and deadline. From there every call reaches its remote and its
422	reply comes back, so every outbound job settles or retries to Dead, which is
423	what `outbound_settles_by_horizon` (below) checks.
424	
425	A realtime workload's settle phase has the same need for a different fault. The
426	subscriber-stall rate is the one fault axis the sim does not inject itself: a
427	workload reads `sim.subscriber_stall()` and drives its own sink's stall closure
428	at that rate. `sim.quiesce_subscriber_stalls()` makes that accessor read 0.0 for
429	the rest of the run, so a stall closure built after it never refuses a send
430	and draws nothing. Call it before a phase whose verdict rests on a delivery
431	completing. A stall there is a fault the property excuses, so a stall that drops
432	the only clean attempt's tail leaves the run with no verdict at all.
433	
434	A tail that opens a kernel needs the clock half too.
435	`sim.quiesce_clock_faults()` ends the clock faults ("Wall time and its faults",
436	below) for the rest of the run, on every clock. No reading steps back and
437	no power cycle jumps a clock forward after it, so each clock's offset stays
438	where the run left it, skew included. Each skipped roll draws nothing, so a
439	run that never calls it replays exactly as before. It does not undo the
440	past: a step back in an earlier phase can leave the clock more than the
441	tolerance behind the latest time the store recorded, and then the tail's open is
442	refused (§7). With the offset frozen, the clock reaches the instant the refusal
443	names as virtual time passes. `clock_reopens_after(text)` (below) reads that
444	instant. Sleep a little past it (`sim.clock().sleep(…)`), restart the process (a
445	refused node exits, and its supervisor starts it again), and boot again. One
446	wait is enough, since nothing moves the clock or the recorded time in between.
447	Bound the loop anyway, and give the run up by name once the bound is spent.
448	`wait_out_clock_refusal(sim, boot)` (below) is that loop, and the worked
449	example in "Calling the outside world in a sim" uses it.
450	
451	### Restarting the process, not the machine
452	
453	`sim.restart()` is a power cycle: every unsynced write survives, tears or
454	vanishes before anything reopens. Most restarts in production are not that. A
455	supervisor restarting a crashed, killed or exited process finds the OS page
456	cache intact: every write the dead process made is still readable, synced or
457	not. `sim.restart_process()` models that. Every open file handle dies, exactly
458	as after `restart`, and nothing else happens. Unsynced writes and directory
459	entries stay pending and readable, and the next `restart()` still collapses
460	them.
461	
462	The difference matters because readable is not durable. A node that reads back
463	what a dead process wrote and persists anything derived from it, before making
464	it durable, has built on data the next power loss can take away. A store
465	outran its own log exactly that way: recovery replayed a WAL frame whose fsync
466	had failed, the store checkpointed past it, and a power cycle dropped the frame.
467	Charpente now syncs what it reads back at boot before it acts on it. A property
468	that only ever power-cycles cannot reach that shape. One that mixes the two can.
469	
470	The sim's kernel is an honest one: a failed sync leaves its writes pending, and
471	the next sync writes them. On Linux a failed fsync can instead mark the pages
472	clean, so the bytes stay readable and never reach the disk. No restart mode
473	models that, and no later sync can repair it.
474	
475	Call `restart_process()` before you drop the old process's `Db` to model a kill:
476	its open files are dead, so nothing it flushes through them on the way out
477	reaches the disk. Only file handles are gated. A destructor that opens a file
478	afresh through a `Disk` it still holds would reach the disk; charpente's own
479	close goes through its open files. Call it after the drop to model an exit.
480	
481	`sim.unsynced_files()` lists the files that hold writes no sync has taken yet.
482	Read it right after `restart_process()` to prove the restart left the next
483	process something unsynced to read back. A property that marks "read back an
484	unsynced write" from that list cannot be satisfied by a restart that quietly
485	flushed.
486	
487	`restart_process()` draws from no random stream and clears no crash countdown,
488	so the sim gained it without re-keying anyone's runs. Calling it does
489	change everything your workload does afterwards, as any restart would. It marks
490	`restart:process`, never `restart`. A crashed disk is power loss, and
491	`restart_process()` refuses it by name: call `restart()` there. It covers the
492	global disk; hosts have no process restart.
493	
494	### Wall time and its faults
495	
496	A workload reads two times. `sim.now()` is virtual time, the one dimension every
497	host shares; `SimSource` horizons and `push_at` times are on it. A clock's
498	`wall()` (`sim.clock()`, or a host's `host.clock()`) is the wall time a node
499	sees: `sim.true_wall()` (virtual time plus 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z) plus that
500	clock's offset. `charpente test --sim` puts three faults on the offset, each on
501	in a quarter of runs, from its own stream:
502	
503	| Axis (`FaultConfig` field) | What it does | Coverage key |
504	|---|---|---|
505	| `clock_skew` | the run's largest skew, up to 120 s: each clock draws its own skew once, uniform within ±`clock_skew`, and reads that far ahead (+) or behind (-) of true time | `clock:skewed`, once per clock, at its first read |
506	| `clock_step_back` | per wall read, the chance the clock steps back by up to 120 s, and stays there | `clock:stepped-back` per step, and `clock:stepped-back:within-tolerance` or `clock:stepped-back:beyond-tolerance` by its size against `CLOCK_TOLERANCE` |
507	| `clock_downtime` | per power cycle (`sim.restart()`, `host.restart()`), the chance the clock jumps forward by up to three days, as if the machine had been off; virtual time stays put, and `restart_process()` is not downtime | `clock:downtime`, per jump, at the first reading that shows it |
508	
509	Each clock's skew, step-backs and jumps are its own, so two hosts' clocks
510	disagree from their first read. The faults compound. A clock's offset is its
511	skew plus every step back and jump it has taken so far, and nothing pulls it
512	back toward true time, just as a clock with no NTP keeps its error, so the
513	offset wanders further as a run goes on. `sim.clock().offset()` (or
514	`host.clock().offset()`) reports it at any moment and draws nothing.
515	The sizes span both sides of `CLOCK_TOLERANCE` (60 s), so a run sees what a node
516	does with a bad clock (§5, §7): it holds its wall reading at the latest time it
517	used for a step back within the tolerance, stops by name for one beyond it
518	(`clock went backwards: …`) or for a hold that lasts longer than the tolerance
519	(`clock stalled: …`), and refuses to open while its clock is more than the
520	tolerance behind the latest time its data directory recorded (`refusing to
521	open: this node's wall clock …`). `clock_refused` names the stops and the
522	refusal (below). They are fallout only where a clock fault acted:
523	`clock_fallout(sim, text)` excuses one once a clock in this run has read with
524	its own skew, stepped back, or shown a jump, and `is_fault_fallout` alone never
525	does. A node whose clock is right is refused only by a bug, and the platform's
526	suites run with the clock axes off, so a refusal there fails. An app workload's
527	filter is `|t| is_fault_fallout(t) || clock_fallout(sim, t)`. The fault-free
528	tail above quiesces the clock and then waits out a refusal.
529	
530	A property that judges expiry and lateness judges two things. Against each
531	node's own clock readings it holds the node to what it promises (below), which
532	is exact. Against `sim.true_wall()` it states what that promise means in true
533	time, written through each clock's offset, since a skewed clock is the thing
534	under test and a bound that assumes the node's reading is true time fails on
535	correct code. The platform's own suites (`run_universes_swarm!`, `Sim::new`,
536	`FaultConfig::default()` and `none()`) leave the three axes off; a platform
537	property turns them on in `run_universes_swarm_with!`'s `adjust`, which is
538	handed the run's seed with its config (`|seed, cfg| …`), so any value it
539	draws comes from a stream keyed by that seed.
540	
541	`tests/clock.rs` in the `charpente` crate (`crates/charpente/tests/clock.rs` in
542	a checkout) is the worked example. It runs four platform properties with all
543	three axes on (sessions, a one-second schedule, retries, and the stops and
544	refusals themselves, on one node and on a follower promoted on its own host's
545	clock) and a victim clock that fails two of them by name. It shows how to write
546	the bounds.
547	
548	Write a bound through each clock's offset, the reading minus `sim.true_wall()`
549	at that instant, never through `clock_skew`. A step back within the tolerance
550	is held and then caught up, so step-backs add up, and a clock can run any
551	distance behind true time without a check firing. A bound on `expires_at` that
552	allows only the skew fails on correct code.
553	
554	What a node does guarantee is relative to its own clock. The time it hands out
555	is never behind its clock's reading, and never more than `CLOCK_TOLERANCE`
556	ahead of it: the hold takes the larger, the stop fires past the tolerance, and
557	the open refuses past it. Nor does it stay ahead for longer than the tolerance
558	at a stretch, since the stall stop ends the hold. That gives these bounds:
559	- A session resolves only while the clock judging it reads before its
560	  `expires_at`. In true time, it resolves no later than its TTL plus the
561	  tolerance after it was minted, plus however far the judging clock has fallen
562	  behind the minting one.
563	- A schedule never sits idle once its slot has come on the node's clock.
564	- Two ticks are never further apart in true time than one interval plus the
565	  tolerance, plus the clock's own loss and the time the node was busy.
566	
567	The file records every wall read the kernel makes (a `Clock` wrapper around
568	`sim.clock()`) and steps the kernel by hand. That ties each response, tick and
569	retry to the reading it was decided at.
570	
571	### The checkers
572	
573	`charpente_sim::checks` ships fifteen functions: twelve reusable oracles, and
574	three idioms, one for a boot and two for a tail that waits out a clock
575	refusal. Reach for these before hand-rolling the same logic a fourth time:
576	
577	- `is_fault_fallout(text: &str) -> bool` — classifies an error's *text*:
578	  is this the harness's own injected fault (or its consequences) rather
579	  than a bug your workload should fail on? It recognizes the sim's
580	  injected-fault wording (including the `read_error` axis), the WAL/engine
581	  poison wording, and redb's "close and re-open the database" latch. Used
582	  inside a workload to turn "the disk broke, as instructed" into "no answer
583	  this round" rather than a hard failure — never to swallow anything else.
584	  (`misdirected_write` is not in that list and cannot be: it returns `Ok`, so
585	  it has no wording — what you eventually see is the corrupt frame it left
586	  behind.) **It never excuses the WAL's durable-horizon refusal**, the boot
587	  refused because an already-acknowledged frame failed its check at or below
588	  the store's horizon. That refusal is fallout where `bit_flip` or
589	  `misdirected_write` fired, and a durability bug in the platform everywhere
590	  else (a real one showed itself only as this refusal in 8 of 21 failing
591	  bases), and text cannot say which. So it is `false` here, and an open site
592	  asks `durable_refusal` (below) first, or, for one node of several,
593	  `SimHost::durable_corruption_fired()`. `boot_through_fallout` does that for
594	  you. **Nor does it excuse the kernel's clock stops or open/promote refusal**,
595	  for the same reason: a clock fault or a platform bug produces it, and
596	  `clock_fallout` (below) tells them apart.
597	- `classify(text: &str) -> FaultReason` — the families, typed:
598	  `Injected`, `Poisoned`, `RedbLatch`, `DurableHorizon`, `ClockRefused`, or
599	  `Unrelated` (`is_fault_fallout` is `Injected | Poisoned | RedbLatch`). Use it when your
600	  workload wants to accept some families and fail on others — e.g. "an
601	  injected fault is fallout this round, but a poisoned engine is a finding" —
602	  or to name the family in a coverage key. `DurableHorizon` and
603	  `ClockRefused` are names, never excuses on their own. Matching on a variant instead of on substrings keeps
604	  the prose coupling in one place: if a platform error string is ever
605	  reworded, `classify` is the single site that must change, and it fails by
606	  name instead of leaking a wrong classification into whichever oracle saw
607	  the text first.
608	- `clock_refused(text: &str) -> bool` — true for the kernel's clock stops
609	  (`clock went backwards: …`, `clock stalled: …`) and for its refusal to open or promote a node
610	  whose wall clock is more than `CLOCK_TOLERANCE` behind the latest time its
611	  data directory recorded (`refusing to open: this node's wall clock …`,
612	  `refusing to promote: this node's wall clock …`). A name only: the clock
613	  axes produce both ("Wall time and its faults", above), and so does a
614	  platform bug that refuses a node whose clock is right.
615	- `clock_fallout(sim: &Sim, text: &str) -> bool` — the excuse for those:
616	  true when `clock_refused(text)` holds and a clock fault acted in this run (a
617	  clock read with its own skew, stepped back, or showed a downtime jump: its
618	  `clock:*` coverage key fired). Where no clock fault acted, nothing excuses
619	  the stops or the refusal. An app workload that runs a kernel filters fallout
620	  with `|t| is_fault_fallout(t) || clock_fallout(sim, t)`; a workload that
621	  never builds a kernel cannot see either text.
622	- `clock_reopens_after(text: &str) -> Option<WallTime>` — the instant a clock
623	  stop or refusal names as the one after which the node runs again (its final
624	  "after <instant>", to the millisecond), or `None` for any other text. A
625	  fault-free tail sleeps a little past it after `sim.quiesce_clock_faults()`,
626	  restarts the process and boots again ("A fault-free tail", above). The stall
627	  stop names no instant, so it is `None`: its clock stopped advancing, and no
628	  wait fixes that. A quiesced clock still advances, so a tail's kernel never
