228	### Shrinking a failure
229	
230	A failing run usually carries more than its bug: inputs that play no part, and
231	fault axes that were on but did nothing to it. So the harness replays the first
232	failure of each check with smaller choices and fewer faults, and keeps each
233	smaller run that still fails the same check. The last one it keeps is the run
234	the block shows. The rule is the same for every check.
235	
236	It shrinks the recorded choice sequence, not the values (Hypothesis's approach):
237	each choice is the one its draw used, so a smaller choice is a smaller, simpler
238	value (`lo`, the first item, the identity order), and a draw past the end of
239	the choices reads 0. Its passes run in rounds, repeated until a whole round
240	keeps nothing:
241	
242	1. delete chunks of the choices, 8, 4, 2 and then 1 long, from the end toward
243	   the start;
244	2. set each choice to 0;
245	3. search each choice down toward 0 (galloping up from 1, then bisecting), so a
246	   small value that fails is found even when the values between it and the
247	   recorded choice pass;
248	4. turn off each fault axis that is on, one at a time, in `FaultConfig` field
249	   order. An axis is on when it could fire: a clock axis whose chance is 0 is
250	   off whatever its size, so `faults off:` never lists it;
251	5. lower equal choices together: for each nonzero value two or more choices
252	   hold, set all of them to 0 and then search them down toward 0 as one value,
253	   so a failure that needs the same entity drawn twice (the same lab, the same
254	   product) reaches the lowest one, where lowering either draw alone makes the
255	   two differ and passes. Then, only in a round where everything before kept
256	   nothing, an axis turned off counting as a keep, each pair of those choices
257	   the same way, for a value that also sits where the failure does not need
258	   it. A whole group costs one candidate and a search, as cheap as passes 2
259	   and 3, so whole groups are tried in every round, right after pass 4. The
260	   pairs wait because k equal choices make k(k-1)/2 of them, enough to spend
261	   the whole budget: run while the other passes can still shrink the run,
262	   they could leave on fault axes the failure does not need, or inputs larger
263	   than it needs. Waiting costs a whole round of the other passes first, so
264	   among many choices the budget can run out before a needed pair is tried;
265	   the shrunk run then still fails the check and replays, with more draws
266	   than it needs.
267	
268	A round that keeps nothing ends the shrink on a local minimum: no step of these
269	passes shrinks the run and still fails. They do not search every smaller run,
270	so a smaller one that fails the check can still exist. A shrink that spends its
271	budget (below) ends where the budget ran out, which can be short of a local
272	minimum.
273	
274	A candidate is kept when the same check fails, with any message. One that
275	passes or gives up is not kept, so a clock axis whose removal turns the failure
276	into a clock-excused skip stays on. A smaller input can move where faults land,
277	and a fault turned off can change how many inputs a run draws (a retry loop that
278	no longer retries). Neither breaks anything, because the harness judges a
279	candidate only by replaying it, exactly as the printed repro does.
280	
281	Shrinking runs on the first failure of each check in seed order, never in
282	completion order, and each shrink depends only on its check, seed and first
283	failure. Its budget is 500 replays, counted rather than timed, so the block is
284	identical for any `--jobs` and on any machine. A shrink that spends the budget
285	stops with the smallest run found so far. A workload that panics prints the
286	panic's message on stderr each time a shrink replay panics; the report itself is
287	on stdout, written once every shrink has finished.
288	
289	**A slipped shrink.** Any failure of the same check counts, so the shrunk run
290	can fail it for another reason than the first did. The headline is then the
291	shrunk run's own message, `first:` keeps the original, and `repro:` replays the
292	shrunk run. The original is the seed alone: drop `--inputs` and `--faults-off`
293	from the repro. When the two messages name different bugs, fix the one the
294	repro shows, then rerun the batch.
295	
296	### Re-basing a pinned property: `CHARPENTE_BASE_SEED`
297	
298	Some properties fix their base seed (`run_universes_swarm_with!(BASE, N, …)`)
299	so their `floor:` rates have a stable denominator. That is right for a rate and
300	wrong for a correctness claim: a fixed base means the property only ever
301	examines the same N runs, while a green run reads as though it examined
302	the space.
303	
304	`CHARPENTE_BASE_SEED=0x… cargo test -p <pkg> --test <file>` re-bases every
305	pinned property in that binary, so the claim "this property holds" can actually
306	be tested rather than assumed:
307	
308	```text
309	charpente-sim [realtime]: re-basing 0x000000002eb20001 -> 0x00000000a11ce001 under
310	  CHARPENTE_BASE_SEED — coverage requirements, floors and ceilings skipped (they
311	  are rates measured at the pinned base)
312	```
313	
314	Like `CHARPENTE_SEED`, it takes hex with or without `0x`, and `_` separators
315	are ignored, so a base copied from the source as written (`0x2EB2_5A10`) works
316	as is; a value that is not hex panics naming the variable it was read from.
317	
318	Floors, ceilings and `require:` keys are skipped under the override, for the
319	reason the floor's own panic text gives: they are rates measured AT a base, so
320	evaluating them somewhere else compares against a denominator that was never
321	taken there.
322	What the mode tests is the property's own assertions, which are untouched.
323	
324	**A correctness oracle should pass at every base.** If it passes at its pinned
325	base and fails at others, it is not flaky — it is failing, and the pinned base
326	is hiding it. Two realtime properties were found exactly that way
327	(docs/LEDGER.md 2026-09-07).
328	
329	One caveat worth knowing before you chase a floor panic: an IO call consumes RNG
330	draws, so changing *where* an IO operation happens inside code a property never
331	names reshuffles every run at a pinned base. Floors move for that reason far
332	more often than they move because an oracle decayed.
333	
334	So a floor that falls after such a change is re-measured, not defended and not
335	quietly lowered. Run the property before and after the change at the same ten or
336	more fresh bases (`CHARPENTE_BASE_SEED`) and compare the key's mean. It has
337	decayed if the after-mean sits more than one Welch standard error below the
338	before-mean, where that error is `sqrt(sd_before²/n_before + sd_after²/n_after)`
339	over the per-base counts. Within one standard error, the floor is re-set to its
340	new exact count at its pinned base, with both distributions recorded; beyond
341	it, the fall is the finding. A base where either binary fails on an unrelated,
342	named bug is left out of both sides, and the record says which. One standard
343	error is deliberately strict: pure noise crosses it roughly a sixth to a quarter
344	of the time, which errs toward stopping to look.
345	
346	A cap that rises after such a change asks a different question, because a
347	give-up is not a lost verdict when the same run used to pass having
348	checked nothing. So judge the rise by the verdicts the property reached, over
349	the same ten or more fresh bases: count its passes that covered its reach key
350	(the key its `floor:` counts), and beside them its vacuous passes (runs
351	that passed without covering that key). A cap may rise only if the passes
352	covering the reach key did not fall by more than one Welch standard error.
353	Then the new give-ups replaced vacuous passes, not verdicts, and the cap is
354	re-set by its own convention, with both distributions recorded. If those
355	passes fell by more than one standard error, the rise is the finding. Neither
356	the reach key's own count nor the vacuous passes can decide it alone: 20 more
357	give-ups beside 1 fewer vacuous pass means 19 passes that checked something
358	became give-ups. A pinned cap can read the same
359	number on both binaries while the rate behind it moved, so the test runs
360	whenever the change could have moved it, not only when the pinned count did.
361	That is also why every capped property floors its reach key: without one, the
362	next change that costs it reach passes with every cap still met.
363	
364	At a pinned base both bounds are exact counts. At an ambient base, where the
365	counts move batch to batch, both are margins over ten or more fresh batches.
366	
367	An ambient give-up cap is the larger of two numbers:
368	- twice the largest fresh-batch count;
369	- the smallest k with P(Poisson(lambda) > k) < 1e-4, where
370	  lambda = n x U(x) / N. Here n is the runs in one batch, N the runs
371	  over all the fresh batches, and x the give-ups among them. U(x) is the exact
372	  one-sided 95% Poisson upper bound for x: 2.996 for x = 0, 4.744 for 1, and
373	  6.296 for 2.
374	
375	The second number matters where give-ups are rare. When no batch gave up,
376	twice the largest count is 0, which one legitimately exhausted run fails.
377	When one batch gave up once, it is 2, which a healthy batch fails about once
378	in eighty. Where counts are large the first number is the larger, and the
379	second only confirms it.
380	
381	Two worked examples for the WAL fault matrix, whose 10 fresh batches of
382	n = 512 make N = 5,120:
383	- **x = 0**, as measured. lambda = 512 x 2.996 / 5,120 = 0.30. P(> 3) is
384	  2.6e-4 and P(> 4) is 1.6e-5, so k = 4, and the cap is max(0, 4) = 4.
385	- **x = 1**, as ten bases including 0x9E7C000A would have read: one batch gave
386	  up once. lambda = 512 x 4.744 / 5,120 = 0.47. P(> 4) is 1.4e-4 and P(> 5) is
387	  1.1e-5, so k = 5, and the cap is max(2, 5) = 5, not 2.
388	
389	An ambient reach floor is the mean less four standard deviations. That flakes
390	about once in thirty thousand batches if the counts are near normal, and fails
391	any batch that falls further. So an ambient floor catches a collapse, not a
392	drift. Kernel exactly-once's `job:done` spreads by about 4% of its mean (sd
393	19.1 on 485.2), so its floor sits about 16% below the mean. A fall half that size trips about one batch in
394	forty, which a change can pass by luck. The before-and-after comparison above
395	is the instrument that sees a move that small, so it runs whenever a change
396	could move an ambient floor's rate, as it does for a cap, and not only when a
397	batch goes red.
398	
399	The directory barrier used to be the worst offender, because `sync_dir` is the
400	call a *durability* fix is most likely to add — one such fix moved floors in
401	three separate files in a single day. It now draws from its own fault stream, so
402	adding or relocating a barrier perturbs nothing else. A file sync with nothing
403	to flush is the other exception: it cannot fail and draws no fault, so syncing a
404	file that is already durable moves no roll. That is the shape most durability
405	fixes take after a power cycle. It still counts as a disk operation, so it
406	ticks an armed crash countdown and advances virtual time. No other IO call has
407	either treatment, so the caveat above still holds for the rest of them.
408	
409	### Finding a one-sided property: `charpente test --mutants`
410	
411	A green suite tells you your properties passed. It does not tell you they would
412	have **failed** if the code stopped working. A property that asserts something
413	true whether or not your job ran is *one-sided*: it costs time, reports success,
414	and is not evidence about anything.
415	
416	This is not hypothetical. A helpdesk app built on charpente shipped five such
417	properties — deleting its entire SLA sweep loop left the suite green.
418	
419	The instrument answers one question: **if this code did nothing, would anything
420	go red?** It runs your suite repeatedly against deliberately broken copies of
421	your source (patched in a scratch directory — nothing about the mutation touches
422	your tree or ships), and a mutant that survives is a gap in your oracles.
423	
424	```
425	scripts/mutants.sh --file src/jobs.rs
426	```
427	
428	A mutant reported **MISSED** is the finding. Worked example, from this repo's own
429	fixture app — one job whose whole effect is a counter bump, and two properties
430	that drive it identically and differ only in what they assert:
431	
432	```
433	$ charpente test --mutants --file crates/sim-fixture/src/lib.rs \
434	    --re 'BumpCounter::run.*Ok' --test-package sim-fixture \
435	    --property counter_bump_job_leaves_the_row_readable
436	
437	MISSED   crates/sim-fixture/src/lib.rs:40:9: replace BumpCounter::run -> Result<(), JobError> with Ok(())
438	mutants: 1 total — 0 caught, 1 missed, 0 unviable, 0 timed out
439	  1 MISSED, judged by "counter_bump_job_leaves_the_row_readable" ALONE: that property
440	  runs, reaches a verdict, and does not notice this change — it is ONE-SIDED with
441	  respect to the mutated code, and would pass just the same if the code were deleted.
442	  Fix: assert the EFFECT the mutated code produces (a value that differs when it does
443	  not run), not merely that the surrounding state is still readable. The surviving
444	  diff is in the run directory.
445	```
446	
447	cargo-mutants' own lines pass through (the `MISSED` line above is one). To
448	them the verb adds the summary, a MISSED or TIMED OUT paragraph and, when it
449	derives `--timeout`, its timing line (below); it names no caught mutant. The
450	run directory is cargo-mutants' own per-mutant record, at
451	`target/charpente-mutants/mutants.out/` under the directory the verb ran in
452	(`--dir`, default `.`): `outcomes.json`; `caught.txt`, `missed.txt`,
453	`timeout.txt` and `unviable.txt`, one mutant per line; and `diff/`, one patch
454	per mutant named by its file, line and column, where a MISSED mutant's
455	surviving diff is. The previous run's record moves to `mutants.out.old`. Both
456	sit under `target/`, which the scaffold's `.gitignore` leaves out of the
457	repository.
458	
459	The same mutant, judged by the honest sibling, is **CAUGHT**:
460	
461	```
462	$ charpente test --mutants … --property counter_bump_job_changes_the_row
463	mutants: 1 total — 1 caught, 0 missed, 0 unviable, 0 timed out
464	```
465	
466	Both properties ran 256 runs and reached ~147 verdicts each, so neither
467	result is an artifact of a property that never executed. The only difference is
468	the assertion: one checks the row is still *readable*, the other checks it now
469	reads `hits = 2`.
470	
471	**Scope is part of the claim, and this is the part that misleads.** A mutant is
472	reported CAUGHT if *any* test in scope fails, so one honest sibling hides every
473	one-sided property beside it. `--property NAME` judges the mutants by a single
474	property — that is how you ask whether *that* property earns its place.
475	Similarly `--test-package` decides which packages' suites are allowed to run;
476	without this, the verb judges every mutant with `charpente-core` and
477	`charpente-sim`'s tests — the default target set's oracles — so a `--file`
478	in any other crate must name its own package here, or its mutants are
479	judged by suites that never exercise them and all report MISSED.
480	
481	**Two results that are not findings.** `unviable` means the mutant did not
482	compile — your types rejected it, which is the compile-time contract doing its
483	job. `timed out` means the run did **not resolve**: it is not a catch, and the
484	verb will not let it read as one.
485	
486	The timeout follows the scope too. cargo-mutants times its own baseline over
487	one package, the mutated file's, while every mutant runs all the packages in
488	`--test-package`. So whenever those differ (two or more test packages, or one
489	that is not the `--file`s' package) and no `--timeout` is given, the verb first
490	times one `cargo test` over the test set, passes five times that as the
491	timeout, and prints both numbers:
492	
493	```text
494	mutants: `cargo test` over charpente-core, charpente-sim took 8.6 s of wall time; that is what each mutant runs, and cargo-mutants' own baseline times only the mutated file's package, so the verb is passing --timeout 44 (5x)
495	```
496	
497	Under `--property` each mutant runs that one sim property, less than the set
498	that was timed, so the line says the time is an upper bound on a mutant's run
499	instead. An explicit `--timeout SECS` skips the timing run and is passed through
500	as given.
501	
502	**It is not part of `cargo test`.** Every mutant is a rebuild plus a test run,
503	so this is an on-demand instrument like the edge harness below, not something
504	your inner loop pays for. Scope it at a file or a function (`--file`, `--re`)
505	rather than turning it loose on a whole workspace. It needs the pinned tool:
506	`cargo install cargo-mutants --version 27.1.0 --locked`. The verb checks for it
507	(`cargo mutants --version`) before anything else runs, so a machine without it
508	exits 2 with that install line rather than after a timing run.
509	
510	### A note on the edge harness (platform dev tooling, not app surface)
511	
512	The repo also carries `crates/edge-harness`, which drives real built binaries
513	over real TCP with process- and connection-level faults (`kill -9`,
514	SIGSTOP/SIGCONT, severed or delayed connections) to prove the wire-level
515	versions of three guarantees: acked-implies-durable across a kill and a
516	restart, zero loss over converged writes across `charpente promote`, and exact
517	`Last-Event-ID` SSE resume. **It is not part of your app's testing story and
518	there is nothing to adopt** — `charpente test --sim` above is the app-level
519	interface, and it is where your properties belong. Two things are worth
520	knowing anyway. First, the boundary: `kill -9` is not power loss (killing a
521	process does not drop the OS page cache), so that rig proves ack *ordering*
522	and end-to-end crash recovery through real hyper/TCP, while the simulator
523	above owns power-loss and torn-write durability — if you are reasoning about
524	what charpente's durability claims rest on, they rest on the sim. Second, it
525	makes no seed promise: a scenario's reproduction is a recorded script file, not
526	a seed, which is exactly why app-level properties belong in sim. Its
527	process-touching tests are `#[ignore]`d out of the ordinary sweep and run on
528	demand via `scripts/edge-harness.sh`.

- `--faults-off AXIS,…` — with `--seed`, turn these `FaultConfig` axes off
  (any field but `corruption_scope`, which scopes two axes rather than being
  one). The seed's config is sampled first and these are turned off after, so
  every other field is the seed's own. A name that is not a field is a usage
  error.
- `--master-seed 0x…` — pick where the batch's seed chain starts, instead
  of fresh OS entropy, for a byte-identical repeat of an entire batch
  (every check's every run). Cannot be combined with `--seed`. The batch's
  last line is this flag with the batch's `--runs` and `--filter`.
- `--filter S` — run only the check named `S` when there is one, and
  otherwise every check whose name contains `S`. A failure's `repro:` line
  names its check, so it replays that check alone even when another check's
  name contains it (`charge` and `charge_twice`). Filtering happens
  **before** any seed is drawn, so a filtered batch consumes a different (but
  still fully reproducible) prefix of the seed chain than an unfiltered one
  — this is why every individual failure's repro line carries its own
  run's seed rather than relying on the batch's master seed.
- `--jobs N` — how many runs to run in parallel (default: the host's
  available parallelism). Every run's seed is pre-derived on the main
  thread, in registry order, before any work is handed out, so `--jobs 1`
  and `--jobs 8` run the identical seed sequence and produce byte-identical
  reports — worker scheduling is unobservable.
- `--format human|json` — human is the default; `json` emits one object with
  every fact the human report prints, keys in this order: `master_seed`,
  `runs`, `passed`, `failed` and `skipped` (run totals over every check),
  `coverage`, `missing_coverage` (`{check, key}` pairs), `checks` and
  `failures`. Under `--seed`, `seed` stands where `master_seed` does, since
  the replayed seed fed back as `--master-seed` would run another batch. It is
  followed by `inputs`, the choices `--inputs` gave in that flag's encoding,
  when the replay was given them, and `faults_off`, the axes `--faults-off`
  turned off in field order, when it was given those. Each of `checks`, in
  registry order, is `{check, status, passed, failed, skipped, distinct_inputs,
  drew_inputs, skipped_reasons}`: `status` is `ok`, `FAILED` or `untested`
  (under `--seed` too, where the human line says `skipped`), and
  `skipped_reasons` lists every reason, uncapped, as `{reason,
  count}` by count descending then reason, plus `detail` under `--seed`, the one
  run's own text. Each of `failures` lists every failing run, in seed order, as
  `{check, seed, config, fired, message, inputs, faults_off, first_message,
  replays, repro}`, with `config` carrying every fault axis. A check's first
  failure is the one a batch shrinks: its `inputs` are `{name, value}` pairs of
  the shrunk run, `message` is the shrunk run's, `first_message` appears only
  when the shrink slipped to another message, `replays` counts the candidates
  tried and `repro` replays the shrunk run. Every other failure is its own
  unshrunk run: its own drawn `inputs`, `faults_off` `[]`, `replays` 0, no
  `first_message`, and a `repro` that is its seed alone. Seeds are hex strings.
  The two report different totals: the human result line counts checks, and
  the JSON's top-level `passed`, `failed` and `skipped` count runs, each the sum
  of that field over `checks[]`.
- `--dir PATH` — the app crate directory to build and run sim tests from
  (default: `.`). This flag is consumed by the CLI itself; every other flag
  passes straight through to the sim binary the CLI builds and execs.

Exit codes: **0** no run of any selected check failed and every `require`d
coverage key was hit (skipped runs are reported, not failed — see "Giving up"
above; a green batch says how many runs tested each check, and a batch whose
every check is untested exits 0 too, its result line saying `nothing tested`);
**1** at least one run failed, or a coverage requirement went unmet — the
batch itself completed, but something in it was red; **2** the batch never got
that far — a build failure, no
`tests/sim.rs` target found, an unrecognized flag, `--inputs` or
`--faults-off` without `--seed` or with a value they cannot read, a filter
matching no tests, or the sim binary failing to launch or exiting by signal. Exit code
2 means "rerun once this is fixed," not "here is a reproducible bug."

### Reading a batch

A batch prints, on stderr before any run starts, the line that names its master
seed, so a batch you kill still shows the seed that reruns it:

```text
running 3 sim checks, 256 runs each, under random injected faults (master seed 0x0000000000000001)
```

Its report, on stdout, has the shape of `cargo test`'s ("Giving up" above
shows two). Like `cargo test`'s, it closes with a line per check directly
above the result, so the last lines of the output carry every check's status
and counts beside the verdict. In order:

- **One failure block per failing check**: its first failure in seed order,
  shrunk ("Reading a failure" and "Shrinking a failure" below). The check's
  other failing runs print no block; its line counts them, and `--format json`
  lists each one.
- **A line per unmet requirement**: `sim coverage requirement failed in
  <check>: "<key>" never occurred in <n> runs`, with what to do about it.
- **The skipped runs' reasons**, under each check that skipped any, most
  frequent first and then in byte order, each with its count. A check that
  tested nothing is headed `— never tested: every run was skipped`. A check
  lists at most eight reasons and counts the rest on one line; `\n`, `\r` and
  `\t` in a reason print as those two-character escapes, so every reason stays
  on one line.
- **The checks that draw no inputs**, named, when any check with a tested run
  drew none: each of their runs tested the same scripted case.
- **A line per check**, in registry order: `check <name> ... <status>
  (<counts>)`. A run that passed or failed *tested* the check; a run that gave
  up was *skipped*. The status is `FAILED` when a run failed or a `require`d
  key never occurred, `untested` when no run tested the check, and `ok`
  otherwise. The counts are how many runs tested it (`52 tested`), how many
  distinct inputs those runs drew when it draws any (`203 tested over 181
  distinct inputs`, "Drawing inputs" above), how many failed when any did
  (`64 tested: 16 failed`), how many were skipped when any were (`52 tested,
  12 skipped`), and the keys that never occurred (`required "restart" never
  occurred`).
- **The result**: `sim result: ok`, `FAILED`, or `nothing tested` when no check
  passed and none failed, then how many checks passed, failed and (if any)
  were untested, and how many of the batch's runs tested a check.
- **The rerun command**: `rerun exactly this batch: charpente test --sim
  --master-seed 0x…`, with `--runs` when the batch ran another count than 256
  and `--filter` when it had one. Pasted, it prints this report again, byte
  for byte, for any `--jobs`.

There is no line for the faults that fired. To confirm that a fault a property
depends on actually happened, `require` its coverage key (`sim_tests! {
orders_charge_once require ["fault:outbound_refused"] }`): an unmet requirement
fails the check, and its line names the key. That makes "the refused reply was
exercised" a claim the batch checks rather than a number someone has to read.

The human report is for reading, not parsing: read `--format json` in a
program.

```text
  shrunk: 3 draws to 2, faults off: bit_flip, read_error, in 87 replays
  first:  exactly-once violated: hits 3, done 1 for key 812
  repro:  charpente test --sim --filter receipts_exactly_once --seed 0x8bee1752811ae873 --inputs 03c801 --faults-off bit_flip,read_error
```

This is a check's first failure in the batch, shrunk ("Shrinking a failure"
below): every line but `first:` describes the smallest run the harness found
that still fails the check, and `repro:` replays exactly that run. Each line,
in order:

- The first line is that run's own `Err` message (or an absorbed panic
  payload) — the actual claim that failed.
- `seed` is the one `u64` that determined this entire run: virtual
  time, every entropy draw, the fault matrix's decisions and, unless the
  repro passes `--inputs`, every `sim.input()` draw.
- `config` is the run's `FaultConfig` — the fault rates and latency ranges
  that were ENABLED (per-run swarm sampling, glossed under the checkers
  above): the seed's sampled config with the axes on the `shrunk:` line
  turned off. It is a set of probabilities, so it tells you what kind of
  trouble was *possible*: `crash_torn: 0.664668` means torn writes were
  likely in this run, not that any occurred. Do not read a diagnosis
  off this line — that is the next one's job. The last three fields are the
  clock axes ("Wall time and its faults"): here each clock drew its own skew
  within ±41.2 s of true time, no reading stepped back, and each power cycle
  had an even chance of a jump of up to three days.
- `fired` is what ACTUALLY happened: the run's coverage map, every
  fault and event that really occurred, with counts. This is the line to
  reason from. A high probability whose key is absent here never fired, and
  an explanation resting on it is wrong. `fired: nothing` is a real and
  valuable answer — it means no injected fault was involved and the failure
  is a plain bug. (This line exists because it once did not: a durability
  finding was attributed to `dir_entry_loss: 0.477` by three separate
  readers, none of whom could have known whether that axis fired, because
  the failure path discarded coverage entirely — docs/LEDGER.md 2026-09-07.)
- `inputs` is every `sim.input()` draw the run made, by name, in draw order
  ("Drawing inputs" above). A run that drew nothing has no `inputs:` line.
- `shrunk` says how far shrinking got: how many inputs the first failure
  drew and how many the shrunk run drew, counted as the `inputs:` line lists
  them; the fault axes it turned off (`none` when it needed them all); and
  how many runs it replayed. The shrunk run can draw more than the first: a
  fault turned off can let a loop run longer. `shrunk: nothing smaller fails, in N replays`
  means no smaller run failed the check, so the block is the first failure's
  own and its repro is the seed alone.
- `first` is the first failure's message, printed only when the shrunk run
  failed the check with another one (a slipped shrink, below).
- `repro` is not advice, it **is** the reproduction: paste that exact line
  and the same run happens again, byte for byte. `--seed` replays a literal
  seed; `--inputs` appears only when the shrunk run's choices are not the
  ones the seed draws, and `--faults-off` only when it turned axes off (both
  above). There is no separate "figure out how to reproduce this" step —
  the failure message already did that work. Replaying it prints the same
  block without `shrunk:` and `first:`, since a replay is one run and shrinks
  nothing.

The check's other failures in the batch print no block: its check line counts
them (`64 tested: 16 failed`), and `--format json` lists each one, unshrunk,
with a repro that is its seed alone.

The same discipline extends outward: `run_universes!`/`run_universes_swarm!`
(the frozen internal-suite macros the platform's own tests use) and
`charpente test --sim` share one seed→behavior mapping, except that only
`charpente test --sim` samples the clock axes. So `CHARPENTE_SEED=0x… cargo
test -p <pkg> --test <file>` and `charpente test --sim --seed 0x…` are the
same idea at two different layers, each replaying its own layer's run: a
failure's seed is always enough, on its own, to see the exact same run
again.

### Shrinking a failure

A failing run usually carries more than its bug: inputs that play no part, and
fault axes that were on but did nothing to it. So the harness replays the first
failure of each check with smaller choices and fewer faults, and keeps each
smaller run that still fails the same check. The last one it keeps is the run
the block shows. The rule is the same for every check.

It shrinks the recorded choice sequence, not the values (Hypothesis's approach):
each choice is the one its draw used, so a smaller choice is a smaller, simpler
value (`lo`, the first item, the identity order), and a draw past the end of
the choices reads 0. Its passes run in rounds, repeated until a whole round
keeps nothing:

1. delete chunks of the choices, 8, 4, 2 and then 1 long, from the end toward
   the start;
2. set each choice to 0;
3. search each choice down toward 0 (galloping up from 1, then bisecting), so a
   small value that fails is found even when the values between it and the
   recorded choice pass;
4. turn off each fault axis that is on, one at a time, in `FaultConfig` field
   order. An axis is on when it could fire: a clock axis whose chance is 0 is
   off whatever its size, so `faults off:` never lists it;
5. lower equal choices together: for each nonzero value two or more choices
   hold, set all of them to 0 and then search them down toward 0 as one value,
   so a failure that needs the same entity drawn twice (the same lab, the same
   product) reaches the lowest one, where lowering either draw alone makes the
   two differ and passes. Then, only in a round where everything before kept
   nothing, an axis turned off counting as a keep, each pair of those choices
   the same way, for a value that also sits where the failure does not need
   it. A whole group costs one candidate and a search, as cheap as passes 2
   and 3, so whole groups are tried in every round, right after pass 4. The
   pairs wait because k equal choices make k(k-1)/2 of them, enough to spend
   the whole budget: run while the other passes can still shrink the run,
   they could leave on fault axes the failure does not need, or inputs larger
   than it needs. Waiting costs a whole round of the other passes first, so
   among many choices the budget can run out before a needed pair is tried;
   the shrunk run then still fails the check and replays, with more draws
   than it needs.

A round that keeps nothing ends the shrink on a local minimum: no step of these
passes shrinks the run and still fails. They do not search every smaller run,
so a smaller one that fails the check can still exist. A shrink that spends its
budget (below) ends where the budget ran out, which can be short of a local
minimum.

A candidate is kept when the same check fails, with any message. One that
passes or gives up is not kept, so a clock axis whose removal turns the failure
into a clock-excused skip stays on. A smaller input can move where faults land,
and a fault turned off can change how many inputs a run draws (a retry loop that
no longer retries). Neither breaks anything, because the harness judges a
candidate only by replaying it, exactly as the printed repro does.

Shrinking runs on the first failure of each check in seed order, never in
completion order, and each shrink depends only on its check, seed and first
failure. Its budget is 500 replays, counted rather than timed, so the block is
identical for any `--jobs` and on any machine. A shrink that spends the budget
stops with the smallest run found so far. A workload that panics prints the
panic's message on stderr each time a shrink replay panics; the report itself is
on stdout, written once every shrink has finished.

**A slipped shrink.** Any failure of the same check counts, so the shrunk run
can fail it for another reason than the first did. The headline is then the
shrunk run's own message, `first:` keeps the original, and `repro:` replays the
shrunk run. The original is the seed alone: drop `--inputs` and `--faults-off`
from the repro. When the two messages name different bugs, fix the one the
repro shows, then rerun the batch.

### Re-basing a pinned property: `CHARPENTE_BASE_SEED`

Some properties fix their base seed (`run_universes_swarm_with!(BASE, N, …)`)
so their `floor:` rates have a stable denominator. That is right for a rate and
wrong for a correctness claim: a fixed base means the property only ever
examines the same N runs, while a green run reads as though it examined
the space.

`CHARPENTE_BASE_SEED=0x… cargo test -p <pkg> --test <file>` re-bases every
pinned property in that binary, so the claim "this property holds" can actually
be tested rather than assumed:

```text
charpente-sim [realtime]: re-basing 0x000000002eb20001 -> 0x00000000a11ce001 under
  CHARPENTE_BASE_SEED — coverage requirements, floors and ceilings skipped (they
  are rates measured at the pinned base)
```

Like `CHARPENTE_SEED`, it takes hex with or without `0x`, and `_` separators
are ignored, so a base copied from the source as written (`0x2EB2_5A10`) works
as is; a value that is not hex panics naming the variable it was read from.

Floors, ceilings and `require:` keys are skipped under the override, for the
reason the floor's own panic text gives: they are rates measured AT a base, so
evaluating them somewhere else compares against a denominator that was never
taken there.
What the mode tests is the property's own assertions, which are untouched.

**A correctness oracle should pass at every base.** If it passes at its pinned
base and fails at others, it is not flaky — it is failing, and the pinned base
is hiding it. Two realtime properties were found exactly that way
(docs/LEDGER.md 2026-09-07).

One caveat worth knowing before you chase a floor panic: an IO call consumes RNG
draws, so changing *where* an IO operation happens inside code a property never
names reshuffles every run at a pinned base. Floors move for that reason far
more often than they move because an oracle decayed.

So a floor that falls after such a change is re-measured, not defended and not
quietly lowered. Run the property before and after the change at the same ten or
more fresh bases (`CHARPENTE_BASE_SEED`) and compare the key's mean. It has
decayed if the after-mean sits more than one Welch standard error below the
before-mean, where that error is `sqrt(sd_before²/n_before + sd_after²/n_after)`
over the per-base counts. Within one standard error, the floor is re-set to its
new exact count at its pinned base, with both distributions recorded; beyond
it, the fall is the finding. A base where either binary fails on an unrelated,
named bug is left out of both sides, and the record says which. One standard
error is deliberately strict: pure noise crosses it roughly a sixth to a quarter
of the time, which errs toward stopping to look.

A cap that rises after such a change asks a different question, because a
give-up is not a lost verdict when the same run used to pass having
checked nothing. So judge the rise by the verdicts the property reached, over
the same ten or more fresh bases: count its passes that covered its reach key
(the key its `floor:` counts), and beside them its vacuous passes (runs
that passed without covering that key). A cap may rise only if the passes
covering the reach key did not fall by more than one Welch standard error.
Then the new give-ups replaced vacuous passes, not verdicts, and the cap is
re-set by its own convention, with both distributions recorded. If those
passes fell by more than one standard error, the rise is the finding. Neither
the reach key's own count nor the vacuous passes can decide it alone: 20 more
give-ups beside 1 fewer vacuous pass means 19 passes that checked something
became give-ups. A pinned cap can read the same
number on both binaries while the rate behind it moved, so the test runs
whenever the change could have moved it, not only when the pinned count did.
That is also why every capped property floors its reach key: without one, the
next change that costs it reach passes with every cap still met.

At a pinned base both bounds are exact counts. At an ambient base, where the
counts move batch to batch, both are margins over ten or more fresh batches.

An ambient give-up cap is the larger of two numbers:
- twice the largest fresh-batch count;
- the smallest k with P(Poisson(lambda) > k) < 1e-4, where
  lambda = n x U(x) / N. Here n is the runs in one batch, N the runs
  over all the fresh batches, and x the give-ups among them. U(x) is the exact
  one-sided 95% Poisson upper bound for x: 2.996 for x = 0, 4.744 for 1, and
  6.296 for 2.

The second number matters where give-ups are rare. When no batch gave up,
twice the largest count is 0, which one legitimately exhausted run fails.
When one batch gave up once, it is 2, which a healthy batch fails about once
in eighty. Where counts are large the first number is the larger, and the
second only confirms it.

Two worked examples for the WAL fault matrix, whose 10 fresh batches of
n = 512 make N = 5,120:
- **x = 0**, as measured. lambda = 512 x 2.996 / 5,120 = 0.30. P(> 3) is
  2.6e-4 and P(> 4) is 1.6e-5, so k = 4, and the cap is max(0, 4) = 4.
- **x = 1**, as ten bases including 0x9E7C000A would have read: one batch gave
  up once. lambda = 512 x 4.744 / 5,120 = 0.47. P(> 4) is 1.4e-4 and P(> 5) is
  1.1e-5, so k = 5, and the cap is max(2, 5) = 5, not 2.

An ambient reach floor is the mean less four standard deviations. That flakes
about once in thirty thousand batches if the counts are near normal, and fails
any batch that falls further. So an ambient floor catches a collapse, not a
drift. Kernel exactly-once's `job:done` spreads by about 4% of its mean (sd
19.1 on 485.2), so its floor sits about 16% below the mean. A fall half that size trips about one batch in
forty, which a change can pass by luck. The before-and-after comparison above
is the instrument that sees a move that small, so it runs whenever a change
could move an ambient floor's rate, as it does for a cap, and not only when a
batch goes red.

The directory barrier used to be the worst offender, because `sync_dir` is the
call a *durability* fix is most likely to add — one such fix moved floors in
three separate files in a single day. It now draws from its own fault stream, so
adding or relocating a barrier perturbs nothing else. A file sync with nothing
to flush is the other exception: it cannot fail and draws no fault, so syncing a
file that is already durable moves no roll. That is the shape most durability
fixes take after a power cycle. It still counts as a disk operation, so it
ticks an armed crash countdown and advances virtual time. No other IO call has
either treatment, so the caveat above still holds for the rest of them.

### Finding a one-sided property: `charpente test --mutants`

A green suite tells you your properties passed. It does not tell you they would
have **failed** if the code stopped working. A property that asserts something
true whether or not your job ran is *one-sided*: it costs time, reports success,
and is not evidence about anything.

This is not hypothetical. A helpdesk app built on charpente shipped five such
properties — deleting its entire SLA sweep loop left the suite green.

The instrument answers one question: **if this code did nothing, would anything
go red?** It runs your suite repeatedly against deliberately broken copies of
your source (patched in a scratch directory — nothing about the mutation touches
your tree or ships), and a mutant that survives is a gap in your oracles.

```
scripts/mutants.sh --file src/jobs.rs
```

A mutant reported **MISSED** is the finding. Worked example, from this repo's own
fixture app — one job whose whole effect is a counter bump, and two properties
that drive it identically and differ only in what they assert:

```
$ charpente test --mutants --file crates/sim-fixture/src/lib.rs \
    --re 'BumpCounter::run.*Ok' --test-package sim-fixture \
    --property counter_bump_job_leaves_the_row_readable

MISSED   crates/sim-fixture/src/lib.rs:40:9: replace BumpCounter::run -> Result<(), JobError> with Ok(())
mutants: 1 total — 0 caught, 1 missed, 0 unviable, 0 timed out
  1 MISSED, judged by "counter_bump_job_leaves_the_row_readable" ALONE: that property
  runs, reaches a verdict, and does not notice this change — it is ONE-SIDED with
  respect to the mutated code, and would pass just the same if the code were deleted.
  Fix: assert the EFFECT the mutated code produces (a value that differs when it does
  not run), not merely that the surrounding state is still readable. The surviving
  diff is in the run directory.
```

cargo-mutants' own lines pass through (the `MISSED` line above is one). To
them the verb adds the summary, a MISSED or TIMED OUT paragraph and, when it
derives `--timeout`, its timing line (below); it names no caught mutant. The
run directory is cargo-mutants' own per-mutant record, at
`target/charpente-mutants/mutants.out/` under the directory the verb ran in
(`--dir`, default `.`): `outcomes.json`; `caught.txt`, `missed.txt`,
`timeout.txt` and `unviable.txt`, one mutant per line; and `diff/`, one patch
per mutant named by its file, line and column, where a MISSED mutant's
surviving diff is. The previous run's record moves to `mutants.out.old`. Both
sit under `target/`, which the scaffold's `.gitignore` leaves out of the
repository.

The same mutant, judged by the honest sibling, is **CAUGHT**:

```
$ charpente test --mutants … --property counter_bump_job_changes_the_row
mutants: 1 total — 1 caught, 0 missed, 0 unviable, 0 timed out
```

Both properties ran 256 runs and reached ~147 verdicts each, so neither
result is an artifact of a property that never executed. The only difference is
the assertion: one checks the row is still *readable*, the other checks it now
reads `hits = 2`.

**Scope is part of the claim, and this is the part that misleads.** A mutant is
reported CAUGHT if *any* test in scope fails, so one honest sibling hides every
one-sided property beside it. `--property NAME` judges the mutants by a single
property — that is how you ask whether *that* property earns its place.
Similarly `--test-package` decides which packages' suites are allowed to run;
without this, the verb judges every mutant with `charpente-core` and
`charpente-sim`'s tests — the default target set's oracles — so a `--file`
in any other crate must name its own package here, or its mutants are
judged by suites that never exercise them and all report MISSED.

**Two results that are not findings.** `unviable` means the mutant did not
compile — your types rejected it, which is the compile-time contract doing its
job. `timed out` means the run did **not resolve**: it is not a catch, and the
verb will not let it read as one.

The timeout follows the scope too. cargo-mutants times its own baseline over
one package, the mutated file's, while every mutant runs all the packages in
`--test-package`. So whenever those differ (two or more test packages, or one
that is not the `--file`s' package) and no `--timeout` is given, the verb first
times one `cargo test` over the test set, passes five times that as the
timeout, and prints both numbers:

```text
mutants: `cargo test` over charpente-core, charpente-sim took 8.6 s of wall time; that is what each mutant runs, and cargo-mutants' own baseline times only the mutated file's package, so the verb is passing --timeout 44 (5x)
```

Under `--property` each mutant runs that one sim property, less than the set
that was timed, so the line says the time is an upper bound on a mutant's run
instead. An explicit `--timeout SECS` skips the timing run and is passed through
as given.

**It is not part of `cargo test`.** Every mutant is a rebuild plus a test run,
so this is an on-demand instrument like the edge harness below, not something
your inner loop pays for. Scope it at a file or a function (`--file`, `--re`)
rather than turning it loose on a whole workspace. It needs the pinned tool:
`cargo install cargo-mutants --version 27.1.0 --locked`. The verb checks for it
(`cargo mutants --version`) before anything else runs, so a machine without it
exits 2 with that install line rather than after a timing run.

### A note on the edge harness (platform dev tooling, not app surface)

The repo also carries `crates/edge-harness`, which drives real built binaries
over real TCP with process- and connection-level faults (`kill -9`,
SIGSTOP/SIGCONT, severed or delayed connections) to prove the wire-level
versions of three guarantees: acked-implies-durable across a kill and a
restart, zero loss over converged writes across `charpente promote`, and exact
`Last-Event-ID` SSE resume. **It is not part of your app's testing story and
there is nothing to adopt** — `charpente test --sim` above is the app-level
interface, and it is where your properties belong. Two things are worth
knowing anyway. First, the boundary: `kill -9` is not power loss (killing a
process does not drop the OS page cache), so that rig proves ack *ordering*
and end-to-end crash recovery through real hyper/TCP, while the simulator
above owns power-loss and torn-write durability — if you are reasoning about
what charpente's durability claims rest on, they rest on the sim. Second, it
makes no seed promise: a scenario's reproduction is a recorded script file, not
a seed, which is exactly why app-level properties belong in sim. Its
process-touching tests are `#[ignore]`d out of the ordinary sweep and run on
demand via `scripts/edge-harness.sh`.

## 13. describe — the machine-readable contract

`charpente describe` renders the full shape of a mounted `App` — every table (with its
version, structural fingerprint, indexes, migration chain, and whether it's tenant-scoped),
every route (method, pattern, name, whether it requires auth, the tenant scope it admits every caller to if it is declared `public(Org)`, by that tenant type's `NAME`, whether it declared `cross_tenant`, whether it's an SSE stream),
every registered event (name, payload type, and the tenant it belongs to if it is `scoped_by` — §11), every job (name, retry policy, the tenant scope it acts in if it is `scoped_by`, by its `NAME`, whether it declared `cross_tenant`, and its `outbound` host and `timeout_ms`, or `null` for a pure job), every cron entry
(name, interval), every declared `Host` as `outbound_hosts` (the host, the variable NAMES it reads, the header names those fill, and its two caps; never a value — §6), and the app's config — as one JSON (or human-readable) document. It is a pure walk of the app's own registries (DESIGN §7): no
disk writes beyond the ephemeral describe run itself, no socket, no kernel loop. This is
the "what exists" query an agent would otherwise burn context reconstructing by reading
every `#[table]`/`#[route]`/`#[job]` item across the crate by hand.

There are two ways to ask for it: from inside the app binary itself (`charpente::launch`,
below), or from the outside without running the app at all (`charpente describe`, the CLI
verb, further below).

### The one-line main: `charpente::launch`

`charpente::launch(addr, data_dir, build)` replaces a hand-rolled `fn main` that calls
`App::open` and `charpente::serve::serve` directly (§5, §7). It owns argv dispatch: no
verb serves the app exactly as before; `describe [--format json|human]` renders the
contract to stdout and exits, without ever touching `data_dir`. `build` is the same
`fn(Box<dyn Disk>, Box<dyn Entropy>) -> io::Result<App>` shape used everywhere else an
app hands its construction over to the platform (sim tests, the CLI verb below) — the
one function this migration asks you to factor `fn main`'s body into.

```rust
use charpente::core::io::{Disk, Entropy};
use charpente::core::table::Id;
use charpente::http::{ApiError, App, AppConfig};
use charpente::{Schema, Tx, View, Wire, route, routes, table};
use serde::Deserialize;

#[table(global)]
struct Note {
    id: Id<Note>,
    text: String,
}

#[derive(Wire, Deserialize)]
struct NoteBody {
    text: String,
}

#[route(POST "/notes/:id", public)]
fn create_note(tx: &mut Tx, id: Id<Note>, body: NoteBody) -> Result<Id<Note>, ApiError> {
    tx.put(&Note {
        id,
        text: body.text,
    });
    Ok(id)
}

fn build_app(disk: Box<dyn Disk>, entropy: Box<dyn Entropy>) -> std::io::Result<App> {
    Ok(App::open(disk, Schema::new().table::<Note>(), entropy, AppConfig::default())?
        .mount(routes![create_note]))
}

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    charpente::launch("0.0.0.0:8080", "./data", build_app)
}
```

exactly as a hand-rolled `main` would; `myapp describe` and `myapp describe --format json`
are new, for free — and so is `restore` (§15). The serve form takes the operator's outbound
flags (§5), each repeatable for a different host or CA file, which `launch` hands to
`serve_with`: `myapp --outbound-base pay.example=https://127.0.0.1:8443 --outbound-ca
./ca.pem`. An unrecognized verb, a bad `--format` value, or a serve flag that is unknown,
missing its value, naming a host or CA file a second time, or (for `--outbound-base`) not
`HOST=URL` exits 2 with a pinned usage message, before the data directory is touched:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
usage: <app> [describe [--format json|human]]
       <app> restore --from BUCKET --prefix PREFIX [--to DIR] [--force]
       <app> [--outbound-base HOST=URL]... [--outbound-ca PATH]...  — no verb serves the app
```

(`launch.rs`'s `the_guide_quotes_the_usage_text_the_binary_actually_prints` `include_str!`s
this file and asserts the block above is the constant verbatim, so the two cannot drift
apart silently again — they did once, when §15 was added.)

never `serve_replicated`, so neither a witness conflict nor a strict-witness deadline can
happen here; those are `charpente::serve_replicated`-only stops) comes from one of three
distinct moments, each with its own line on stderr:

- **Before any kernel exists.** The data directory cannot be opened — its parent is missing
  or the node cannot read it (§1), the path is empty, or it is not a directory you can
  create: `charpente failed to start: the data directory "<path>" ...` or `charpente failed
  to start: could not fsync directory "<parent>" ...`, naming the cause and the fix. Or opening
  `/dev/urandom` (`ProdEntropy::new`) or `build` (`App::open`) fails — a table-gate barrier
  from a schema this binary cannot open, or an ordinary platform IO failure (the store, the
  log): `charpente refused to start: ...`/`charpente failed to start — fix the store/log and
  restart: ...`. Or the outbound client's setup refuses (§5, §6) — an unset or malformed
  credential variable, a bad `--outbound-base`, an unreadable `--outbound-ca`:
  `charpente refused to start: ...`, the refusal's own text naming the fix. Or the outbound
  client cannot be built for want of resources, its runtime or its thread: `charpente failed
  to start: outbound: the client's runtime could not be built: ...` or `... the client's
  thread could not be spawned: ...`, each ending `— raise the process's thread and file
  limits, then restart`. Or the HTTP bind fails, which `serve_with` attempts after the client
  is built and before it spawns the kernel thread: `charpente failed to start — could not
  bind <addr>: <the OS error> — free that address, or change the one the app passes to
  launch`.
- **The kernel stops on its own account** — a Pending job of a foreign shape (§6), a
  migration step this binary has no registration for, or a platform IO failure — and its
  stop line names which: `charpente kernel refused to start`/`stopped on a
  refusal`/`stopped on a platform IO failure`.
- **The HTTP edge thread ends before the kernel does** (most likely a panic — v0 has no
  admin-triggered shutdown): `charpente kernel stopped: the request channel closed, ...`.

In every case the line names the fix before `launch` exits.

### `charpente describe` — the CLI verb

The CLI verb builds and runs any app crate's binary from the outside — no code changes to
the app required, not even the `launch` migration above (it works against any binary that
calls `charpente::launch`, which is what makes it a description of the app rather than
something the app has to expose over HTTP itself):

<!-- pinned -->
```text
usage: charpente describe [--dir PATH] [--format json|human] [--bin NAME]
       --dir PATH   the app crate directory to build and describe (default: .)
       --bin NAME   which binary to describe when the crate has several (default: the sole binary, else the one named like the package)
```

```bash
charpente describe --dir ./myapp --format json
```

`--dir` defaults to the current directory. `charpente describe` runs `cargo build` in
that directory, picks its one binary target (or the one matching `--bin`, or the one
named like the package when several exist and none is named), and execs it with
`describe --format <F>` — the exact same argv path `charpente::launch` handles above.
Cargo's own errors (a missing `Cargo.toml`, a build failure) are forwarded verbatim,
never wrapped in a framework message.

### The invoicing contract

### Where the guarantee stops

**The guarantee is about the typed surface the framework hands your app.** A
route handler receives a `Tx`, and a scoped job the `ScopedTx` of the tenant it
was enqueued in; through a `Tx`, a scoped table is unreachable without
`tx.scope::<Org>(org, ctx)?`. That is the property a
reviewer checks by reading one line per handler, and the compiler enforces it.

It is **not** a sandbox around the process. Your own `main` builds the `App` it
hands to `launch`, so it holds `App::db()` — and a `Db` reaches every tenant:
`Db::snapshot()` exposes scoped and raw reads that take a scope on the caller's
word with no `authorize` on the path (replication seeding, the archive and
`restore` are built on them; operator code and a sim oracle read one tenant's
rows with `get_scoped(scope, id)`, `scan_scoped(scope)`, `scan_from_scoped(scope,
from_id, limit)` and `scan_by_scoped(scope, index, key)`, `scope` being the
tenant's raw id), and `Db::begin_group` can mint the `CrossTenant`
token, for the length of that group's borrow. Whoever holds the `Db` holds the store, with the same standing as
whoever holds the data directory: an operator, not a request.

**It covers the platform's own tables too.** The job queue (`JobRow`) holds every tenant's
job payloads and the tenant each job runs in, the event log (`EventRow`) holds every
tenant's events, and the migration record (`SchemaVersion`) is the migration gate's own
state. No app code reads or writes one through a transaction, whether a handler's or a
job's, on a bare `Tx` or through a `ScopedTx`'s deref (§6). rustc prints this for a read of any of the
three, with your row type in place of `<row>`:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
`<row>` is one of the platform's tables, and a transaction does not read it
`<row>` is read through `Db::snapshot`, never through a transaction
the platform's tables — the job queue (`JobRow`), the event log (`EventRow`) and the migration record (`SchemaVersion`) — are the platform's own state, and the first two hold every tenant's rows, so neither a handler nor a job reads them; code that holds the `Db` reads them through a snapshot:
    db.snapshot()?.scan::<<row>>()?
a route that shows a job's progress or an event's history reads a table of the app's own, written in the same transaction as the enqueue or the emit, or subscribes to the events
```

So an admin job list or an activity feed is a table of the app's own, written in the same
transaction as the enqueue or the emit and scoped like any other, or, for a live feed, a
`Subscription` (§11). Operator code reads the platform's tables through `db.snapshot()`, as
§8's oracles do, since whoever holds the `Db` holds every tenant already. The one
transaction that reads a job row is the dispatcher's own: `Tx::get_job` takes the
`TenantAdmission` only a `Group` mints, which no handler or job holds.

The read seal is on the table's name as well as its type, as the write seal is. A
hand-written `Row` whose `TABLE` is one of the three names, scoped or not, fails to build at
each read the binary can reach, on a bare `Tx`, a `ScopedTx` or an `across_tenants` scan,
reported by `cargo build` and not `cargo check`:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
this Row's TABLE is "charpente.jobs", the platform's job queue — a transaction does not read the platform's tables, because the queue holds every tenant's job payloads and the tenant each one runs in; give this table a name of its own, and read the queue through `db.snapshot()` from code that holds the `Db`
this Row's TABLE is "charpente.events", the platform's event log — a transaction does not read the platform's tables, because the log holds every tenant's events; give this table a name of its own, and read the log through `db.snapshot()` from code that holds the `Db`, or subscribe to its events
this Row's TABLE is "charpente.schema_versions", the platform's migration record — a transaction does not read the platform's tables, because the record is the migration gate's own state; give this table a name of its own, and read the record through `db.snapshot()` from code that holds the `Db`
```

**Sessions and API keys are the app's own.** `Session` and `ApiKey` (§5) are ordinary
`#[table(global)]` tables that `App::open` registers for you, and a handler reads and
writes them like any other global table. They carry no tenant data, and revoking a key is
`tx.delete::<ApiKey>(id)`, an ordinary write, by design. Being global, any id reaches any
subject's key, so a revoke checks the row's `subject` against the caller's first (§5's
`revoke_key`).

**Code outside a handler never takes a scope on its own word.** A job declares
`#[job(scoped_by = Org)]` and runs in the tenant its enqueuer opened or its fan-out
named (§6). Nothing else decides which, because no app code can write the job row that
carries that tenant, and an enqueue inside a tenant of another scope type is refused.
**Operator code that must act inside one tenant** — seeding, a test oracle, an admin
step in `main` — does not take a scope on its own word either. It begins a group, mints
a `TenantAdmission` from it, and opens the tenant with `admit_scope`:

```rust
use charpente::auth::Principal;
use charpente::http::ApiError;
use charpente::{Db, Id, Tenant, Tx, TxError, table};

#[table(global)]
struct Org {
    id: Id<Org>,
    name: String,
}

impl Tenant for Org {
    const NAME: &'static str = "Org";
    type Who = Principal;
    type Error = ApiError;
    fn authorize(_tx: &Tx, _who: &Principal, _scope: Id<Org>) -> Result<(), ApiError> {
        // Refuses everyone: the seed below never asks.
        Err(ApiError::Unauthorized)
    }
}

#[table(scoped_by = Org)]
struct Memo {
    id: Id<Memo>,
    text: String,
}

/// Seeds one tenant's first memo. `db.begin_group()` is the operator's
/// handle, and the admission it mints is what `admit_scope` asks for.
fn seed(db: &mut Db, org: Id<Org>) -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let mut group = db.begin_group()?;
    let admission = group.tenant_admission();
    let staged = group.stage(|tx| {
        tx.admit_scope::<Org>(org, &admission).put(&Memo {
            id: Id::from_raw(1),
            text: "welcome".to_string(),
        });
        Ok::<(), std::io::Error>(())
    });
    // `commit` on every path: a group dropped with staged writes panics.
    group.commit().map_err(|failure| failure.error)?;
    match staged {
        Ok(()) => Ok(()),
        Err(TxError::App(e)) | Err(TxError::Io(e)) => Err(e),
        Err(other) => Err(std::io::Error::other(format!("{other:?}"))),
    }
}
```

No `authorize` runs there. The operator has no principal to ask about, and already
holds the store. The admission carries the seal `CrossTenant` carries: its field is
private and `Group::tenant_admission` is its only constructor. So a handler, which holds
a `Tx` and a `Ctx` and never a `Group`, cannot mint one; `TenantAdmission(())` is
`error[E0423]`. Nor can anyone keep one: like `CrossTenant`, a `TenantAdmission`
borrows what its group borrows and is not `Clone`, so it goes out of reach with the group's
borrow of the `Db`, and a `static` or `thread_local!` refuses it — unless operator code
leaks its `Db`, which is the operator's standing used on purpose. The one-scope rule is the same contract whichever way a scope was
entered. Do not build an app-internal helper that takes a raw scope and reads through
`Db::snapshot`: that is the one shape that looks tenant-aware and is not.

### Deliberately not built

Stated so you do not go looking:

- **Nested or hierarchical scopes** (Org → Project → …). One level.
- **Cross-tenant writes in one transaction.** A transaction opens one scope.
- **Platform-derived tenancy.** There is no `Principal → Org` resolver hook;
  the tenant is named by your code at the `tx.scope` line and nowhere else.
- **Retrofitting existing tables.** Every table declares `scoped_by` or
  `global`, but no migration is forced: `global` is what a bare table
  always was, and a table cannot gain a scope in place — see the refusal
  above.
- **Tenant-local ids.** Ids stay globally unique and app-minted.
- **Permissions.** This answers *which tenant*, never *what may this principal
  do*; API-key scopes and permissions are their own future design.

transaction that reads a job row is the dispatcher's own: `Tx::get_job` takes the
`TenantAdmission` only a `Group` mints, which no handler or job holds.

The read seal is on the table's name as well as its type, as the write seal is. A
hand-written `Row` whose `TABLE` is one of the three names, scoped or not, fails to build at
each read the binary can reach, on a bare `Tx`, a `ScopedTx` or an `across_tenants` scan,
reported by `cargo build` and not `cargo check`:

<!-- pinned -->
```text
this Row's TABLE is "charpente.jobs", the platform's job queue — a transaction does not read the platform's tables, because the queue holds every tenant's job payloads and the tenant each one runs in; give this table a name of its own, and read the queue through `db.snapshot()` from code that holds the `Db`
this Row's TABLE is "charpente.events", the platform's event log — a transaction does not read the platform's tables, because the log holds every tenant's events; give this table a name of its own, and read the log through `db.snapshot()` from code that holds the `Db`, or subscribe to its events
this Row's TABLE is "charpente.schema_versions", the platform's migration record — a transaction does not read the platform's tables, because the record is the migration gate's own state; give this table a name of its own, and read the record through `db.snapshot()` from code that holds the `Db`
```

**Sessions and API keys are the app's own.** `Session` and `ApiKey` (§5) are ordinary
`#[table(global)]` tables that `App::open` registers for you, and a handler reads and
writes them like any other global table. They carry no tenant data, and revoking a key is
`tx.delete::<ApiKey>(id)`, an ordinary write, by design. Being global, any id reaches any
subject's key, so a revoke checks the row's `subject` against the caller's first (§5's
`revoke_key`).

**Code outside a handler never takes a scope on its own word.** A job declares
`#[job(scoped_by = Org)]` and runs in the tenant its enqueuer opened or its fan-out
named (§6). Nothing else decides which, because no app code can write the job row that
carries that tenant, and an enqueue inside a tenant of another scope type is refused.
**Operator code that must act inside one tenant** — seeding, a test oracle, an admin
step in `main` — does not take a scope on its own word either. It begins a group, mints
a `TenantAdmission` from it, and opens the tenant with `admit_scope`:

```rust
use charpente::auth::Principal;
use charpente::http::ApiError;
use charpente::{Db, Id, Tenant, Tx, TxError, table};

#[table(global)]
struct Org {
    id: Id<Org>,
    name: String,
}

impl Tenant for Org {
    const NAME: &'static str = "Org";
    type Who = Principal;
    type Error = ApiError;
    fn authorize(_tx: &Tx, _who: &Principal, _scope: Id<Org>) -> Result<(), ApiError> {
        // Refuses everyone: the seed below never asks.
        Err(ApiError::Unauthorized)
    }
}

#[table(scoped_by = Org)]
struct Memo {
    id: Id<Memo>,
    text: String,
}

/// Seeds one tenant's first memo. `db.begin_group()` is the operator's
/// handle, and the admission it mints is what `admit_scope` asks for.
fn seed(db: &mut Db, org: Id<Org>) -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let mut group = db.begin_group()?;
    let admission = group.tenant_admission();
    let staged = group.stage(|tx| {
        tx.admit_scope::<Org>(org, &admission).put(&Memo {
            id: Id::from_raw(1),
            text: "welcome".to_string(),
        });
        Ok::<(), std::io::Error>(())
    });
    // `commit` on every path: a group dropped with staged writes panics.
    group.commit().map_err(|failure| failure.error)?;
    match staged {
        Ok(()) => Ok(()),
        Err(TxError::App(e)) | Err(TxError::Io(e)) => Err(e),
        Err(other) => Err(std::io::Error::other(format!("{other:?}"))),
    }
}
```

No `authorize` runs there. The operator has no principal to ask about, and already
holds the store. The admission carries the seal `CrossTenant` carries: its field is
private and `Group::tenant_admission` is its only constructor. So a handler, which holds
a `Tx` and a `Ctx` and never a `Group`, cannot mint one; `TenantAdmission(())` is
`error[E0423]`. Nor can anyone keep one: like `CrossTenant`, a `TenantAdmission`
borrows what its group borrows and is not `Clone`, so it goes out of reach with the group's
borrow of the `Db`, and a `static` or `thread_local!` refuses it — unless operator code
leaks its `Db`, which is the operator's standing used on purpose. The one-scope rule is the same contract whichever way a scope was
entered. Do not build an app-internal helper that takes a raw scope and reads through
`Db::snapshot`: that is the one shape that looks tenant-aware and is not.

### Deliberately not built

Stated so you do not go looking:

- **Nested or hierarchical scopes** (Org → Project → …). One level.
- **Cross-tenant writes in one transaction.** A transaction opens one scope.
- **Platform-derived tenancy.** There is no `Principal → Org` resolver hook;
  the tenant is named by your code at the `tx.scope` line and nowhere else.
- **Retrofitting existing tables.** Every table declares `scoped_by` or
  `global`, but no migration is forced: `global` is what a bare table
  always was, and a table cannot gain a scope in place — see the refusal
  above.
- **Tenant-local ids.** Ids stay globally unique and app-minted.
- **Permissions.** This answers *which tenant*, never *what may this principal
  do*; API-key scopes and permissions are their own future design.

content.content:
## 14. The TypeScript client

`crates/charpente-tsgen` turns one mounted app's `describe` contract (§13) into a
TypeScript client: branded id types and a declaration for every wire type — an `interface`
for a struct, a `type` union for an enum — a discriminated `Result<T, E>` per route, and
per-event dispatch for every SSE route that declared `emits(...)`. Nothing here is
hand-written per app — the emitter is a pure function of the contract — so getting the
generated client right is entirely a matter of getting the WIRE right.

### Deriving `Wire`

Every type that reaches a route's params, request body, response, or error, and every
`#[event]` payload, must implement `Wire` — the trait describing what a value looks like
once serde has encoded it, not what its Rust shape merely suggests. `#[derive(Wire)]`
reads serde's OWN attributes, so the schema matches what serde actually emits, and it
rejects, by name, any attribute it has no logic for — a schema that silently disagreed
with the wire would be worse than a compile error.

Read faithfully: `rename`, `rename_all` (`camelCase`, `snake_case`, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE`,
`kebab-case`), `skip`/`skip_serializing` (the field never appears in the schema at all, not
merely marked optional), `skip_serializing_if` (marks the field `optional` — see "64-bit
integers" below for what that means at an `Int64` position), and `#[serde(crate = "...")]`
(accepted and ignored: it only redirects serde_derive's own generated paths, and changes no
field, name, or shape).

Rejected, with the fix named in the message: `flatten` (hoists the inner type's fields in a
way the wire IR cannot express); `default` (changes whether a field may be absent — say
`Option<T>` or `skip_serializing_if` instead, so the wire semantics are explicit);
`skip_deserializing` (the field IS still emitted on the wire; only reads are affected);
`untagged` (an untagged value carries no discriminator for the schema to key on); a
struct-level `tag` (tagging is an enum concern, resolved on the enum itself); and the split
`rename(serialize = ..., deserialize = ...)` form (a wire schema is one shape, and
divergent serialize/deserialize names can't be represented).

```rust
use charpente::wire::{WireI64, WireU64};
use charpente::Wire;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Wire, Serialize, Deserialize)]
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")]
struct LineItemView {
    #[serde(rename = "sku")]
    item_code: String,
    unit_amount_cents: WireI64,
    quantity: WireU64,
    #[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]
    note: Option<String>,
}
```

An enum derives `Wire` too, and describes whichever of serde's *tagged* representations it
actually uses — a unit-only enum as a TypeScript string union, otherwise externally
(serde's default), internally (`tag = "..."`), or adjacently (`tag` + `content`) tagged;
`untagged` is refused for the same reason it is on a struct.

### 64-bit integers: `bigint` on both sides of the wire

A bare `u64`/`i64` at any wire position is a compile error naming the fix — above 2^53 a
JSON number silently loses precision in JavaScript, so `Wire` has no impl for either type
(DESIGN §3). `WireU64`/`WireI64` are the sanctioned carriers: they serialize as decimal
strings, and the generated TypeScript type is `bigint`. Every TypeScript fragment below is
copied verbatim from `ts-fixture/src/generated/client.ts` — the committed output of
`charpente gen-client` against `crates/ts-fixture-app`'s contract — not written from
memory:

```ts
export interface LimitExceeded {
  maxCents: bigint;
}
```

**Outbound (client to server)** needs no schema knowledge: `request()`'s `JSON.stringify`
runs a replacer that converts every `bigint` it meets to its decimal string BEFORE
serialization, unconditionally — dedented here out of the conditional spread it actually
sits inside, `request()`'s own `body` option:

```ts
JSON.stringify(body, (_k, v) =>
  typeof v === "bigint" ? v.toString() : v,
)
```

— which is sound because a type-checked call site can only ever hand this a `bigint`
where the schema put one.

**Inbound (server to client)** needs a schema-directed walk instead, because `JSON.parse`
has already parsed the string into a JavaScript value by the time anything could revive
it. The one primitive every generated walker calls:

```ts
function reviveInt64(v: unknown): bigint {
  return typeof v === "string" ? BigInt(v) : (v as bigint);
}
```

A generated method wraps `this.request(...)` for a route whose response or error
transitively contains an `Int64`, and calls a per-type revive function that converts just
those positions back to `bigint`:

```ts
async getInvoice(id: InvoiceId): Promise<Result<InvoiceView, ApiError>> {
  const r = await this.request<InvoiceView, ApiError>("GET", `/invoices/${encodeURIComponent(id)}`);
  return r.ok ? { ok: true, data: reviveInvoiceView(r.data) } : { ok: false, error: r.error };
}
```

A route whose response and error carry no `Int64` anywhere keeps the plain one-line
`return this.request(...)` — nothing extra is emitted for the common case:

```ts
async createCustomer(id: CustomerId, body: CreateCustomerBody): Promise<Result<CustomerView, ApiError>> {
  return this.request<CustomerView, ApiError>("POST", `/customers/${encodeURIComponent(id)}`, body);
}
```

**Absence is two different shapes, and the emitter answers them differently.** An
`Option<WireI64>` field the server always writes a key for sends an explicit `null` when
absent, and the walker guards it the same way:

```ts
adjustmentCents: (v.adjustmentCents) == null ? null : (reviveInt64(v.adjustmentCents)),
```

A bare `WireI64` behind `#[serde(skip_serializing_if = ...)]` never writes `null` — the key
is OMITTED entirely — so its TypeScript type is `?: bigint`, never `?: bigint | undefined`
(under `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, which `ts-fixture/tsconfig.json` turns on, those are
different declarations, and only the first is a document the server can actually send), and
the walker omits the key with a conditional spread rather than materializing it as
`undefined`:

```ts
...(v.lateFeeCents === undefined ? {} : { lateFeeCents: reviveInt64(v.lateFeeCents) }),
```

The opposite call goes the opposite way, deliberately, for an INPUT type an app author
builds rather than a wire type the server sends: every OPTIONAL member of `SubscribeOptions`
is `?: T | undefined` (`onEvent` and `onEnd` are required, no `?`), because there absence and
`undefined` mean the same thing (neither is serialized) and `?: T` alone would refuse the
ordinary pass-through
`function tail(api: Api, cursor?: string) { return api.feed({ cursor, … }); }`.

### Ending a stream: `StreamEnd`

`onEnd` is how a subscribed stream tells its caller it stopped, typed as `StreamEnd`,
which carries four kinds:
960:`token_hash`/`key_hash` are lowercase-hex SHA-256 of the raw credential; the
1014:2. Any other bearer — SHA-256'd and matched against the `ApiKey` index, then

usage: charpente test --mutants [--file PATH]… [--re REGEX] [--dir PATH] [--timeout SECS] [--jobs N]
--file PATH  a source file to mutate (repeatable; default: the oracle-bearing set)
--re REGEX   only mutants whose description matches
--dir PATH   the workspace directory to run in (default: .)
--jobs N     cargo-mutants' parallelism (also CARGO_MUTANTS_JOBS); refused above 1 when CARGO_TARGET_DIR is inherited
--test-package NAME  whose tests judge the mutants (repeatable). Without this, the verb judges every mutant with charpente-core and charpente-sim's tests — the default target set's oracles — so a --file in any other crate must name its own package here, or its mutants are judged by suites that never exercise them and all report MISSED.

## GUIDE sections re-read, and why

- **§5 "Auth"**, three times: to find how an operator gets its *first*
  credential. §5 shows `ctx.create_api_key` minting a key for the caller's own
  subject and says "the first credential comes from something the app trusts,
  such as an IdP or a signup route". It never shows a key minted for another
  subject (an operator issuing a key to a source); I inferred that
  `create_api_key(tx, "source:<id>")` is allowed because the signature takes any
  subject.
- **§16 "Where the guarantee stops"**: to check whether operator code holding
  the `Db` could mint an `ApiKey` row directly. It can write the row, but the
  row stores a SHA-256 of a raw key, and nothing in the docs exposes the hashing
  or a mint outside a request. So I abandoned that path.
- **§8 "Giving up" and "The checkers"**, twice: to settle which losses
  `durable_corruption_fired` may excuse. The answer, an acked *setup* step cut
  by `misdirected_write`, is the same rule applied to setup rather than to the
  property's own write. GUIDE only shows it for the latter.
- **§8 "Driving the whole app in a sim"**: to learn whether a stopped
  `Kernel` can be `run` again or must be rebuilt. It says a kernel can be `run`
  again after its source is exhausted, but not what happens after `run`
  returned `Err`. I rebuild it after a process restart (`restart_process`, or
  `restart` where `disk_crashed`).
- **§14 "64-bit integers"**: to confirm `WireI64`/`WireU64` serialize as
  decimal strings, which the sim's JSON oracles compare against.
EOF
OUTER
)" && ./box 'tail -3 /root/mutants1.log'
